question: The electronic configuration of an element is 1S2 2S2 2P6 3S2 3P3. How many unpaired electrons are there in the element?
solution:
Idea tested: reading an electron configuration and counting electrons that are alone in an orbital.

An orbital can hold only two electrons. When electrons enter a set of orbitals of equal energy (a subshell), they go in one at a time first, and only pair up when every orbital already has one electron. This is Hund's rule.

  • 1s2 → 2 electrons, paired (0 unpaired).
  • 2s2 → 2 electrons, paired (0 unpaired).
  • 2p6 → 3 orbitals, all full (0 unpaired).
  • 3s2 → 2 electrons, paired (0 unpaired).
  • 3p3 → 3 orbitals, but only 3 electrons arrive. Each orbital takes one electron, so all 3 orbitals have a single, lonely electron.

So the only unpaired electrons are the three in 3p. The atom is phosphorus (15 electrons) and it has 3 unpaired electrons.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 5 is the total number of electrons in the third shell (3s2 3p3), not the number that are unpaired.
  • 4 would mean four lonely electrons, but there are only three orbitals in a p subshell.
  • 2 would be true only if two of the 3p electrons had paired up, which does not happen while empty orbitals are still available.

question: Which of the following can be obtained by fractional distillation?

option.c: Iodine from solution of Iodine in carbon tetrachloride
option.d: Sulphur from the solution of sulphur in carbon disulphide

solution:
Idea tested: fractional distillation separates liquids that boil at different temperatures.

In fractional distillation a mixture of liquids is warmed in a fractionating column. The liquid with the lowest boiling point turns to vapour first, rises to the top and is collected. Later, the liquid with the higher boiling point distils over. It is used when the components are miscible liquids (they mix completely) whose boiling points are far apart.

Liquid air is mainly nitrogen (boiling point −196 °C) and oxygen (boiling point −183 °C). Because their boiling points differ by about 13 °C, warming liquid air in a fractionating column lets nitrogen boil off first and be collected separately. That is how nitrogen is obtained from liquid air.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Sodium chloride from sea water is obtained by evaporation or crystallisation of the water, leaving the salt behind.
  • Iodine from iodine in carbon tetrachloride is obtained by allowing the solvent to evaporate (or by crystallisation), not by fractional distillation of the two liquids.
  • Sulphur from sulphur in carbon disulphide is obtained by evaporating the carbon disulphide, leaving sulphur crystals.

Only the air example is a normal fractional distillation of two mixed liquids with different boiling points.

question: Duralumin consists of aluminum, copper?
solution:
Idea tested: the composition of duralumin, an important alloy of aluminium.

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements, made to improve its properties. Duralumin is made mostly of aluminium (about 90–95 %) with small amounts of copper (about 4 %), magnesium (about 0.5 %) and manganese (less than 1 %).

So, apart from aluminium and copper, duralumin contains manganese and magnesium.

Duralumin is light like aluminium, but much stronger and harder. That is why it is used for aircraft bodies, bicycle frames and vehicle parts.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Zinc and gold — gold is never added to duralumin; it is far too soft and expensive. Zinc is not part of duralumin either.
  • Lead and manganese — lead is heavy and soft, so it would destroy the lightness and strength of the alloy.
  • Nickel and silver — silver is a precious metal and is not used here; nickel is not one of the duralumin components.

question: An example of a polysaccharide is?
solution:
Idea tested: telling a polysaccharide apart from simple sugars.

Sugars are carbohydrates. A monosaccharide is one single sugar unit, a disaccharide is two units joined together, and a polysaccharide is a very long chain of many sugar units (monosaccharides) joined by glycosidic bonds.

Starch is made of hundreds of glucose units joined in a long chain, so it is a polysaccharide. Plants store food as starch (in seeds, tubers such as cassava and yam), and our bodies break it back down into glucose during digestion. Other common polysaccharides are cellulose (plant cell walls) and glycogen (animal storage).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Glucose is a single sugar unit — a monosaccharide.
  • Dextrose is just another name for glucose, so it is also a monosaccharide.
  • Mannose is a single sugar unit as well — a monosaccharide.

Long chain = polysaccharide, single unit = monosaccharide, and only starch is the long chain here.

question: 8g of CH4 occupies 11.2 at S.T.P. What volume would 22g of CH3CH2CH3 occupy under the same condition?
solution:
Idea tested: equal numbers of moles of any gas occupy the same volume at the same temperature and pressure (Avogadro's law).

First, check what 8 g of methane tells us. The molar mass of CH4 is 12 + 4(1) = 16 g/mol, so

n=816=0.5 mol

0.5 mol occupies 11.2 dm3, so 1 mol would occupy 22.4 dm3 at S.T.P. That confirms the molar volume of a gas at S.T.P.

Now the second gas is propane, CH3CH2CH3 (C3H8). Its molar mass is 3(12) + 8(1) = 44 g/mol, so

n=2244=0.5 mol

Both samples contain exactly the same number of moles (0.5 mol), and at the same conditions equal moles take up equal volumes. Therefore the propane also occupies 11.2 dm3.

Check with the molar volume:

V=n×22.4=0.5×22.4=11.2dm3

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 3.7 dm3 would need about 0.165 mol, which is not the amount present.
  • 22.4 dm3 is the volume of a whole mole, but we only have half a mole.
  • 33 dm3 does not match any sensible mole value for 22 g of propane.

question: The best treatment for a student who accidentally poured conc tetraoxosulphate(vi) on his skin in the laboratory is to wash his skin with?
solution:
Idea tested: first aid for acid spills on the skin — dilute the acid and cool the area with plenty of water.

Concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid (sulphuric acid, H2SO4) is very corrosive, and it produces a lot of heat when it mixes with water. Acting quickly matters:

  1. Wash the skin with plenty of cool running water for many minutes. The water washes the acid off the skin and dilutes what is left, so it does less damage.
  2. The cool water also carries heat away, which reduces the burning sensation and further injury.
  3. Do not rub the skin, and get medical help if the burn is bad.

So the best treatment is cool running water.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Sodium hydroxide solution is a strong alkali. Neutralising an acid with a strong alkali produces even more heat and can burn the skin again, so it is dangerous.
  • Iodine solution is an antiseptic for small cuts; it is not used to remove acid and would add another chemical to the burn.
  • Sodium trioxonitrate(V) solution (sodium nitrate solution) does not neutralise the acid and would just leave another substance on the damaged skin.

question: Which of the gas laws does this graph illustrate?
solution:
Idea tested: recognising which gas law a volume–temperature graph represents.

The gas laws describe how the pressure, volume and temperature of a fixed mass of gas are related:

  • Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional (PV=constant). Its graph is a curve.
  • Charles' law: at constant pressure, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature. Its graph is a straight line, and the volume rises as the temperature rises.
  • Gay-Lussac's law: at constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
  • Graham's law: the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its density.

The graph plots volume against temperature for a gas kept at constant pressure and shows a straight line rising steadily with temperature. That is exactly Charles' law:

VT=constantat constant P

If the line is extended backwards it would meet the temperature axis at −273 °C (0 K), where the volume would be zero.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Boyle would give a pressure–volume graph shaped like a curve.
  • Gay-Lussac would give a pressure–temperature straight line, not volume against temperature.
  • Graham is about rates of diffusion, which is not what this graph shows.

question: What are the possible oxidation numbers of an element if its atomic number is 17?
solution:
Idea tested: working out oxidation numbers from an element's electron configuration.

Atomic number 17 means the element has 17 electrons. Its configuration is 2, 8, 7, so it has seven outer electrons — it is chlorine, a Group 7 (halogen) element. Elements in this group are one electron short of a full outer shell of eight.

There are two natural ways to reach a stable arrangement:

  1. Gain one electron → 8 outer electrons, giving an oxidation number of −1 (as in NaCl, where chlorine is Cl−).
  2. Lose (or share) all seven outer electrons → the outer shell is empty, leaving the full shell underneath, giving an oxidation number of +7 (as in HClO4, where chlorine is +7).

So the possible oxidation numbers are −1 and +7.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • −1 and 6 — +6 is typical of Group 6 elements such as sulphur, not of chlorine.
  • −3 and 5 — these are typical of Group 5 elements such as nitrogen and phosphorus.
  • −2 and 6 — these are typical of Group 6 elements such as oxygen and sulphur.

question: What process would coal undergo to give coal gas, coal tar, ammoniacal liquor and coke?
solution:
Idea tested: destructive distillation of coal and the products it gives.

Destructive distillation means heating a substance strongly in the absence of air. Because no oxygen is present, the coal cannot simply burn away; instead its large molecules break down into smaller substances, which are collected.

When coal is heated this way, four main products are obtained:

  • Coal gas — a mixture rich in hydrogen and methane, used as a fuel.
  • Coal tar — a thick black liquid that is the source of benzene, phenol, dyes and medicines.
  • Ammoniacal liquor — a solution of ammonia in water, used to make fertilisers.
  • Coke — the solid left behind, mostly carbon, used to reduce metal ores in the blast furnace.

These are exactly the four products named in the question, so the process is destructive distillation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Steam distillation passes steam through a substance to carry over volatile oils; it does not break coal down.
  • Liquefaction means changing a gas or solid into a liquid (for example, cooling a gas), not heating coal without air.
  • Hydrolysis is the breaking of a bond by water, as when starch is boiled with acid; it is not used on coal.

question: Liquid black soap is made by boiling palm oil with liquid extract of ash. The function of the ash is to provide the ?
solution:
Idea tested: saponification — making soap by boiling fat or oil with an alkali.

Palm oil is a fat (an ester of glycerol and long-chain alkanoic acids). To turn it into soap, the ester must be broken by an alkali. This reaction is called saponification:

fat+alkali→soap+glycerol

The liquid extract of ash (called lye) is alkaline because wood ash contains potassium carbonate, which dissolves to give a solution of potassium hydroxide. That alkali splits the fat into soap and glycerol. So the ash provides the alkali.

Soap molecules have a long water-hating (hydrocarbon) tail and a water-loving ionic head, which is why they can lift grease and dirt off the skin and cloth into water.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Acid would do the opposite — an acid cannot split a fat into soap; it would only free the fatty acids.
  • Ester of alkanoic acid is what the palm oil already is; adding more ester does not make soap.
  • Alkanol is an alcohol such as ethanol; glycerol is an alkanol that is produced by the reaction, not the substance that drives it.

question: When water drops are added to calcium carbide in a container and the gas produced is passed through a jet and lighted, the resultant flame is called an?
solution:
Idea tested: the reaction of calcium carbide with water to make ethyne (acetylene) and the flame it burns with.

When water drops fall on calcium carbide, the carbide reacts with the water:

CaC2+2H2O→Ca(OH)2+C2H2

The gas produced is ethyne (C2H2), which is also called acetylene. When this gas is passed through a jet and lit in a supply of pure oxygen, it burns with a very hot, bright flame of about 3000 °C:

2C2H2+5O2→4CO2+2H2O

Because the flame is produced by burning acetylene in oxygen, it is called the oxyacetylene flame. It is hot enough to melt and join metals, so it is used for welding and cutting steel.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Oxyethene flame is not a real name; there is no gas called ethene in this reaction.
  • Oxyhydrocarbon flame is too general — it does not name the gas that is actually burning.
  • Oxymethane flame would involve methane, but calcium carbide and water do not produce methane.

question: Which of the following substances is a mixture?
solution:
Idea tested: the difference between a mixture and a pure substance.

A mixture contains two or more substances that are simply mixed together. They are not chemically joined, so the parts keep their own properties and can be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation or distillation. Also, the parts can be present in any ratio.

Sea water is water with many salts dissolved in it (mainly sodium chloride, plus magnesium and calcium salts). The salts and water are not chemically combined, and you can get the salt back by evaporating the water. So sea water is a mixture.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Granulated sugar is sucrose, a single compound with a fixed formula (C12H22O11). All its molecules are the same.
  • Sodium chloride is a compound of Na+ and Cl− ions in a fixed 1:1 ratio held by ionic bonds; it cannot be separated by simple physical means.
  • Iron filings contain only iron atoms — a single element.

question: If the quantity of oxygen occupying 2.76L container at a pressure of 0.825 atm and 300k is reduced by one-half, what is the pressure exerted by the remaining gas?
solution:
Idea tested: the ideal gas law and what happens to pressure when the amount of gas changes at constant volume and temperature.

Start from the ideal gas equation:

PV=nRT

Rearrange it to make pressure the subject:

P=nRTV

The gas stays in the same 2.76 L container, and the temperature is not changed. Since V, T and R are all constant, pressure is directly proportional to the number of moles:

P2P1=n2n1

The quantity of gas is reduced by one-half, so n2=12n1. Substituting:

P2=12P1=12×0.825=0.4125 atm

Rounding to three decimal places gives 0.413 atm. This makes sense: remove half the gas molecules and you get half as many collisions with the walls, so the pressure halves.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 1.650 atm is double 0.825 atm — that would happen if the gas were doubled, not halved.
  • 0.825 atm means no change at all, which would only be true if the amount of gas stayed the same.
  • 0.275 atm is 0.825 divided by three, which does not match the one-half given in the question.

question: Four elements P, Q, R and S have atomic numbers of 4, 10, 12 and 14 respectively. Which of these elements is noble gas?
solution:
Idea tested: using atomic number to write electron configurations and identify a noble gas.

The atomic number tells us the number of electrons in a neutral atom. Fill the shells as 2, 8, 8 …

  • P, atomic number 4: 2, 2. Beryllium — two outer electrons, so it is a metal that loses them.
  • Q, atomic number 10: 2, 8. Neon — the outer shell holds the maximum of eight electrons.
  • R, atomic number 12: 2, 8, 2. Magnesium — two outer electrons.
  • S, atomic number 14: 2, 8, 4. Silicon — four outer electrons.

A noble gas has a complete outer shell (a duet for helium, an octet for the others), which makes it very stable and almost unreactive. Only Q (neon, 2, 8) has a full outer shell, so the noble gas is Q.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • P (2, 2) and R (2, 8, 2) are metals in Group 2 that react by losing two electrons.
  • S (2, 8, 4) is silicon, a Group 4 element that shares electrons in covalent bonds.

question: The products of the thermal decomposition of ammonium trioxonitrate(v) are?
solution:
Idea tested: the unusual thermal decomposition of ammonium trioxonitrate(V) (ammonium nitrate).

Ammonium nitrate contains two nitrogen-containing ions: the ammonium ion NH4+ and the nitrate ion NO3−. On strong heating, the two ions react with each other inside the same compound:

NH4NO3→N2O+2H2O

So the products are nitrogen(I) oxide (dinitrogen monoxide, N2O) and water.

You can see why with oxidation numbers. Nitrogen in NH4+ is −3 and nitrogen in NO3− is +5. In N2O each nitrogen is +1, which lies between −3 and +5 — the two nitrogen atoms have moved towards each other, one being oxidised and the other reduced. That is why this is a special case among nitrates.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Ammonia and oxide — ammonia is not a final product here; it would be driven off only from ammonium salts of non-oxidising acids.
  • Nitrogen and water would need the nitrate to lose all its oxygen in a simple way, which is not what happens; N2O is formed instead.
  • Nitrogen(IV) oxide and water is what heavy metal nitrates such as lead(II) nitrate and copper(II) nitrate give on heating, together with the metal oxide. Ammonium nitrate is different because its cation can take part in the reaction.

question: How many valence electrons are contained in the element 3115P?
solution:
Idea tested: using the atomic number and electron configuration to count valence electrons.

The symbol 3115P tells us that phosphorus has atomic number 15 and mass number 31. The atomic number is the number of protons, and in a neutral atom it is also the number of electrons.

So phosphorus has 15 electrons. The shells fill in the order 2, 8, 5:

2,8,5

The outermost shell has 5 electrons. Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell, so the answer is 5 (option a).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 4 would be right for a Group 4 element such as carbon, not phosphorus.
  • 15 is the total number of electrons in the atom, not the number in the outer shell.
  • 31 is the mass number (protons + neutrons), not an electron count.

question:
The number of molecules of Carbon(iv)Oxide produced when 10.0g of CaCO3 is treated with 0.2dm3 of 1 Mole of HCL in the equation

CaCO3 + 2HCL ⇒  CaCl2  + H2 O + CO2  , is?
solution:
Idea tested: mole–mole ratios in a balanced equation and Avogadro's number.

Write the balanced equation and note the mole ratio:

CaCO3+2HCl→CaCl2+H2O+CO2

1 mole of CaCO3 gives 1 mole of CO2.

Step 1: moles of CaCO3 (molar mass = 40 + 12 + 3(16) = 100 g/mol)

n=mM=10.0100=0.1 mol

Step 2: moles of acid available (0.2 dm3 of 1 mol/dm3)

n=c×V=1×0.2=0.2 mol

The equation needs 2 mol of HCl for every 1 mol of CaCO3, so 0.1 mol of CaCO3 needs exactly 0.2 mol of HCl. The acid is just enough, so all the CaCO3 reacts.

Step 3: moles of CO2 formed = 0.1 mol (same as the CaCO3).

Step 4: number of molecules using Avogadro's number, NA=6.02×1023

N=n×6.02×1023=0.1×6.02×1023=6.02×1022

So 6.02 × 1022 molecules of CO2 are produced.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 1.00 × 1023 would need about 0.166 mol of CO2, but only 0.1 mol is formed.
  • 6.02 × 1023 is the number of molecules in a whole mole; we have only one tenth of a mole.
  • 6.02 × 1024 is ten times too big — it would need 10 moles of CO2.

question: The volume occupied by 1.58g of a gas at S.T.P is 500cm3. What is the relative molecular mass of the gas?  [ G.M.V at S.T.P = 22.4dm3 ]
solution:
Idea tested: using the molar volume of a gas at S.T.P. to find a relative molecular mass.

At S.T.P., 1 mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm3, which is the same as 22 400 cm3.

The sample has a volume of 500 cm3 and a mass of 1.58 g. First find how many moles that volume represents:

n=50022400=0.02232 mol

Now find the mass of one mole (the molar mass):

M=mn=1.580.02232≈70.8 g/mol

The same thing in one line, using proportion:

M=22400×1.58500=44.8×1.58≈70.8≈71

So the relative molecular mass is 71 (this is the value for chlorine gas, Cl2, since 2 × 35.5 = 71).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 28 is the mass of nitrogen, N2; 1.58 g of it would occupy about 1264 cm3, not 500 cm3.
  • 32 is the mass of oxygen, O2; 1.58 g would occupy about 1106 cm3.
  • 44 is the mass of carbon dioxide, CO2; 1.58 g would occupy about 804 cm3.

question: Which of the following gases will rekindle a brightly splint?
solution:
Idea tested: the test for an oxidising gas — it makes a glowing splint burst into flame.

A glowing splint is a wooden splint that is still red-hot but not burning with a flame. If it is placed in a gas that releases oxygen easily, the extra oxygen makes it burst into flame. We say the gas rekindles the splint.

Nitrogen(I) oxide, N2O, contains oxygen and breaks down when heated by the splint:

2N2O→2N2+O2

The oxygen released feeds the glowing wood, so the splint relights. That is why N2O is used in dentists' laughing-gas mixtures and is sometimes called "laughing gas".

Note a detail: N2O rekindles a brightly glowing splint but may put out a faintly glowing one, because the faint splint is not hot enough to decompose the gas and release oxygen.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • NO2 (nitrogen(IV) oxide) is a brown, poisonous gas that does not supply oxygen to a splint in this way.
  • NO (nitrogen(II) oxide) is a colourless gas that reacts with oxygen in air to form NO2; it does not rekindle a glowing splint.
  • Cl2 is a greenish-yellow poisonous halogen; it does not release oxygen, so it cannot rekindle the splint.

question: The shape of ammonia molecule is?
solution:
Idea tested: predicting molecular shape from bond pairs and lone pairs (VSEPR theory).

Nitrogen has 5 outer electrons. In ammonia, NH3, three of these electrons are shared with three hydrogen atoms, giving 3 bond pairs. The remaining two electrons stay on nitrogen as 1 lone pair.

So nitrogen is surrounded by 4 electron pairs. These pairs repel one another and arrange themselves towards the corners of a tetrahedron.

One corner is occupied by the lone pair, so the three hydrogen atoms occupy the other three corners. The resulting shape is a triangular pyramid, called trigonal pyramidal (option a).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Octahedral needs 6 electron pairs around the central atom, as in SF6.
  • Square planar has four atoms lying flat in a square, which ammonia does not have.
  • Tetrahedral describes four atoms at the corners, as in methane, CH4. Ammonia has only three hydrogen atoms plus a lone pair.

question: A few drop of conc HCL are added to about 10cm3 of a solution of PH 3.4. The PH of the resulting mixture is?

option.d: the same as that of the pure water

solution:
Idea tested: what pH measures and what happens to pH when an acid is added.

pH measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is. It is defined as:

pH=−log⁡[H+]

Because of the minus sign, more hydrogen ions mean a smaller pH. The scale runs from 0 (very acidic) to 14 (very alkaline), with 7 neutral.

The original solution has pH 3.4, so it is acidic. Concentrated hydrochloric acid is a strong acid that adds a large amount of H+ ions. Adding it makes the mixture more acidic, so the concentration of H+ increases and the pH value goes down:

pHnew<3.4

So the pH of the resulting mixture is less than 3.4.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Greater than 3.4 would mean the mixture became less acidic, but we added acid, not alkali.
  • Unaltered would only happen if we added something neutral that did not change the H+ concentration.
  • The same as pure water (pH 7) would mean the acid had been neutralised, which is the opposite of what happened.

question: Chromatography is used to separate components of mixture which differ in their rates of ?
solution:
Idea tested: the principle of chromatography.

In chromatography, a spot of the mixture is placed on the stationary phase (for example, filter paper or a coated plate) and a solvent, the mobile phase, creeps through it.

Each component of the mixture dissolves in the moving solvent and is also held back by the paper. Components that dissolve well in the solvent travel along quickly; components that stick strongly to the paper travel slowly. Because the components move at different rates, they separate into separate spots.

So chromatography separates the components of a mixture that differ in their rates of migration (how fast they move through the stationary phase).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a region of high concentration to low concentration; it is not what drives the separation on the paper.
  • Reaction — chromatography is a physical separation; the components do not react with each other.
  • Sedimentation is the settling of solid particles at the bottom of a liquid, used in decantation and centrifugation, not in chromatography.

question: Deliquescent substances are also?
solution:
Idea tested: the three ways substances behave towards water vapour in the air.

  • Hygroscopic substances absorb water vapour from the air but do not dissolve in it. Examples: quicklime, silica gel, concentrated sulphuric acid.
  • Deliquescent substances absorb so much water vapour from the air that they dissolve in it and form a solution. Example: calcium chloride, CaCl2.
  • Efflorescent substances do the opposite: they lose their water of crystallisation to the air and crumble into powder. Example: washing soda, Na2CO3·10H2O.

Deliquescence is simply an extreme case of taking up moisture from the air. A deliquescent substance first absorbs water vapour (hygroscopic behaviour) and keeps going until it dissolves. So every deliquescent substance is also hygroscopic.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Efflorescent is the opposite behaviour — losing water instead of absorbing it.
  • Anhydrous means "containing no water of crystallisation"; deliquescent salts can be anhydrous to begin with, so this is not the link being tested.
  • Insoluble is wrong: deliquescent salts dissolve very readily in the water they absorb.

question: Helium is used in observation of ballons because it is?
solution:
Idea tested: the properties that make helium the safest gas for filling balloons.

For a balloon to rise, the gas inside must be lighter (less dense) than air. Air has an average relative molecular mass of about 29. Helium is a single atom with a relative atomic mass of only 4, so it is much lighter than air and the balloon floats.

Helium is also a noble gas in Group 0. Its outer shell is complete (2 electrons), so it is unreactive and does not burn. That is very important: hydrogen is even lighter, but it is highly flammable and caused terrible airship accidents, so helium is preferred.

Therefore helium is light and non-combustible — the ideal combination for observation balloons and party balloons.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Light and combustible describes hydrogen, not helium.
  • Heavy and combustible is wrong twice: helium is light, and it does not burn.
  • Heavy and non-combustible — helium certainly does not burn, but it is not heavy; a heavy gas would keep the balloon on the ground.

question: 32g of anhydrous copper(ii)tetraoxosulphate(vi) dissolved in 1dm3 of water generated 13.0kj of heat. The heat solution is?
solution:
Idea tested: converting the heat released by a mass of a substance into the heat change per mole (molar heat of solution).

Dissolving anhydrous copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI), CuSO4, in water gives out heat — the process is exothermic. We are told 32 g of it released 13.0 kJ.

Step 1: molar mass of CuSO4

M=64+32+4(16)=160 g/mol

Step 2: moles in 32 g

n=32160=0.2 mol

Step 3: heat per mole — if 0.2 mol gives 13.0 kJ, then 1 mol gives

13.00.2=65.0 kJ/mol

So the molar heat of solution is 65.0 kJ/mol (exothermic).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 26.0 kJ/mol would come from dividing 13.0 by 0.5, which is not the number of moles present.
  • 130.0 kJ/mol would come from multiplying 13.0 by 10, a slip with the decimal place.
  • 260.0 kJ/mol would treat 32 g as only 0.05 mol, which is wrong because 32 g is 0.2 mol.

question:
A gaseous metallic chloride MCl consists of 20.22% of M by mass. The formula of the chloride is?

[ M = 27, Cl = 35.5]
solution:
Idea tested: finding an empirical formula from percentage composition.

Assume 100 g of the chloride. Then it contains 20.22 g of M and (100 − 20.22) = 79.78 g of chlorine.

Step 1: convert each mass to moles (M = 27, Cl = 35.5)

n(M)=20.2227=0.749 mol

n(Cl)=79.7835.5=2.247 mol

Step 2: divide both by the smaller number

M:0.7490.749=1

Cl:2.2470.749≈3

Step 3: write the formula. The ratio M : Cl is 1 : 3, so the formula is MCl3. This also fits the group: M = 27 is aluminium, which forms Al3+, so three chloride ions are needed for each aluminium ion.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • MCl would need 43.6 % M by mass for M = 27 (27 out of 62.5), not 20.22 %.
  • MCl2 would need about 27.6 % M by mass (27 out of 98), too high.
  • M2Cl6 is just MCl3 written doubled; the empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio, MCl3.

question: What quantity of electricity will liberate 0.125 mole of oxygen molecules during the electrolysis of dilute sodium chloride solution?
solution:
Idea tested: Faraday's laws — the quantity of electricity needed to liberate a given amount of a substance at an electrode.

In the electrolysis of dilute sodium chloride solution, the ions present are Na+, H+ (from water), Cl− and OH−. At the anode, hydroxide ions are discharged and oxygen is given off:

4OH−→2H2O+O2+4e−

This equation shows that 1 mole of O2 needs 4 moles of electrons, and 1 mole of electrons carries 1 faraday (F) = 96 500 C:

1 mol O2→4F=4×96500=386000 C

Step: scale down to 0.125 mol of O2

Q=0.125×4×96500=48250 C

So 48 250 C of electricity is needed.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 24 125 C is half of the correct value — it would be right if 1 mole of O2 needed only 2 faradays.
  • 72 375 C would come from using 6 faradays per mole of oxygen, which is not what the anode equation shows.
  • 96 500 C is the charge of just 1 faraday, enough for only 0.25 mol of O2.

question: Which of the following types of bonding does not involve the formation of new substances?
solution:
Idea tested: what a metallic bond is and how it differs from the bonds that join different atoms into compounds.

In a metal, the atoms pack together and lose their outer electrons into a shared "sea" of delocalised electrons. The metal is held together by the attraction between these electrons and the positive metal ions they leave behind. That attraction is the metallic bond.

Notice that only one kind of atom is involved, and no atoms are joined into a new chemical compound: a piece of copper is still copper, it has not turned into a new substance. Metallic bonding simply explains the properties of metals, such as their shine, malleability and ability to conduct heat and electricity.

Covalent bonding joins atoms by sharing electrons (as in H2O), electrovalent (ionic) bonding joins ions by transferring electrons (as in NaCl), and co-ordinate bonding forms when one atom donates a lone pair to another (as in the ammonium ion). In all three cases atoms or ions of different elements combine chemically and a new substance is produced.

So the type of bonding that does not involve forming a new substance is metallic.

question: An organic compound that does not undergo a reaction with both hydrogen cyanide and hydroxylamine can be?
solution:
Idea tested: which functional group reacts with hydrogen cyanide and hydroxylamine, and which one does not.

Both hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and hydroxylamine (NH2OH) attack a carbonyl group, the C=O double bond found in aldehydes and ketones:

  • With HCN, the carbonyl compound forms a cyanohydrin.
    RCHO+HCN→RCH(OH)CN
  • With hydroxylamine, it forms an oxime.
    R2CO+NH2OH→R2C=NOH+H2O

An alkene has a carbon–carbon double bond (C=C) and no carbonyl carbon at all, so it has nothing for HCN or hydroxylamine to add to. It does not undergo these reactions.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Alkanal (aldehyde) has the −CHO group and readily forms cyanohydrins and oximes.
  • Alkanone (ketone) has the C=O group and also forms cyanohydrins and oximes.
  • Alkanoic acid contains a carboxyl group (−COOH). Its carbonyl carbon is already attached to an −OH group and is much less reactive towards these reagents, so it is not the group that gives the classic cyanohydrin/oxime reactions — and it is certainly not the answer here, because the alkene has no carbonyl group at all.

question: The substance often used for vulcanization of rubber is?
solution:
Idea tested: vulcanisation of rubber and the element that carries it out.

Natural rubber is made of long, flexible chains of polyisoprene. The chains can slide over one another, so raw rubber is soft, sticky and weakens when warm, and it hardens and cracks when cold.

Vulcanisation means heating rubber with sulphur. Sulphur atoms form short bridges (cross-links) between neighbouring rubber chains:

chain−S−S−chain

These cross-links stop the chains from sliding freely past each other. The rubber becomes stronger, harder, more elastic and less affected by temperature changes — exactly what is needed for tyres, shoes and hoses. This process is called vulcanisation, and the substance used is sulphur.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Chlorine can react with rubber (chlorination) but it is not the standard vulcanising agent; it tends to make the surface hard and brittle.
  • Hydrogen peroxide is an oxidising bleach, not a cross-linking agent for rubber.
  • Tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid (sulphuric acid) is a strong acid that would destroy rubber, not strengthen it.

question: The chlorinated alkane often used industrially to remove grease is?
solution:
Idea tested: the uses of chlorinated alkanes (chloroalkanes) as industrial solvents.

Tetrachloromethane is CCl4 — one carbon atom with four chlorine atoms attached. It is a non-polar liquid, so it dissolves other non-polar substances such as oils, fats, grease, waxes, resins and varnish, but it does not mix with water.

This makes it an excellent solvent for cleaning grease off machinery, electrical equipment and clothes in dry cleaning. Because it does not conduct electricity and does not catch fire, it was also used in fire extinguishers. So the chlorinated alkane used industrially to remove grease is tetrachloromethane.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Chloromethane (CH3Cl) is a gas at room temperature, so it cannot be used as a liquid cleaning solvent.
  • Trichloromethane (CHCl3, chloroform) is a liquid but is mainly known as an old anaesthetic and a laboratory solvent, not the classic grease remover.
  • Dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) is used as a paint stripper and in some cleaning, but the standard industrial grease-removal solvent named in the syllabus is tetrachloromethane.

question: What mass of water is produced when 8.0g of hydrogen reacts with excess oxygen?
solution:
Idea tested: mass–mass calculations using a balanced equation.

Write the balanced equation for hydrogen burning in oxygen:

2H2+O2→2H2O

Step 1: moles of hydrogen (H2 = 2 g/mol)

n=8.02=4.0 mol

Step 2: moles of water. From the equation, 2 mol of H2 give 2 mol of H2O, so the ratio is 1 : 1:

n(H2O)=4.0 mol

Step 3: mass of water (H2O = 18 g/mol)

m=n×M=4.0×18=72 g

So 72.0 g of water is produced. Oxygen is in excess, so all 8 g of hydrogen reacts.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 8.0 g just repeats the mass of hydrogen; mass is not conserved per element like that, because oxygen adds mass.
  • 16.0 g comes from using H instead of H2, which halves the moles of hydrogen wrongly.
  • 36.0 g is the mass of water from 4 g of hydrogen (2 mol), only half of what we have.

question: Proteins in acid solution undergo?
solution:
Idea tested: the structure of proteins and what happens when they are boiled with acid.

Proteins are natural polymers. Their building blocks are amino acids, joined in long chains by peptide bonds (−CO–NH–). A protein may contain hundreds or thousands of amino acid units.

Hydrolysis means breaking a bond by adding water. When a protein is heated with acid (acid hydrolysis), water is added across each peptide bond, the chain is split and the protein breaks down into its individual amino acids:

protein+nH2O→amino acids

The same kind of breakdown happens in your stomach, where enzymes and acid digest protein from food into amino acids that the body can absorb and reuse.

So proteins in acid solution undergo hydrolysis.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Substitution replaces one atom or group by another in a molecule; it does not break a polymer into its units.
  • Fermentation is the breakdown of sugars by micro-organisms (as in making palm wine or bread); it does not act on proteins in acid.
  • Polymerisation is the opposite process — joining small units into a big chain. Here the chain is being taken apart, not built.

question: The general formula for the Alkanals is?
solution:
Idea tested: the general formulas of the main homologous series.

Alkanals are the aldehydes. Their functional group is −CHO, a carbonyl carbon (C=O) that still carries one hydrogen. So the general formula is RCHO, where R is an alkyl group (or hydrogen, in the case of methanal, HCHO).

For example, ethanal is CH3CHO. Aldehydes are easily oxidised to the corresponding alkanoic acids and give a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • R2CO is the general formula of the alkanones (ketones), where the carbonyl carbon is joined to two carbon groups, e.g. propanone, CH3COCH3.
  • ROH is the general formula of the alkanols (alcohols), such as ethanol, C2H5OH.
  • RCOOR is the general formula of the esters, such as ethyl ethanoate, CH3COOC2H5.

Only RCHO ends in a carbonyl carbon that still has one hydrogen — the signature of an alkanal.

question: When cathode rays are deflected onto the electrode of an electrometer, the instrument becomes?
solution:
Idea tested: the nature of cathode rays and the evidence that they are negatively charged.

Cathode rays are produced in a discharge tube when a high voltage is applied. They are streams of electrons, given off by the negative electrode (the cathode) and travelling towards the anode.

Because they are made of electrons, they carry a negative charge. Two classic observations prove this:

  • They travel from the cathode towards the anode, i.e. towards the positive side.
  • They are bent towards a positively charged plate and away from a negatively charged plate in an electric field.

So when cathode rays are directed onto the electrode of an electrometer, they deliver electrons to it, and the instrument becomes negatively charged.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Bipolar would mean carrying both charges at once, which cathode rays do not.
  • Positively charged is the opposite of the truth; positive rays (canal rays) are the ones that would do this.
  • Neutral would be true only if the rays had no charge, but they are deflected by electric fields, which only happens to charged particles.

question: When a solid substance disappears completely as a gas on heating, the substance is said to have undergone?
solution:
Idea tested: change of state — the special case where a solid turns straight into a gas.

Sublimation is when a solid changes directly into a gas without becoming a liquid first. The solid appears to "disappear" and a gas with a smell or visible fumes takes its place. On cooling, the gas changes straight back into a solid, which is called deposition.

Examples you may know: solid carbon(IV) oxide ("dry ice") forms a dense vapour without melting; iodine crystals give off purple vapour on gentle heating; ammonium chloride, camphor and naphthalene (mothballs) also sublime.

The word "sublimate" also describes the solid collected after sublimation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Crystallisation is the reverse process — forming solid crystals from a solution or a melt, not turning a solid into a gas.
  • Distillation separates a liquid from a solution by boiling it and condensing the vapour; it needs a liquid stage.
  • Evaporation is a liquid turning into a gas at its surface, again a liquid–gas change, not solid–gas.

question: An electron can be added to a halogen atom to form a halide ion with?
solution:
Idea tested: how a halogen atom forms a halide ion and why the octet matters.

Halogens are Group 7 elements (F, Cl, Br, I). Their atoms have seven electrons in the outer shell, e.g. chlorine is 2, 8, 7.

Eight outer electrons give the stable noble-gas arrangement, so a halogen atom simply gains one electron:

Cl2,8,7+e−→Cl−,2,8,8

The ion formed has eight valence electrons and a single negative charge (a halide ion such as Cl− or F−). That is why halide ions are very stable and why halogens react by gaining an electron (acting as oxidising agents).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 7 valence electrons describes the neutral halogen atom, before it gains the extra electron.
  • 2 valence electrons describes helium or a Group 2 metal after losing electrons, not a halide ion.
  • 3 valence electrons belongs to Group 3 elements such as boron or aluminium.

question: Aluminum hydroxide is used in the dyeing industry as a?
solution:
Idea tested: the role of aluminium hydroxide in the dyeing industry.

A dye often does not stick firmly to cloth by itself, so its colour can wash out. To solve this, a mordant is used: a substance that combines with the dye and fixes it firmly onto the fabric fibres, making the colour fast.

Aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3, is a gelatinous precipitate that clings to the fibres. It holds the dye molecules on the cloth and often deepens and brightens the colour. Aluminium salts such as alum are also used for this purpose. That is why aluminium hydroxide is used in the dyeing industry as a mordant.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Dye — aluminium hydroxide is white and gives no colour; the colour comes from the dye itself.
  • Dispersant — a dispersant keeps tiny particles spread throughout a liquid; that is not its role in dyeing.
  • Salt — although it is an ionic compound, calling it a "salt" does not describe the job it does in fixing the dye.

question: The most important element on the earth's crust is?
solution:
Idea tested: the most abundant element in the Earth's crust.

The Earth's crust is the solid outer skin of the planet — the rocks, sand and soil under our feet. By mass, its composition is roughly:

  • Oxygen — about 46.6 %
  • Silicon — about 27.7 %
  • Aluminium — about 8.1 %
  • Iron — about 5.0 %
  • Calcium, sodium, potassium and magnesium — the rest

Oxygen is so abundant because it is combined in nearly every rock mineral (silicates, oxides, carbonates) and in water. Nearly half the mass of the crust is oxygen, so the most important (most abundant) element in the Earth's crust is oxygen.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the air (about 78 %), but it makes up only a tiny fraction of the crust.
  • Hydrogen is the lightest element and very common in the universe and in water, but it is a small part of the crust's mass.
  • Fluorine occurs mainly in minerals such as fluorspar, in very small amounts compared with oxygen.

question: To obtain pure carbon(ii)oxide from its mixture with carbon(iv)oxide, the mixture should be?
solution:
Idea tested: separating two gases by using the different acid–base behaviour of their oxides.

A mixture of carbon(II) oxide (CO) and carbon(IV) oxide (CO2) contains one neutral oxide and one acidic oxide.

  • CO2 is an acidic oxide. It dissolves in and reacts with alkalis.
  • CO is a neutral oxide. It does not react with alkalis (it is only slightly soluble in water).

So if the gas mixture is bubbled through concentrated sodium hydroxide solution, the carbon(IV) oxide is absorbed and removed:

CO2+2NaOH→Na2CO3+H2O

The CO passes through unchanged, so pure carbon(II) oxide is collected. This is also why the CO2 left over from making CO by passing CO2 over red-hot carbon is removed with concentrated NaOH.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Heated copper(II) oxide would oxidise the CO to CO2 — it destroys the gas we want to keep.
  • Bubbling through water only dissolves a little CO2 and leaves most of it in the gas, so the CO is not purified.
  • Concentrated H2SO4 is a drying agent; it removes water vapour, not CO2.

question: Give the common name for the following compound (CH3)2 CH CH2 -Br
solution:
This question tests how to read the structure of a halogenoalkane and give its common name.

The structure is CH3–CH(CH3)–CH2–Br. Follow these steps:

  1. Count the carbon atoms: there are four carbon atoms, so the parent alkane is butane.
  2. Find the longest chain that contains the carbon carrying the bromine: that chain has three carbons (propane).
  3. The bromine sits on carbon 1 and a methyl group (–CH3) sits on carbon 2, so the IUPAC name is 1-bromo-2-methylpropane.
  4. A four-carbon group shaped like (CH3)2CH–CH2– is called an isobutyl group, so the common name is isobutyl bromide.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Methyl bromide is CH3Br – only one carbon, so it is far too small.
  • Propyl bromide is CH3CH2CH2Br – a straight three-carbon chain with no branch.
  • Butyl bromide is the straight-chain CH3CH2CH2CH2Br. Our molecule is branched, not straight, so it is the iso isomer.

question: The enzyme that converts glucose to ethyl alcohol is?
solution:
This question tests the fermentation of sugar and the enzyme that produces ethanol.

Yeast contains a mixture of enzymes that work one after another on sugar. The final step is:

C6H12O6→zymase2C2H5OH+2CO2

So one glucose molecule gives two molecules of ethanol (ethyl alcohol) and two molecules of carbon dioxide. The catalyst for this step is zymase.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Maltase breaks maltose (a two-sugar) into two glucose units. It does not make alcohol.
  • Diastase breaks starch down into maltose. It acts earlier in the chain.
  • Invertase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose. It also stops before alcohol is formed.

Only zymase catalyses the last step, turning sugar into ethanol.

question: The scientist who stated that matter can be converted into energy is?
solution:
This question tests the idea of mass–energy equivalence.

Albert Einstein showed that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing and can be changed into each other. His famous equation is:

E=mc2

Here E is energy, m is mass and c is the speed of light, about

3×108m/s

Because c2 is enormous, even a tiny mass can release a huge amount of energy. This is exactly what happens inside the sun and in nuclear reactors.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Boyle is known for Boyle’s law of gases: at constant temperature, PV=constant.
  • Lavoisier is known for the law of conservation of mass in chemical reactions.
  • Avogadro is known for Avogadro’s law and Avogadro’s number of particles in a mole.

question: What is the IUPAC name for the following compound? HC≡CCH3
solution:
Idea tested: naming alkynes using IUPAC rules.

The structure is HC≡CCH3. The longest carbon chain has 3 carbon atoms.

For 3 carbons the prefix is prop-, and a triple bond uses the suffix -yne. Putting them together gives propyne (option b).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Acetylene is the common name for ethyne, which has only 2 carbon atoms.
  • Butanol is an alcohol containing an –OH group; this compound has no oxygen.
  • Decanoic acid is a 10-carbon carboxylic acid with a –COOH group, completely different from this alkyne.

question: What is the chemical name for the compound CuCO3?
solution:
This question tests how the charge on a metal ion is worked out from a compound’s formula.

The compound is CuCO3. The carbonate ion is CO32−, so it carries a charge of −2.

A compound is electrically neutral, so the positive charge on copper must balance the negative charge:

charge on Cu+(−2)=0 ⇒charge on Cu=+2

So the copper ion is Cu2+, and the correct name is copper(II) carbonate.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Copper(III) carbonate would need a Cu3+ ion, but copper only forms +1 and +2 ions in its common compounds.
  • Copper(I) carbonate would be Cu2CO3, with two copper ions for every carbonate ion.
  • Copper alone is just the name of the metal element, not the name of this compound.

question: A 'breath test' used by traffic police to check drunken driving uses?

option.b: Silica gel coated with saliva nitrate

solution:
This question tests the redox reaction used in the traditional breath test for alcohol.

When a driver breathes out, any ethanol vapour in the breath is passed through orange acidified potassium dichromate solution. Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid, while the dichromate ion is reduced to green chromium(III) ions:

Cr2O72− + 14H+ + 6e− → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O

The visible sign is a colour change from orange to green. The sulphuric acid supplies the H+ ions the reaction needs.

The option says “dichromatic”, which is a spelling slip for dichromate – the reagent meant is potassium dichromate, K2Cr2O7.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Turmeric on filter paper is a test for alkalis (bases); it changes colour with a base, not with alcohol vapour.
  • Silica gel coated with saliva nitrate is not a standard test reagent; silica gel is used to absorb moisture.
  • Potassium permanganate–sulphuric acid can also oxidise alcohol (purple fading to colourless), but the classic breath test uses the dichromate reagent.

question: Which one of the following is not a mixture?
solution:
This question tests the difference between a mixture and a pure substance.

A mixture contains two or more substances that are just mixed together, not chemically joined. A pure substance (an element or a compound) contains only one kind of particle.

  • Air is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
  • Milk is a mixture: tiny fat droplets and protein spread through water (an emulsion).
  • Cement is a mixture of compounds such as calcium silicates, aluminates and gypsum.
  • Mercury is an element, Hg, made of only mercury atoms, so it is not a mixture.

Therefore mercury is the only pure substance here.

Remember: a mixture can be separated by physical methods (filtering, distillation), while an element cannot be broken down into a simpler substance by any chemical means.

question: Which of the following is a non-metal that remains liquid at room temperature?
solution:
This question tests the physical states of the non-metals at room temperature.

Most non-metals are gases or solids at room temperature. Bromine is the exception: it is a deep red-brown liquid that gives off a brown vapour.

Bromine is in Group 17 (the halogens), with atomic number 35. Going down the group the melting and boiling points rise, so chlorine is a gas, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Chlorine is a pale green-yellow gas at room temperature.
  • Phosphorus is a solid (white or red) at room temperature.
  • Helium is a gas; it is a noble gas that hardly reacts at all.

So bromine is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature.

question:
Which of the following are chemical changes? 

I. cooking of food
II. digestion of food
III. freezing of water
IV. water is heated up
solution:
This question tests the difference between a chemical change and a physical change.

In a chemical change a new substance is formed and the change is usually hard to reverse. In a physical change no new substance is formed; only the state, shape or size changes, and the change is easily reversed.

  1. Cooking of food – chemical. Heat causes reactions such as browning and the breaking down of proteins; the cooked food cannot be turned back into raw food.
  2. Digestion of food – chemical. Enzymes break large food molecules into new, smaller substances such as glucose and amino acids.
  3. Freezing of water – physical. Water simply changes to ice; melt the ice and you get water again.
  4. Heating water – physical. Water changes to steam and condenses back to water on cooling.

Only I and II are chemical changes, so the answer is I and II.

question: The atomic weight of nitrogen is?
solution:
This question tests the meaning of relative atomic mass (atomic weight) and the value for nitrogen.

Atomic weight is the average mass of an element’s atoms compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. It is measured in atomic mass units (u).

For nitrogen:

  • The atomic number is 7, so an atom has 7 protons.
  • The common nitrogen atom, N-14, has 7 neutrons.
mass number=protons+neutrons=7+7=14

So the atomic weight of nitrogen is 14. Its molecule is N2, and its molar mass is 28 g/mol, but the question asks about a single atom.

Why the other options are wrong: 10 is close to the mass of boron-10, 12 is the mass of carbon-12, and 16 is the mass of oxygen-16. None of them is nitrogen.

question: The gas which causes global warming is?
solution:
This question tests which gas is mainly responsible for global warming.

Sunlight warms the earth, and the earth gives the heat back as infrared radiation. Certain gases in the atmosphere absorb this infrared radiation and send part of it back down, so the planet stays warmer than it would otherwise be. This is the greenhouse effect, and these gases are called greenhouse gases.

Carbon dioxide, CO2, is the main greenhouse gas produced by human activity, because burning fuels such as petrol, coal and wood releases it:

C + O2 → CO2

More CO2 means more heat trapped, so the average temperature of the earth rises – global warming, which causes climate change, melting ice and rising sea levels.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • O2 (oxygen) is needed for breathing and burning; it does not absorb infrared radiation in a way that traps heat.
  • N2 (nitrogen) makes up about 78% of air but is not a greenhouse gas.
  • He (helium) is a noble gas and does not trap heat.

question: Oxygen is absent in?
solution:
This question tests what kerosene is made of.

Kerosene is a fraction obtained from crude oil. It is a mixture of hydrocarbons – compounds that contain only carbon and hydrogen, with roughly 12 to 18 carbon atoms per molecule (C12 to C18).

Since a hydrocarbon contains only C and H, there is no oxygen in kerosene. When kerosene burns in plenty of air, the oxygen comes from the air, not from the fuel:

CnH2n+2+3n+12O2→nCO2+(n+1)H2O

Why the other options contain oxygen:

  • Soil holds water (H2O), air (which contains O2) and mineral oxides.
  • Glass is mainly silica, SiO2, mixed with oxides of sodium and calcium.
  • Cement is made of oxides and silicates of calcium, silicon, aluminium and iron.

question: A sample of any of the following substances disappears after some time when exposed to air like camphor, naphthalene, or dry ice. This phenomenon is called?
solution:
This question tests the change of state called sublimation.

Sublimation is the direct change of a solid into a gas without first becoming a liquid. The reverse process, gas to solid, is called deposition.

Camphor, naphthalene (mothballs), iodine, menthol and dry ice (solid CO2) all sublime at ordinary conditions. Their particles have enough energy to escape straight from the solid surface into the air, so the solid slowly disappears.

This property is also used to purify substances: the solid is warmed and the vapour is collected and cooled back to a pure solid, leaving impurities behind.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Evaporation is a change from liquid to gas, for example water drying from a puddle.
  • Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a region of high concentration to one of low concentration, such as a smell filling a room.
  • Radiation is the transfer of energy by waves (for example heat from the sun); it is not a change of state.

question: The maximum electron in N shell is?
solution:
This question tests the maximum number of electrons a shell can hold.

Shells are numbered outwards from the nucleus: K is n = 1, L is n = 2, M is n = 3 and N is n = 4.

The maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by:

maximum electrons=2n2

For the N shell, n=4, so:

2×42=2×16=32

So the N shell can hold up to 32 electrons.

Why the others are wrong: 2 is the maximum for the K shell (n = 1), 8 is the maximum for the L shell (n = 2), and 18 is the maximum for the M shell (n = 3).

question: Neutrons were discovered by?
solution:
This question tests who discovered each part of the atom.

James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. He found a particle with no charge and about the same mass as a proton, and he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935 for this work.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Ernest Rutherford discovered the nucleus and the proton (from his gold-foil experiment), and he described alpha and beta rays.
  • J. J. Thomson discovered the electron using cathode rays; he pictured the atom as a positive sphere with electrons embedded in it.
  • John Dalton put forward the atomic theory, saying that matter is made of tiny indivisible atoms.

A simple summary: Thomson found the electron, Rutherford found the proton, and Chadwick found the neutron.

question:
Which of the following is a form of calcium carbonate?

I. limestone
II. marble
III. chalk
Iv. egg-shells
solution:
This question tests the natural sources of calcium carbonate.

Calcium carbonate has the formula CaCO3. It is one of the most common compounds in the earth’s crust, and all four substances listed are forms of it:

  • Limestone – a sedimentary rock made mainly of CaCO3; it is the main raw material for making quicklime and cement.
  • Marble – limestone that has been changed by great heat and pressure, giving larger crystals.
  • Chalk – a soft, white form built from the shells of tiny sea creatures.
  • Egg-shells – made almost completely of calcium carbonate crystals.

A simple test for any of them is to add dilute acid: calcium carbonate fizzes and gives off carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.

CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2

Since all four are forms of calcium carbonate, the answer is I, II, III and IV.

question: Soaps clean surfaces on the principle based on?
solution:
This question tests how soap works, which is a matter of surface tension.

Water molecules pull on one another strongly, so the surface of water behaves like a stretched skin. This pull is called surface tension. It stops water from wetting greasy dirt properly, so plain water does not clean well.

A soap molecule has two ends:

  • a long hydrocarbon tail that dissolves in grease and oil;
  • an ionic head that dissolves in water.

When soap is added, its molecules push between the water molecules at the surface and lower the surface tension. Water can then spread over the cloth and the greasy dirt. The tails bury themselves in the grease while the heads stay in the water, so the grease is pulled off the cloth in tiny balls called micelles and washed away.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Viscosity is a liquid’s thickness or resistance to flowing; soap does not clean by changing viscosity.
  • Floatation means floating, and is used in separating ore from waste rock by froth flotation, not in washing with soap.
  • Elasticity is the ability of a material to return to its shape after being stretched, which has nothing to do with cleaning.

question: The reactivity of fluorine is due to?
solution:
This question tests why fluorine is the most reactive non-metal.

Electronegativity is the strength with which an atom pulls electrons towards itself in a bond. Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of all elements (about 4.0 on the Pauling scale).

Because its nucleus is small and holds its seven outer electrons very tightly, fluorine attracts other electrons very strongly and gains the one electron it needs to complete its outer shell:

F + e− → F−

This readiness to grab electrons makes fluorine extremely reactive – it even reacts with glass, water and many metals.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Small size of the fluorine atom helps, but small size alone does not explain reactivity; the key factor is its very high electronegativity.
  • Availability of d-orbitals is not true for fluorine, which is in period 2 and has no d-orbitals.
  • A strong F–F bond would make fluorine less reactive, because energy would be needed to break it. In fact the F–F bond is unusually weak, which adds to fluorine’s reactivity.

question: The mass number of a nucleus is?

option.a: Always less than its atomic number
option.b: The sum of the number of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus
option.c: Always more than the atomic weight

solution:
This question tests the meaning of mass number.

An atom is made of protons and neutrons in the nucleus, with electrons orbiting outside.

  • Atomic number (Z) = number of protons.
  • Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons.
A=Z+n

where n is the number of neutrons. Electrons are not counted because their mass is about 1/1840 of a proton’s mass, so it is negligible.

Example: sodium-23 has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so

11+12=23

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Always less than its atomic number is impossible, because the mass number includes the atomic number.
  • Always more than the atomic weight is not necessarily true; for many elements the mass number is close to or less than the atomic weight (for example chlorine has atoms of mass number 35 and 37 but an atomic weight of 35.5).
  • A fraction is wrong: protons and neutrons are whole particles, so the mass number is a whole number.

question: The mass of one Avogadro number of helium atoms is?
solution:
This question tests the mole concept and molar mass.

Avogadro’s number is the number of particles in one mole of a substance:

NA=6.022×1023particles per mole

So “one Avogadro number of helium atoms” means one mole of helium atoms.

The relative atomic mass of helium is 4, so its molar mass is:

M=4g/mol

Now use the mole formula:

n=NNA=1mol mass=n×M=1×4=4.00g

So the mass is 4.00 gram.

Why the others are wrong: 1.00 g would be one mole of hydrogen atoms (mass 1), 6.00 g and 8.00 g do not match the mass of any one mole of helium.

question: 220g of carbon dioxide contains ----- moles
solution:
This question tests how to convert a mass into moles.

First find the molar mass of carbon dioxide, CO2:

M=12+2×16=12+32=44g/mol

One mole of CO2 therefore has a mass of 44 g.

Now use the mole formula, where n is moles, m is mass and M is molar mass:

n=mM=22044=5mol

So 220 g of carbon dioxide contains 5 moles.

Why the others are wrong: 220 g is five 44 g portions. If you divide by the wrong molar mass you get a different number – for example 220/44 is 5, not 6, 3 or 4. (Using 44 g per mole is the only correct step.)

question: The inherited traits of an organism are controlled by?
solution:
This question tests the chemical that carries inherited information.

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is the molecule that stores the instructions an organism inherits from its parents. A DNA molecule is a long chain of repeating units, and the order of those units spells out the “code” for features such as eye colour, blood group and height. DNA is passed from parents to offspring when cells divide.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Nucleotides are the single building blocks (units) that join together to make DNA and RNA. On their own they do not carry a full set of instructions.
  • RNA molecules help to read and carry out the DNA instructions, for example by carrying the message to the ribosomes to make proteins. RNA is a helper, not the store of inherited traits.
  • Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions in the body. They do the work, but they do not hold the inherited plan.

A useful comparison: DNA is like the recipe book, RNA is the copy of one recipe, and enzymes are the cooks.

question: The most abundant rare gas in the atmosphere is?
solution:
This question tests the composition of the air, especially the noble (rare) gases.

Dry air is roughly:

  • nitrogen (N2) about 78%
  • oxygen (O2) about 21%
  • argon (Ar) about 0.93%
  • carbon dioxide (CO2) about 0.04%
  • the other noble gases in very tiny amounts

Among the noble gases, argon is by far the most abundant, because it makes up nearly 1% of the air. Neon, helium, krypton and xenon are present only in traces.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • He (helium) is very rare in air – only a few parts per million.
  • Ne (neon) is also present in very small amounts (about 18 parts per million).
  • Xe (xenon) is the rarest of these four in the atmosphere.

Argon is obtained industrially by fractional distillation of liquid air.

question: The heat required to raise the temperature of the body by 1k is called?
solution:
This question tests the difference between heat capacity and specific heat capacity.

Thermal capacity (also called heat capacity) is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of the whole body by 1 K (which is the same size as 1 °C). Its unit is J/K.

The heat taken in is calculated with:

Q=mcΔθ

If the temperature changes by 1 K, then Δθ=1, so Q=mc. The quantity mc is the thermal capacity of the body.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Specific heat (specific heat capacity) is the heat needed to raise 1 kg of the substance by 1 K; its unit is J/(kg·K). It is a property of the material, not of the whole body.
  • Water equivalent is the mass of water that would need the same heat to warm up by the same amount; it is measured in kg, not J/K.
  • None of the above is wrong because thermal capacity fits the definition exactly.

question: The nucleus of a hydrogen  atom consist of a?
solution:
This question tests the structure of the simplest atom, hydrogen.

A hydrogen atom has atomic number 1 and mass number 1. Using the rules:

protons=atomic number=1 neutrons=mass number−protons=1−1=0

So the nucleus of an ordinary hydrogen atom is just one proton, with no neutron, and one electron moves around it outside the nucleus.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 1 proton, 2 neutrons would be tritium with an extra neutron and a mass number of 3; that is a rare isotope, not the ordinary hydrogen atom.
  • 1 neutron only is impossible, because the nucleus must carry a positive charge and neutrons have no charge.
  • 1 electron only is wrong because electrons move outside the nucleus, not inside it.

question: The metal used to recover copper from a solution of copper sulphate is?
solution:
This question tests displacement reactions and the reactivity series.

A more reactive metal can push a less reactive metal out of its salt solution. In the reactivity series the order is roughly:

Na > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > Cu > Ag > Au

Iron is above copper, so iron can displace copper from copper sulphate solution:

Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu

In terms of ions, iron atoms lose two electrons and copper ions gain them:

Fe → Fe2+ + 2e−    (oxidation)

Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu    (reduction)

The blue colour of the solution fades to pale green and a reddish-brown deposit of copper appears. Iron is cheap and does not react violently with water, so it is a good choice.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Na (sodium) is far too reactive: it reacts violently with the water in the solution, so it cannot be used this way.
  • Ag (silver) is below copper in the series, so it cannot displace copper.
  • Hg (mercury) is also below copper and cannot displace it.

question: The nucleus of an atom consists of?
solution:
This question tests the structure of the atom.

An atom has two main parts:

  • a small, dense nucleus at the centre, containing protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge);
  • electrons (negative), which move around the nucleus in shells.

So the nucleus contains protons and neutrons. The protons give the nucleus its positive charge, and the neutrons add mass without adding charge. Almost all of the atom’s mass is in the nucleus, but the electrons occupy most of its volume.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Electrons and neutrons – electrons are not in the nucleus.
  • Electrons and protons – again, electrons orbit outside the nucleus.
  • None of the above is wrong because protons and neutrons is the correct answer.

question: A solution contains 20g of solute in 180g of solvent. If the solvent is water, what is the concentration of the solution in terms of mass by mass percentage
solution:
This question tests how to calculate concentration as mass by mass percentage.

Given: mass of solute = 20 g, mass of solvent (water) = 180 g.

Step 1: find the mass of the whole solution.

msolution=msolute+msolvent msolution=20+180=200g

Step 2: use the percentage formula.

mass %=msolutemsolution×100% mass %=20200×100%=0.1×100%=10%

So the concentration is 10%.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • 11.1% comes from dividing by the mass of the solvent only: 20/180 × 100. The definition uses the mass of the whole solution.
  • 22.2% comes from 20/90 or a similar slip; it is not what the numbers give.
  • 20% would be right only if the solution had a total mass of 100 g, but here it is 200 g.

question: The only metal that is anti-bacterial is?
solution:
This question tests a special property of copper.

Copper is the metal, among the options given, that is well known for killing bacteria. Copper ions damage the cell walls and the genetic material of bacteria, so germs cannot multiply on a copper surface. That is why copper is used for door handles in hospitals and for water pipes.

Copper also conducts electricity and heat very well, which is why it is used for electrical wires and cooking pots.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Iron is strong and cheap and is used for building and tools, but it is not the metal known for antibacterial action; it can even rust.
  • Sodium is a very soft, very reactive metal that reacts violently with water, so it cannot be used on ordinary surfaces.
  • Aluminium is light and forms a protective oxide layer, which makes it good for foil and pots, but it is not the antibacterial metal being described.

So the answer is copper.

question: An element having the atomic number 17 will resemble which of the following elements having atomic number as given below?
solution:
This question tests how the periodic table groups elements with similar properties.

An element’s group is decided by the number of electrons in its outermost shell. Element 17 is chlorine:

Cl: 2,8,7

It has 7 outer electrons, so it belongs to Group 17 (Group VII), the halogens.

Now check the options:

  • Element 35 is bromine: 2, 8, 18, 7 – also 7 outer electrons, so it is in Group 17 too.
  • Element 33 is arsenic: 2, 8, 18, 5 – Group 15.
  • Element 18 is argon: 2, 8, 8 – a complete outer shell, Group 18 (a noble gas).
  • Element 19 is potassium: 2, 8, 8, 1 – Group 1 (an alkali metal).

Elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons, so they react in similar ways. Chlorine and bromine both form salts with metals and both are coloured, reactive non-metals. The answer is 35.

question: A chemical process in which there is a gain of electrons is known as?
solution:
This question tests the definition of reduction in terms of electrons.

A handy memory aid is OIL RIG:

  • Oxidation Is Loss of electrons.
  • Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

So a process in which a particle gains electrons is reduction. For example, a copper ion gains two electrons to become a copper atom:

Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu

Reduction can also be described as a loss of oxygen or a decrease in oxidation number. Here the oxidation number of copper falls from +2 to 0, which confirms it is reduced.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Sublimation is a solid changing directly to a gas; no electrons are transferred.
  • Oxidation is the opposite – a loss of electrons.
  • Distillation is a separation method based on different boiling points; it is a physical process.

question: The reactions involving simultaneous oxidation and reduction?
solution:
This question tests the name for reactions in which oxidation and reduction happen together.

Electrons cannot simply disappear. If one substance loses electrons (is oxidised), another substance must gain them (is reduced). When both happen in the same reaction, we call it a redox reaction (a short form of reduction + oxidation).

Example: a zinc strip in copper sulphate solution.

Zn → Zn2+ + 2e−    (zinc is oxidised)

Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu    (copper is reduced)

Overall: Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu

The electrons lost by zinc are exactly the electrons gained by the copper ions, so the two changes are linked.

Why the other options are wrong: “Automatic reactions”, “alternate reactions” and “reduction agency” are not standard chemical terms for this. (A reducing agent is a substance that gives electrons away, but that is only one partner in a redox reaction, not the name of the reaction.)

question: A binary compound of oxygen with another element is referred to as?
solution:
This question tests the naming of binary compounds containing oxygen.

A binary compound is made of two elements only. When one of those elements is oxygen, the compound is called an oxide.

Examples:

  • MgO – magnesium oxide (a metal with oxygen)
  • CO2 – carbon(IV) oxide, or carbon dioxide (a non-metal with oxygen)
  • SO2 – sulphur(IV) oxide
  • Al2O3 – aluminium oxide

In each case oxygen is combined with just one other element, so the name ends in -oxide.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom, such as iron or oxygen; it is not a compound at all.
  • Carbon and Nitrogen are the names of elements, not of compounds with oxygen.

question: The process or act of extracting a metal from its ore and refining it is called?
solution:
This question tests the correct word for obtaining a metal from its ore.

Metallurgy is the science and technology of extracting metals from their ores and then purifying (refining) them for use. The usual stages are:

  1. Mining – digging the ore out of the ground.
  2. Concentration – removing rocky impurities (gangue) from the ore.
  3. Roasting or calcination – heating the ore in air or without air to change it chemically.
  4. Reduction – removing oxygen, for example with carbon or by electrolysis.
  5. Refining – purifying the crude metal, for example by electrolysis.

All of these steps together are called metallurgy.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Extraction is a general word for taking something out; it is only one part of the whole process.
  • Metal mining only means digging the ore out of the ground.
  • Prospecting means searching for deposits of ore before mining even begins.

question: The compounds made up of only carbon and hydrogen are called?
solution:
This question tests the definition of a hydrocarbon.

A hydrocarbon is a compound made up of only carbon and hydrogen. Nothing else – no oxygen, no nitrogen, no halogen.

Examples:

  • methane, CH4
  • ethane, C2H6
  • ethene, C2H4
  • benzene, C6H6

Hydrocarbons are the main substances in petroleum, natural gas and coal, and they are the starting materials for making plastics, fuels and many medicines.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Carbon compounds is too broad: it also covers CO2, carbonates and many other substances that contain other elements.
  • Atoms are the smallest particles of an element, not compounds.
  • Carbon hydrolysis is not a real chemical term. Hydrolysis means a substance being split by water.

question: Which of the following is a physical property of monosaccharides?

option.c: They are highly vital to the exploration of metals
option.d: They can be reduced to sugar alcohols

solution:
Idea tested: distinguishing physical properties from chemical properties.

A physical property can be observed without forming a new substance. Monosaccharides are white crystalline solids that dissolve easily in water and taste sweet. This is a physical property, so option b is correct.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Getting charred on strong heating is a chemical change — the sugar decomposes into black carbon and other products.
  • Being "highly vital to the exploration of metals" is not a property of monosaccharides at all.
  • Reduction to sugar alcohols is a chemical reaction, because a new substance is formed.

question: In troposphere, the two types of pollutants are?
solution:
This question tests the types of pollutants found in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere.

The troposphere is where we live, where weather happens and where the air we breathe is found. Pollutants in this layer are grouped by their physical form into two types:

  • Gaseous pollutants – gases such as sulphur(IV) oxide (SO2), carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen oxides (NO and NO2) and hydrocarbons.
  • Particulate pollutants – tiny solid particles or droplets such as dust, soot, smoke, ash and aerosols.

So the two types of tropospheric pollutants are gaseous and particulate pollutants.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Carbon and metallic pollutants – this leaves out gaseous pollutants such as SO2 and NO2, and “carbon pollutant” is not a proper class.
  • Natural and man-made pollutants – this describes where a pollutant comes from (its source), not the physical type of pollutant in the troposphere.
  • Sulphuric and nitrogenous pollutants – these are only some examples of gaseous pollutants and do not cover dust, soot and other particles.

question: The molar enthalpy change accompanying the removal of an electron from a gas phase atom or ion in its ground state is called?
solution:
This question tests the definition of ionisation enthalpy (ionisation energy).

Ionisation enthalpy is the energy needed to remove one electron from a gaseous atom or ion in its ground state. For the first electron of an atom M:

M(g)→M+(g)+e−ΔH>0

The value is positive because energy must be supplied to pull the negative electron away from the positive nucleus – the process is endothermic. The molar value is quoted in kJ/mol.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Electron gain enthalpy is the enthalpy change when a gaseous atom gains an electron, forming a negative ion: M(g) + e− → M−(g). It is usually negative (energy released).
  • Enthalpy change is a general term for the heat change in any reaction, not specifically for removing an electron.
  • Enthalpic gas removal is not a real chemical term.

question: The fourteen elements (atomic number 90-103) after actinium are called?
solution:
This question tests the name of the series of elements that follows actinium.

The elements with atomic numbers 89 to 103 form the actinoid (actinide) series – actinium itself and the fourteen elements after it. They are named after the first member, actinium.
