Their special feature is that the inner 5f subshell is being filled as you move along the series. They are all heavy metals and all are radioactive, which is why they are studied in nuclear chemistry. The best known member is uranium, used as nuclear fuel; plutonium is another.

Similarly, the series that follows lanthanum is called the lanthanoids (rare earths), filling the 4f subshell.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Nucleotides are the units that make up DNA and RNA; they are not elements at all.
  • Pre-actinium elements is not a standard name for any series.
  • Atomic elements is not a recognised classification of the periodic table.

question: The process by which salt and water reacted in a limited way to form an acid or a base is?
solution:
This question tests salt hydrolysis.

Hydrolysis means a reaction in which water breaks a bond in a substance. In salt hydrolysis, one of the ions from a dissolved salt reacts with water and makes the solution acidic or basic.

Example 1 – sodium ethanoate (a salt of a weak acid and a strong base) makes the solution alkaline:

CH3COO− + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + OH−

The OH− ions make the solution basic.

Example 2 – ammonium chloride (a salt of a weak base and a strong acid) makes the solution acidic:

NH4+ + H2O ⇌ NH4OH + H+

The H+ ions make the solution acidic.

A salt of a strong acid and a strong base, such as NaCl, does not hydrolyse, so its solution stays neutral.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Neutral process – not a standard term; neutralisation is a different reaction (acid + base → salt + water), not a salt reacting with water.
  • Basic acidic process – not a real chemical name.
  • Sublimation – a solid changing directly to a gas, which has nothing to do with salts and water.

question: The sub-atomic particles located in the nucleus of an atom are?
solution:
This question tests the parts of an atom and where each part is found.

An atom has a tiny, heavy centre called the nucleus, and light electrons move around it in shells.

  • The nucleus holds two kinds of particles: protons, which carry a positive charge, and neutrons, which carry no charge at all.
  • Electrons carry a negative charge and are never inside the nucleus.

So the sub-atomic particles in the nucleus are the neutron and the proton, which is option a.

Why the others are wrong:

  • proton and electron – the electron lives outside the nucleus, in the shells.
  • proton and ions – an ion is a whole atom (or group of atoms) that has gained or lost electrons; it is not a sub-atomic particle.
  • neutron and electron – again the electron is outside the nucleus.

question: The IUPAC nomenclature of the structure is?
solution:
This question tests how to name an alkane that carries substituent groups, using IUPAC rules.

  1. Find the longest chain of carbon atoms. Here the longest chain has 4 carbon atoms, so the parent name ends in -butane.
  2. Name the groups attached to the chain. There is one chlorine atom (chloro) and one methyl group (CH3).
  3. Number the chain from the end that gives the groups the smallest numbers. Counting from the end nearer the substituted carbon, both groups sit on carbon 2.
  4. Put the groups in alphabetical order before the parent name (chloro comes before methyl), and give each group its number: 2-chloro-2-methylbutane.

So the correct name is option d.

Why the others are wrong:

  • 3-chloro-3-methylbutane – the numbering is done from the wrong end, so it gives 3 instead of 2; a chain must always be numbered to give the lowest numbers.
  • 2,2-dichloro-3-methylbutane – this name claims two chlorine atoms, but only one chlorine is present, and a butane chain cannot have a methyl group on carbon 3 and two chlorines on carbon 2 while still matching the structure.
  • 3-methylchlorobutane – the substituents are written as one word in the wrong order and without proper numbering; correct IUPAC names separate each substituent with its own number.

question:
SO2 + O2 → 2SO3

In the reaction above, the most suitable catalyst is?
solution:
This question tests the catalyst used in the industrial manufacture of sulphuric acid by the Contact Process.

The important step in the Contact Process is turning sulphur dioxide into sulphur trioxide:

2SO2+O2⇌2SO3

This reaction is slow on its own, so it is passed over a solid vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, V2O5, at about 450 °C and 2–3 atmospheres. The catalyst speeds up the reaction without being used up, so option d is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • chromium(VI) oxide (CrO3) – a strong oxidising agent, not the catalyst for this step.
  • iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3) – an oxide of iron used as an ore and as a catalyst in other reactions, but not here.
  • copper(I) oxide (Cu2O) – a red copper compound, not used as the catalyst in the Contact Process.

question: In the preparation of salts, the method employed will depend on the?
solution:
This question tests what decides the method we use to prepare a salt.

Different salts need different preparation methods (acid + metal, acid + carbonate, acid + base, precipitation, or direct combination), and the method is chosen after checking the properties of the salt, especially how it behaves when heated.

  1. Some salts break down when heated, for example ammonium carbonate and most nitrates, so they must not be made by heating to dryness.
  2. Some salts contain water of crystallisation (hydrated salts) and lose that water on strong heating, changing the salt.
  3. Salts such as sodium chloride are stable to heat, so evaporating their solutions is safe.

Because the choice of method depends on whether the salt survives heating, the answer is stability to heat, option c.

Why the others are wrong:

  • composition – far too general; every salt has a composition, so it does not tell you which method to use.
  • dissociating ability – this describes how well a substance splits into ions in water (its strength as an electrolyte), not the preparation method.
  • precipitating ability – precipitation is only one of the methods used, so it cannot be the thing that all methods depend on.

question: The following non-metal form acidic oxides with oxygen except?
solution:
This question tests which non-metal oxides are acidic and which are not.

Most non-metals burn in oxygen to give acidic oxides, which dissolve in water to form acids and react with alkalis.

  • Phosphorus gives phosphorus(V) oxide, P4O10, which forms phosphoric acid.
  • Sulphur gives sulphur dioxide, SO2, which forms sulphurous acid.
  • Chlorine gives oxides such as Cl2O7, which form acidic solutions.

Carbon is the exception. It does form the acidic gas CO2, but it also forms carbon monoxide, CO, when there is not enough oxygen. Carbon monoxide is a neutral oxide: it does not react with acids or with alkalis. So carbon is the non-metal that does not only give acidic oxides, making option c correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • phosphorus – its oxide P4O10 is acidic.
  • sulphur – its oxide SO2 is acidic (it is the gas that helps form acid rain).
  • chlorine – its oxides are acidic.

question: How many neutrons are present in atom with mass number and atomic number 37 and 17 respectively?
solution:
This question tests how mass number, atomic number and neutrons are linked.

Remember the meaning of the two numbers:

  • Atomic number (Z) = number of protons.
  • Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons.

So the neutrons are found by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number:

neutrons=A−Z=37−17=20

So there are 20 neutrons, which is option b.

Why the others are wrong:

  • 18 – would need a mass number of 35, not 37.
  • 37 – that is the mass number, which counts protons and neutrons together.
  • 17 – that is the number of protons (the atomic number).

question: The sulphide that is commonly used in coating electric fluorescent tubes is?
solution:
This question tests a useful compound of zinc and the property that makes it glow.

The white solid painted on the inside of fluorescent tubes and television screens is zinc sulphide, ZnS.

Zinc sulphide is a phosphor: when energy such as ultraviolet light or radiation hits it, it absorbs the energy and then gives it out again as a flash of visible light. This glowing effect is called luminescence (when caused by radiation it is radioluminescence). That is exactly what is needed inside a fluorescent tube, so option c is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • iron(II) sulphide (FeS) – a black solid used as a source of hydrogen sulphide with acids; it does not glow.
  • tin(II) sulphide (SnS) – a dark brown/black solid, not a phosphor.
  • lead(IV) sulphide (PbS) – a black solid (the mineral galena), used as a lead ore; it does not glow.

question: An organic compound which liberate carbon(iv)oxide from trioxocarbonate(iv) solution is likely to be?
solution:
This question tests which class of organic compound is acidic enough to release carbon dioxide from a trioxocarbonate(IV) (carbonate) solution.

Carbonates such as sodium carbonate, Na2CO3, fizz with acids because the acid gives hydrogen ions that turn the carbonate into carbon dioxide gas:

2CH3COOH+Na2CO3→2CH3COONa+H2O+CO2

Ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, is a carboxylic acid, so it contains the −COOH group whose hydrogen can be lost as H+. That makes option d correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • C2H5OH – ethanol, an alcohol; its −OH hydrogen is not acidic enough to react with a carbonate.
  • C3H4 – propyne, a hydrocarbon with a triple bond; hydrocarbons are not acidic and do not fizz with carbonates.
  • C6H6 – benzene, a hydrocarbon; also unreactive towards carbonates.

question: Addition of sodium chloride to water to form a solution would  lead to?

option.a: increase in freezing point and increase the boiling point
option.b: increase in freezing point and decrease the boiling point
option.c: decrease in freezing point and decrease the boiling point
option.d: decrease in freezing point and increase the boiling point

solution:
This question tests how dissolving a solid in water changes the freezing point and the boiling point of the water.

Salt particles take up space among the water molecules, and this makes it harder for the water to freeze and harder for it to boil. These effects are called colligative properties:

  • Freezing point depression: the solution freezes at a lower temperature than pure water (pure water freezes at 0 °C).
  • Boiling point elevation: the solution boils at a higher temperature than pure water (pure water boils at 100 °C).

So adding sodium chloride decreases the freezing point and increases the boiling point, which is option d. This is why salt is spread on icy roads to melt the ice.

Why the others are wrong:

  • increase in freezing point and increase in boiling point – the freezing point always goes down, never up, when a solute is added.
  • increase in freezing point and decrease in the boiling point – both changes are stated the wrong way round.
  • decrease in freezing point and decrease in the boiling point – the boiling point goes up, not down.

question: A chemical widely used as a fertilizer is?
solution:
This question tests the names of common materials and which one is a fertiliser.

A fertiliser must supply a plant nutrient, mainly nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium.

Nitrochalk (calcium ammonium nitrate, CAN) is made from ammonium nitrate and calcium carbonate. It is rich in nitrogen and is spread on farms to help crops grow green and strong, so option d is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • galena – lead(II) sulphide, PbS; it is the main ore of lead, a metal, and contains no plant nutrient.
  • bauxite – the ore of aluminium (mainly Al2O3); used to make aluminium, not to feed plants.
  • emerald – a green gemstone (a form of beryl), a precious stone, not a fertiliser.

question: On the basis of the electrochemical series, which of these ions will show the greater tendency to be discharged at the cathode in an electrolytic cell
solution:
This question tests the electrochemical series and which ion is easiest to discharge at the cathode.

At the cathode, positive ions gain electrons (they are reduced) and become atoms. The ion that gains electrons most easily is the one whose metal is least reactive, that is, the metal lowest down in the electrochemical series.

The series, from most reactive to least reactive, runs:

K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Sn > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au

Among Zn, Fe, Sn and Cu, copper is lowest, so copper is least reactive and Cu2+ is reduced most readily:

Cu2++2e−→Cu

So option a is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • Cu2+ < Sn2+ – tin lies above copper in the series, so it is more reactive and harder to discharge.
  • Fe2+ – iron is more reactive than tin and copper, so it is discharged less easily.
  • Zn2+ – zinc is the most reactive of the four, so it is the hardest of them to discharge.

question: Addition of charcoal to the filter bed of sand during water treatment for township supply is to?
solution:
This question tests the stages of treating water for a town supply and the job of charcoal.

Water from rivers contains dirt, germs and dissolved gases that make it smell and taste unpleasant. After screening, coagulation, settling and filtration through sand, the water may still carry dissolved gases and substances that cause a bad taste and smell.

Charcoal (especially activated carbon) is full of tiny pores, giving it a huge surface area. Particles of gas and smelly organic matter stick to that surface – a process called adsorption – so the water comes out fresh. That is why option c is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • prevent goitre – goitre is prevented by iodine, which is added to table salt, not to water by charcoal.
  • prevent tooth decay – this needs fluoride, sometimes added in tiny amounts to water.
  • kill germs – germs are killed by chlorine (or ozone/UV light), not charcoal; charcoal only removes smells and tastes.

question: Using the metal activity series, the metal that can liberate hydrogen gas from steam is?
solution:
This question tests the metal activity series and which metals are reactive enough to release hydrogen from steam.

Only fairly reactive metals (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc and iron) can pull oxygen out of steam. When steam passes over red-hot iron:

3Fe+4H2O→Fe3O4+4H2

Iron takes the oxygen, and hydrogen gas is set free. So option a is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • copper – copper is below hydrogen in the activity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from water or steam.
  • tin – tin is also below hydrogen; it reacts only with strong acids, not with steam.
  • lead – lead is below hydrogen as well and does not react with steam to give hydrogen.

question: An organic compound with fishy smell is likely to have a general formula?
solution:
This question tests the general formula of the organic family that smells like fish.

Amines are compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms of ammonia, NH3, have been replaced by carbon groups (R groups). Their general formula is R−NH2.

  • Ammonia itself has a sharp, choking smell.
  • Liquid amines keep a similar smell, which people describe as fishy or like stale fish – this is why fish that is going bad smells of amines.

So the fishy compound is an amine, RNH2, which is option c.

Why the others are wrong:

  • RCONHR1 – this is a substituted amide (two carbon groups on the nitrogen); amides are usually solids with little smell.
  • RCONH2 – a primary amide such as ethanamide, an odourless white solid.
  • RCOR1 – a ketone, whose small members smell more like nail-varnish remover (propanone), not fish.

question:
N2O4 ⇔ 2NO2          (ΔH = +ve)

From the reaction above, which of these conditions would produce the highest equilibrium yield for N2O4?
solution:
Idea tested: using Le Chatelier's principle to predict the effect of temperature and pressure on an equilibrium.

The equilibrium is N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 with ΔH = +ve, so the forward reaction is endothermic. We want the highest yield of N2O4, which is the reactant, so the equilibrium must shift to the left.

  • Lower temperature: the forward reaction absorbs heat. Cooling removes heat, so the system shifts left to release heat and make more N2O4.
  • Higher pressure: the left side has 1 mole of gas and the right side has 2 moles. High pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, which is the left side, so more N2O4 is formed.

Therefore, low temperature and high pressure give the highest yield of N2O4 — option a.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Low temperature and low pressure: low pressure favours the side with more gas molecules (the right), so it reduces the N2O4 yield.
  • High temperature and low pressure: both changes shift the equilibrium to the right, producing more NO2 and less N2O4.
  • High temperature and high pressure: high pressure helps, but high temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right, so the N2O4 yield is not highest.

question:
Zn + 2HCL → ZnCl2 + H2 

What happens to zinc in the above reaction?
solution:
This question tests oxidation and reduction using changes in oxidation number.

Write the equation with oxidation numbers:

Zn0+2HCl+1→ZnCl2+2+H20

  1. Zinc goes from oxidation number 0 to +2. It loses electrons, and loss of electrons is oxidation.
  2. Hydrogen goes from +1 in HCl to 0 in H2. It gains electrons, so it is reduced.

Zinc is therefore oxidised, which is option a.

Why the others are wrong:

  • reduced – that describes hydrogen, not zinc; zinc loses electrons, so it cannot be reduced.
  • a reactant – true but not the answer; being a reactant says nothing about the chemical change.
  • a metal – also true but not the answer; the question asks what happens to zinc in the reaction.

Zinc is the reducing agent because it gives electrons away, while HCl is the oxidising agent.

question: An organic functional group which can likely decolorize ammoniacal silver nitrate is?
solution:
This question tests a test used to recognise a terminal alkyne.

Ammoniacal silver nitrate solution (Tollens' reagent) contains silver ions, Ag+.

In a terminal alkyne the triple bond is at the end of the chain, so one carbon still carries a hydrogen atom: R−C≡C−H. That hydrogen is slightly acidic and can be replaced by silver:

R−C≡C−H+Ag+→R−C≡C−Ag+H+

A white precipitate of silver alkynide forms, and the reagent is used up (decolourised). So option c is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • alkene – the C=C double bond does not react with ammoniacal silver nitrate; alkenes are tested with bromine water instead.
  • alkane – alkanes are saturated and unreactive towards this reagent.
  • alkanol – the −OH hydrogen of an alcohol is not acidic enough to form a silver compound.

question: A colored gas that is known to be poisonous and can readily damage the mucous lining of the lungs is?
solution:
This question tests the physical properties and health effects of common gases.

The gas described is chlorine, Cl2:

  • It is a greenish-yellow gas, so it has a colour.
  • It has a sharp, bleach-like smell and is very poisonous.
  • When breathed in, it dissolves in the moisture of the nose, throat and lungs, forming acid that burns the mucous lining, causing coughing, a sore throat and, in large amounts, fluid in the lungs.

So the answer is option c.

Why the others are wrong:

  • hydrogen sulphide – poisonous with a rotten-egg smell, but it is colourless.
  • carbon(II) oxide – very poisonous because it takes the place of oxygen in the blood, but it is colourless and odourless.
  • sulphur(IV) oxide – choking and harmful to the lungs, but it is colourless too.

question: In order to electroplate spoon with silver, the arrangement of the electrolytic cell is?

option.a: the anode is a silver rod and the cathode is the spoon
option.b: the anode is the spoon and the cathode is a silver rod
option.c: the electrolyte is silver trioxonitrate(v)( solution and the cathode is a silver rod.
option.d: the electrolyte  is silver trioxonitrate(v) solution and the anode is the spoon

solution:
This question tests how an electroplating cell is arranged.

To plate a metal onto an object, the object must gain the metal, and metal atoms are deposited where ions gain electrons – at the cathode (the negative electrode).

  1. Cathode: the spoon, the object to be plated.
  2. Anode: a rod of pure silver, the plating metal. It dissolves and keeps replacing the silver ions used up.
  3. Electrolyte: a solution of a silver salt, usually silver trioxonitrate(V), AgNO3, so that silver ions are available.

At the cathode: Ag++e−→Ag

So the anode is a silver rod and the cathode is the spoon, which is option a.

Why the others are wrong:

  • anode is the spoon and cathode is a silver rod – this is reversed; the silver would leave the spoon instead of coating it.
  • electrolyte is silver trioxonitrate(V) solution and the cathode is a silver rod – the electrolyte is right, but the cathode must be the spoon, not the silver rod.
  • electrolyte is silver trioxonitrate(V) solution and the anode is the spoon – the electrolyte is right, but if the spoon were the anode it would dissolve rather than be plated.

question: An organic compound which decolorizes bromine water is likely to be?
solution:
This question tests the reaction that shows a compound is unsaturated.

Bromine water is orange-brown. When it is shaken with a compound that has a carbon-to-carbon double bond, the bromine adds across the double bond and the colour disappears (the water turns colourless).

C2H4+Br2→C2H4Br2

C2H4 is ethene, an alkene (general formula CnH2n, so it has one double bond), so it decolourises bromine water. That makes option d correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • C3H8 – propane, an alkane (CnH2n+2); it is saturated and does not react with bromine water.
  • C2H6 – ethane, also an alkane, so no reaction.
  • C4H10 – butane, another alkane, so no reaction.

question: Crude petroleum is converted to useful products by the process of?
solution:
This question tests how crude petroleum is separated into useful products.

Crude petroleum is a mixture of many hydrocarbons that differ in the length of their carbon chains. Longer chains have stronger forces between molecules, so they have higher boiling points; shorter chains boil at lower temperatures.

In a refinery the crude oil is heated and the vapour rises up a tall fractionating column. The column is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top, so each fraction condenses at its own level:

  • bottom (very hot): bitumen and heavy fuel oils
  • middle: diesel, kerosene
  • top (cool): petrol, and gases such as LPG

This separation by boiling point is fractional distillation, so option b is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • fractional crystallisation – separates dissolved solids by making them crystallise out; crude oil is a liquid mixture.
  • filtration – separates an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper; it cannot split liquids that mix completely.
  • chromatography – separates small amounts of substances by how fast they move up paper or a column; it is not used to refine petroleum.

question: An organic compound contains 60.0% carbon, 13.3% hydrogen and 26.7% oxygen. Calculate the empirical formula [C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]
solution:
Idea tested: calculating an empirical formula from percentage composition.

Assume we have 100 g of the compound. Then the masses are: carbon 60.0 g, hydrogen 13.3 g and oxygen 26.7 g.

Divide each mass by the relative atomic mass of the element:

C:60.012=5.00, H:13.31=13.3, O:26.716=1.67

Now divide all the answers by the smallest value, 1.67:

C:5.001.67≈3, H:13.31.67≈8, O:1.671.67=1

The simplest whole-number ratio is C : H : O = 3 : 8 : 1, so the empirical formula is C3H8O — option d.

Why the other options are wrong: C4H12O, C3H9O and C4H9O do not match the 3 : 8 : 1 mole ratio obtained from the calculation.

question:
2H2 + O2 → 2H2O

From the equation above, calculate the volume of unreacted oxygen gas if a mixture of 50cm3 of hydroden and 75cm3 of oxygen are involved
solution:
This question tests Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes: gases react in simple whole-number volume ratios.

The equation says 2 molecules of hydrogen react with exactly 1 molecule of oxygen:

2H2+O2→2H2O

So the reacting volumes are in the ratio 2 : 1. Since the temperature and pressure are the same for all the gases, the same ratio holds for volumes.

Step 1: find the oxygen that the hydrogen can use.

VO2=12×50=25cm3

Step 2: subtract the used oxygen from the oxygen supplied.

unreacted=75−25=50cm3

That is 50 cm3, option b.

Why the others are wrong:

  • 85 cm3 – this adds 75 and 10 or similar, which is not how reacting volumes work.
  • 125 cm3 – that is 50 + 75, the total gas mixed, not the leftover oxygen.
  • 55 cm3 – would need 20 cm3 of oxygen used, but 50 cm3 of hydrogen uses 25 cm3.

question: In which of the following will hydrogen form ionic compound?
solution:
This question tests ionic bonding, that is, which compound is held together by ions.

An ionic bond forms when a metal atom transfers electrons to a non-metal atom, making a positive ion and a negative ion that attract each other.

In sodium hydride, NaH:

Na→Na++e−

H+e−→H−

Sodium (a metal) gives its outer electron to hydrogen, so Na+ and H− ions are formed and packed in a giant ionic lattice. So option b is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • HCl – hydrogen chloride is held by a shared pair of electrons (covalent). It only becomes ions when dissolved in water, where it ionises; in the pure state the H–Cl bond is covalent.
  • NH3 – ammonia is covalent; nitrogen shares electron pairs with each hydrogen.
  • CH4 – methane is covalent; carbon shares four pairs of electrons with hydrogen.

question: If the volume of a given mass of a gas at 0ºc is 29.5cm3. What will be the volume of the gas at 15ºc, given that the pressure remains constant.
solution:
This question tests Charles' law: at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute (Kelvin) temperature.

Step 1: change the temperatures to kelvin by adding 273.

T1=0+273=273K

T2=15+273=288K

Step 2: write Charles' law.

V1T1=V2T2

Step 3: make V2 the subject and substitute.

V2=V1×T2T1=29.5×288273=8496273≈31.1cm3

So the new volume is about 31.1 cm3, option d. The gas expands a little because it is warmed at constant pressure.

Why the others are wrong:

  • 31.6 – comes from rounding slips in the arithmetic.
  • 62.2 – about twice the correct answer, as if 15 were doubled.
  • 32.7 – would need a temperature of about 303 K (30 °C), not 288 K.

question: The reactions below represent neutralization reaction, in which of them is the value of ΔH highest?
solution:
This question tests the enthalpy change of neutralisation and how the strength of the acid or base affects it.

When an acid and a base neutralise, the reaction that really happens is:

H++OH−→H2OΔH≈−57kJ/mol

The highest value of ΔH (the most heat released) is obtained when both the acid and the base are strong, because strong acids and strong bases are fully ionised – all their H+ and OH− ions are free to react at once.

With a weak acid or weak base, some energy is used up first to ionise the weak substance before it can react, so less heat is released and ΔH is smaller.

Looking at the options: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O is the only pair of a strong acid and a strong base, so it gives the highest ΔH. Option c is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • CH3CH2COOH + KOH – propanoic acid is a weak acid, so part of the heat is used to ionise it; ΔH is smaller.
  • NH4OH + HCl – ammonium hydroxide is a weak base, so its ΔH is also smaller.
  • CH3COOH + NaOH – ethanoic acid is weak, so this value is smaller than for a strong acid.

question: The pollutant usually presents in a city which generates its electricity from coal?
solution:
This question tests the main air pollutant produced by burning coal to make electricity.

Coal contains small amounts of sulphur mixed in with the carbon. When the coal burns, the sulphur also burns:

S+O2→SO2

So sulphur(IV) oxide, SO2, pours out of the power station chimney. In the air it can be changed into sulphur trioxide and then into sulphuric acid, which falls as acid rain, harming plants, buildings and lakes; it also irritates the lungs. That makes option d correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • fog – fog is tiny water droplets formed when moist air cools; it is weather, not a pollutant from burning coal.
  • carbon(II) oxide – CO is poisonous and can come from burning fuel, but a well-run power station supplies plenty of air, so the carbon is burned to CO2; the pollutant that always comes from coal is the one made from its sulphur.
  • smog – smog is the hazy mixture that forms when sunlight acts on pollutants; it is a result of pollution, not the gas released by burning coal.

question: The dehydration of CH3CH2CH2CH2OH will give?
solution:
This question tests the dehydration of an alkanol (alcohol) to form an alkene.

Dehydration means removing water. With a hot acid catalyst such as concentrated sulphuric acid, the −OH group is removed from one carbon and a hydrogen atom is removed from the neighbouring carbon. The two carbons then join with a double bond:

CH3CH2CH2CH2OH→CH3CH2CH=CH2+H2O

butan-1-ol gives but-1-ene; the double bond can also shift to the middle of the chain to give but-2-ene:

CH3CH=CHCH3

Option d shows exactly that alkene, CH3CH=CHCH3, with a double bond and the formula C4H8, so it is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • HC≡CCH2CH3 – this is but-1-yne, which has a triple bond; removing water from an alcohol gives a double bond, not a triple bond.
  • CH2≡CH2CH3 – the formula is impossible and again shows a triple bond.
  • CH3C≡CCH3 – this is but-2-yne, an alkyne with a triple bond and formula C4H6, not the product of dehydration.

question: When heat is absorbed during a chemical reaction, the reaction is said to be
solution:
This question tests the names of reactions that take in or give out heat.

Every chemical reaction either absorbs heat from its surroundings or releases heat to them.

  • Endothermic (“endo” = in): the reaction absorbs heat, so the mixture feels colder and ΔH is positive.
  • Exothermic (“exo” = out): the reaction releases heat, so the mixture feels hotter and ΔH is negative.

Since the question says heat is absorbed, the reaction is endothermic, option d. A familiar example is the decomposition of limestone, which needs strong heating.

Why the others are wrong:

  • exothermic – the opposite; it gives out heat (burning wood is exothermic).
  • isothermal – means the temperature stays the same; it says nothing about heat being absorbed.
  • thermodynamic – describes the study of energy changes in general, not a type of reaction.

question: Which of the following best represent solid gas mixture?
solution:
This question tests the different kinds of mixture, named by the states of the substances mixed.

A mixture can be described by writing the state of the particles first and the state they are spread through second.

  • Solid in gas: tiny solid particles float in a gas. Smoke is exactly this – fine bits of soot and ash carried in air.
  • Liquid in gas: fog and mist (tiny water droplets in air).
  • Liquid in liquid: milk (fat droplets in water).
  • Solid in solid: soil, an alloy, or a mixture of salts.

Only smoke is a solid scattered through a gas, so option d is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • milk – tiny fat droplets in water, so it is a liquid-in-liquid mixture.
  • kerosene – a liquid fuel; it is a mixture of liquid hydrocarbons, not a solid in a gas.
  • soil – a mixture of solid particles (with some air and water in the gaps), so it is mainly solid in solid, not solid in gas.

question:
H+ + OH− → H2O

The equation above illustrates
solution:
This question tests the ionic equation for the reaction between an acid and a base.

In the equation, one hydrogen ion from the acid joins one hydroxide ion from the base:

H++OH−→H2O

This is what happens whenever an acid neutralises a base: the acid's H+ and the base's OH− combine to form water, and the remaining ions form a salt. Because an acid and a base destroy each other's properties, the reaction is called neutralisation, option d.

For example: HCl+NaOH→NaCl+H2O

Why the others are wrong:

  • precipitation – forming an insoluble solid (a precipitate) from two solutions, for example adding silver nitrate to salt water to get silver chloride.
  • hydration – water molecules attaching themselves to ions or molecules, as when anhydrous copper(II) sulphate turns blue in water.
  • hydrolysis – a substance being broken down by water, such as an ester or a salt of a weak acid splitting in water.

question: Electrons enter into orbitals in order of increasing energy as exemplified by?
solution:
This question tests the order in which electrons fill the shells and orbitals of an atom.

Electrons always fill the lowest energy level available first. The order of increasing energy is:

1s<2s<2p<3s<3p

This tells us two things:

  • The whole 2p subshell is filled before any electron enters the higher-energy 3s orbital.
  • Within the p subshell the three orbitals (px, py, pz) are filled starting from px.

Option b shows 1s2 2s2 2px2 2py1 2pz1, where every electron is still in the 2p level and none has jumped up to 3s. So option b is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • a – puts 2 electrons in px and 2 in py but leaves pz empty while 3s is written with 0; the order within the subshell is not followed.
  • c – places an electron in 3s while 2p is not yet complete, which breaks the rule that the lower level fills first.
  • d – has the same uneven p filling as (a) and still shows an electron pushed into 3s.

question: Wrought iron is obtained by heating cast iron in a furnace with?
solution:
This question tests how cast iron is turned into wrought iron.

Cast iron contains a lot of carbon (about 3–4%). The carbon makes it hard but brittle, so it snaps easily.

To make wrought iron, cast iron is heated in a furnace with haematite, Fe2O3. The haematite supplies oxygen that burns away the extra carbon (and silicon and sulphur) as gases:

C+O→CO2

With most of the carbon removed, the iron becomes soft, tough and easily shaped – wrought iron. So option b is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • magnetite – Fe3O4, another iron ore; the standard process uses haematite.
  • carbon(II) oxide – CO is a reducing agent that is added in the blast furnace to make iron from its ore; it would not remove carbon from cast iron.
  • calcium trioxosilicate(IV) – CaSiO3, the slag that forms in the blast furnace to remove sand; it is a waste product, not the substance used to purify cast iron.

question: In the extraction of iron, hot air is introduced into the blast furnace through?
solution:
This question tests the parts of the blast furnace used to extract iron and how air gets in.

In the blast furnace, coke, limestone and iron ore are fed in at the top and fall down the hot furnace. Hot air is needed near the bottom to burn the coke and make the reducing gas carbon monoxide.

The air is blown in through tuyeres – strong nozzles (pipe openings) set around the lower part of the furnace. The air is preheated to about 600 °C, so it enters as a powerful blast, which is why the furnace is called a blast furnace. That makes option d correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • valves – a valve is simply a tap or gate that opens and closes the flow of a liquid or gas; it is not the opening through which the blast enters.
  • open-hearths – an open-hearth furnace is a different furnace, used for making steel, not part of the iron blast furnace.
  • arcs – an electric arc is the spark of electricity used in an electric-arc furnace for making steel; no arc is used in the blast furnace.

question: How many bonding pair are present in carbon(iv)oxide?
solution:
This question tests how to count shared pairs of electrons (bond pairs) in a molecule.

A single covalent bond is one shared pair of electrons; a double bond is two shared pairs.

Carbon(IV) oxide has a carbon atom joined to two oxygen atoms, and each carbon–oxygen link is a double bond:

O=C=O

Count the bond pairs:

bond pairs=2×2=4

So there are 4 bonding pairs, option a. (Each oxygen also holds unshared pairs of electrons, but those are lone pairs, not bond pairs.)

Why the others are wrong:

  • 3 – that would be one double bond plus one single bond, which CO2 does not have.
  • 2 – that would mean only one double bond in the whole molecule.
  • 1 – that would mean just one single bond, far too few for a molecule with two oxygen atoms joined to carbon.

question: 2-methylprop-1-ene is a structural isomer of?
solution:
This question tests structural isomerism: compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms.

First find the molecular formula of 2-methylprop-1-ene. It has a chain of three carbons with a methyl group on carbon 2 and a double bond starting at carbon 1, giving C4H8.

Now check each option for the same formula:

  • but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3, is also C4H8. Its atoms are arranged differently (a straight chain with the double bond in the middle), so it is a structural isomer. That makes option d correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • but-1-yne – C4H6; it has a triple bond, so it has two hydrogens fewer and cannot be an isomer of C4H8.
  • 2-methylbut-1-ene – C5H10; it has five carbon atoms, so the formula is different.
  • 3-methylprop-1-yne – this name cannot describe a real compound (a three-carbon propyne chain cannot carry a methyl group on carbon 3), and an alkyne has a different formula anyway.

question: Alkanes are used mainly?
solution:
This question tests the main everyday use of the alkanes.

Alkanes are hydrocarbons with only single bonds (general formula CnH2n+2). They react readily with oxygen and burn with a hot flame, giving out plenty of heat:

CH4+2O2→CO2+2H2O+heat

Because they are cheap, easy to store and burn cleanly when there is plenty of air, alkanes are our main fuels: methane (natural gas) for cooking, propane and butane in cylinders, petrol, kerosene and diesel for vehicles and engines. So option c is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • in the textile industry – textiles are made from cotton, wool and synthetic polymers such as nylon and polyester, not from alkanes.
  • in the hydrogenation of oils – this process uses hydrogen gas and a nickel catalyst to harden vegetable oils into margarine; the alkane is not the hydrogen.
  • as fine chemicals – fine chemicals are special chemicals made in small amounts (drugs, dyes, flavouring); alkanes are bulk fuels, not fine chemicals.

question: What volume of (dm3) of water will be added to 10dm3 of 2.0 mol/dm3 HCL acid solution to give a final solution of 0.5 mol/dm3?
solution:
This question tests dilution: adding water to a solution lowers its concentration but leaves the amount (moles) of acid unchanged.

Step 1: find the moles of HCl in the original solution.

n=C×V=2.0mol/dm3×10dm3=20mol

Step 2: use C1V1 = C2V2 to find the total final volume.

2.0×10=0.5×V2

20=0.5V2⇒V2=200.5=40dm3

Step 3: the water added is the final volume minus the volume already there.

Vwater=V2−V1=40−10=30dm3

So 30 dm3 of water must be added, option a.

Why the others are wrong:

  • 40 – that is the total final volume, not the water added.
  • 20 – gives a final volume of only 30 dm3, which would still be about 0.67 mol/dm3, too strong.
  • 50 – gives a final volume of 60 dm3, which is too dilute (about 0.33 mol/dm3).

question:
GAS CO2 N2

O2
% BY VOLUME 4 72 24

The above table shows the compositions of the atmosphere of planet X. Which of these gases are present in higher percentages on earth?
solution:
Idea tested: comparing the composition of Earth's atmosphere with the atmosphere of another planet.

Earth's dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and only about 0.04% carbon dioxide.

Planet X has 72% N2, 24% O2 and 4% CO2. Compare each gas:

  • Nitrogen: 78% on Earth is greater than 72% on planet X, so nitrogen is higher on Earth.
  • Oxygen: 21% on Earth is less than 24% on planet X, so oxygen is lower on Earth.
  • Carbon dioxide: about 0.04% on Earth is far less than 4% on planet X, so carbon dioxide is lower on Earth.

Only nitrogen is present in a higher percentage on Earth. Therefore the correct choice is N2 only — option d.

question: Hard water is water with high concentrations of dissolved ions, in particular calcium and
solution:
This question tests what makes water hard.

Hard water is water that contains a lot of dissolved calcium ions, Ca2+, and magnesium ions, Mg2+. These usually get into the water as it flows over limestone and rocks containing magnesium salts, dissolving them as hydrogencarbonates or sulphates.

These two ions are what stop soap from lathering well: the soap reacts with them to form a grey scum instead of foam. So option a is correct.

Why the others are wrong:

  • nitrogen ions – nitrogen does not form simple ions like this in water; nitrates can be present but they do not cause hardness.
  • phosphorus ions – phosphates may appear in polluted water, but they are not what makes water hard.
  • helium ions – helium is a noble gas; it does not form ions in water at all.

question: What happens to the position of equilibrium, if a reversible exothermic reaction is subjected to a decrease in temperature?

option.a: The position of equilibrium shifts to the left
option.b: The position of equilibrium shifts to the right.
option.c: The position of equilibrium remains unchanged

solution:
This question tests Le Chatelier's principle: how an equilibrium moves when we change the conditions.

In an exothermic reaction heat is given out, so we can pretend heat is one of the products:

A+B⇌C+D+heat
  1. Lowering the temperature means heat is taken away.
  2. The system fights the change by making more heat.
  3. Making heat means going forward — the exothermic direction.
  4. So more products form and the equilibrium position shifts to the right.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Left is the endothermic direction. That is the shift you get when you raise the temperature of an exothermic reaction.
  • (c) Unchanged is wrong because temperature is the one change that actually changes the value of the equilibrium constant, so the position must shift.
  • (d) Stops is wrong because the reaction never stops. Cooling only makes both the forward and backward reactions slower; the particles still react in both directions.

question: Which noble gas is radioactive and is produced as a decay product of uranium and thorium?
solution:
This question tests the noble gases and radioactive decay.

The noble gases sit in the last group (Group 0) of the periodic table: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon. They are very unreactive because their outer shells are full.

  1. Uranium and thorium in rocks break down slowly, giving off particles and turning into a chain of new elements.
  2. One member of that chain is radium, which decays into radon gas.
  3. Radon is itself radioactive, so it goes on decaying and releasing radiation. It seeps out of the ground and can collect in houses, where it is a health hazard.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Argon is a noble gas and is formed when potassium-40 decays, but argon itself is stable — it is not radioactive.
  • (b) Krypton is a noble gas but it is stable and is not a uranium or thorium decay product.
  • (d) Neon is a stable noble gas; it is made inside stars, not in radioactive decay chains.

question: Which of the following reactions would be expected to have the highest entropy change?
solution:
This question tests entropy, which is a measure of how disordered or spread out the particles in a substance are.

The freer the particles, the higher the entropy, so the order is:

solid<liquid<gas
  1. In a solid, particles are packed in place and only vibrate — lowest entropy.
  2. In a liquid, particles are still close but can slide past one another — entropy a little higher.
  3. In a gas, particles fly about freely and spread to fill any container — entropy much higher.

Liquid to gas gives the biggest jump in freedom, so it gives the biggest entropy increase:

ΔS>0

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (b) Solid → liquid does increase entropy, but only slightly, because the particles were already close together.
  • (c) Gas → liquid and (d) gas → solid go the opposite way: the particles become more ordered, so entropy decreases (ΔS<0).

question: What is the sum of the oxidation numbers in a neutral compound?
solution:
This question tests the rule that oxidation numbers in a neutral compound add up to zero.

An oxidation number is a bookkeeping charge we give each atom in a compound, as if all the bonding were ionic. A neutral compound carries no overall charge, so the plus parts and the minus parts must cancel exactly.

  1. Water, H2O: two hydrogens at +1 each and one oxygen at −2.
    2(+1)+(−2)=0
  2. Carbon dioxide, CO2: carbon at +4 and two oxygens at −2 each.
    (+4)+2(−2)=0
  3. Table salt, NaCl: sodium at +1, chlorine at −1.
    (+1)+(−1)=0

So the answer is 0.

Why the other options are wrong: if the sum were +2, +1 or −1, the group of atoms would be a charged ion, not a neutral compound. Those numbers are the charges of ions such as Ca2+, Na+ and Cl−, not the total inside a neutral molecule.

question: According to the kinetic theory of gases, the pressure exerted by a gas is due to

option.b: The weight of the gas particles
option.c: The attractive forces between gas particles
option.d: The collisions of gas particles with the container walls

solution:
This question tests the kinetic theory of gases and where gas pressure comes from.

  1. Gas particles are tiny and far apart, and they move in straight lines at high speed in all directions.
  2. They keep hitting the walls of the container.
  3. Each hit gives the wall a tiny push. Millions of these pushes every second add up to a steady force on the wall.
  4. Pressure is force spread over area:
P=FA

More particles, or hotter particles moving faster, means harder and more frequent collisions, so the pressure goes up.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Vibrations describe particles in a solid. Gas particles travel from place to place; they do not just vibrate.
  • (b) Weight of the gas is far too small to matter, and weight pulls downwards, so it could not push sideways on the walls.
  • (c) Attractive forces are what hold liquid and solid particles together. In a gas they are negligible — attraction is not what pushes on the walls.

question: What is eutrophication?

option.a: The release of harmful chemicals into water bodies
option.b: The excessive growth of algae due to nutrient enrichment
option.c: The presence of heavy metals in water
option.d: The formation of oil slicks on water surfaces

solution:
This question tests eutrophication, which simply means "over-feeding" of a water body.

  1. Rain washes fertilisers (rich in nitrates and phosphates) and sewage into a lake or river.
  2. Those nutrients act like plant food, so algae and water plants grow very fast and form a thick green blanket on the surface (an algal bloom).
  3. The algae soon die. Bacteria then break down the dead algae and use up the dissolved oxygen in the water.
  4. With little oxygen left, fish and other water animals suffocate and die, and the water turns green and smelly.

So eutrophication is the excessive growth of algae caused by nutrient enrichment — option (b).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Release of harmful chemicals is a general description of chemical pollution; eutrophication is specifically caused by extra plant nutrients.
  • (c) Heavy metals in water describes toxic metal pollution, which poisons living things but does not "feed" algae.
  • (d) Oil slicks are oil pollution, which smothers life at the surface; it is a different problem.

question: What is the name of the process by which ammonia is produced on an industrial scale?
solution:
This question tests the industrial manufacture of ammonia, called the Haber process.

N2(g)+3H2(g)⇌2NH3(g)
  1. Nitrogen is obtained from air and hydrogen from natural gas.
  2. The gases are passed over an iron catalyst at about 450 °C and about 200 atmospheres pressure.
  3. Ammonia formed is cooled and liquefied, and unreacted gases are recycled.
  4. The ammonia is used mainly to make fertilisers such as ammonium sulphate and urea.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Nitrogenation is not the name of any standard industrial process.
  • (b) Ammoniation means treating something with ammonia (for example making ammonium salts), not making ammonia itself.
  • (c) Nitrification is a natural soil process in which bacteria turn ammonia into nitrites and then nitrates.

question: Who proposed the planetary model of the atom with electrons orbiting the nucleus?
solution:
This question tests models of the atom and who proposed them.

  1. J.J. Thomson (1897) discovered the electron and pictured the atom as a ball of positive charge with electrons stuck in it — the "plum pudding" model.
  2. Ernest Rutherford (1911) fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but a few bounced back, showing that almost all the mass is packed in a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. He then pictured light electrons circling that nucleus the way planets circle the Sun.
  3. That picture is the planetary model, and it was Rutherford who proposed it.
  4. Niels Bohr (1913) later improved it by putting the electrons in fixed energy shells, and Schrödinger later still described electrons as spread-out clouds (orbitals).

Why the other options are wrong: Bohr refined the planetary idea with quantised shells, so he came after it; Schrödinger gave the modern wave (quantum) model; Thomson's model had no nucleus and no orbits at all.

question: Which of the following is an example of an endothermic reaction?

option.a: Combustion of propane (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></math><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>8</mn></msub></math>) to produce carbon dioxide (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>CO</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>) and water (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>H</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>O).
option.b: Burning of methane (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>CH</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></math>) in the presence of oxygen
option.c: Formation of table salt (NaCl) from sodium (Na) and chlorine (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>Cl</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math>).
option.d: Decomposition of calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) by heat

solution:
Idea tested: recognising endothermic and exothermic reactions.

In an endothermic reaction, heat is absorbed from the surroundings, so the surroundings become cooler. In an exothermic reaction, heat is released to the surroundings.

Burning propane and burning methane are combustions; they release a lot of heat, so they are exothermic. Forming sodium chloride from sodium and chlorine also releases energy overall because a strong ionic lattice is formed, so it is exothermic as well.

Heating limestone (calcium trioxocarbonate(IV)) breaks it down and needs a continuous supply of heat:

CaCO3(s)→CaO(s)+CO2(g)

This decomposition absorbs heat, so it is endothermic — option d.

Why the other options are wrong: combustion reactions release heat (exothermic), and the formation of NaCl releases energy overall (exothermic).

question: What happens to the value of the equilibrium constant (Kc) for a reaction if the reaction is reversed?

option.d: It becomes the reciprocal of the original value

solution:
This question tests what happens to the equilibrium constant Kc when a reaction is written backwards.

For a reaction at equilibrium:

A+B⇌C+D

the constant is products on top, reactants below:

Kc=[C][D][A][B]

Now reverse the equation (C + D ⇌ A + B). The things that were products are now reactants, so the fraction turns upside down:

Kc′=[A][B][C][D]=1Kc

So the new constant is the reciprocal of the old one.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Zero would mean the reaction does not happen at all, which is not true — the same reaction is simply running in the other direction.
  • (b) Negative is impossible: Kc is built from concentrations, and concentrations are always positive numbers.
  • (c) Remains the same is only true if you leave the equation as it is; turning the equation round inverts the fraction and therefore inverts the value.

question: What is the chemical structure of soap and detergent molecules?
solution:
This question tests the structure of soap and detergent molecules — they are "double-ended" molecules.

  1. The head is an ionic or very polar group (in soap, an ionised –COO−Na+ group). It is hydrophilic, meaning water-loving, so it dissolves readily in water.
  2. The tail is a long hydrocarbon chain of about 12 to 18 carbon atoms. It is hydrophobic, meaning water-hating, but it dissolves easily in oil and grease.
  3. In water, many of these molecules gather into a ball called a micelle, with the tails pointing inwards to trap grease and the heads pointing outwards into the water.
  4. The grease is lifted off the cloth and held in the water, then rinsed away — that is how washing works.

So the correct description is a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail — option (a).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (b) If both ends loved water, the molecule could not grab hold of grease.
  • (c) If both ends hated water, the molecule would not dissolve in water at all.
  • (d) These are the same words as (a) but in the wrong order — the head is the water-loving part, not the tail.

question: What does the solubility product constant (Ksp) represent?

option.a: The total mass of solute that can dissolve in a solvent
option.b: The product of the concentrations of the ions in a saturated solution
option.c: The rate at which a solute dissolves
option.d: The pH of a saturated solution

solution:
Idea tested: the meaning of the solubility product constant, Ksp.

For a sparingly soluble salt such as silver chloride, a tiny amount dissolves and sets up an equilibrium:

AgCl(s)⇌Ag+(aq)+Cl−(aq)

Ksp is the product of the concentrations of the ions in the saturated solution, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation:

Ksp=[Ag+][Cl−]

So Ksp represents the ion-concentration product in a saturated solution — option b. It can then be used to work out solubility, but the constant itself is that product.

Why the other options are wrong: Ksp is not a mass, not a rate of dissolving, and not a pH value.

question: Which trace gas in the atmosphere plays a significant role in the greenhouse effect?
solution:
This question tests the greenhouse effect and which gas is responsible for it.

  1. Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface.
  2. The warm surface gives out heat as invisible infrared radiation.
  3. Carbon dioxide molecules in the air absorb this infrared radiation and send part of it back towards the Earth.
  4. So heat is trapped near the surface and the planet warms, just like a blanket keeps you warm.

Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04% of the air — a trace — but it is the greenhouse gas released in the largest amounts when fuels are burnt.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Oxygen (about 21% of air) is a main gas, but it does not absorb infrared radiation well, so it does not trap heat.
  • (b) Argon is a noble gas with a full outer shell; it neither reacts nor absorbs infrared radiation.
  • (d) Nitrogen (about 78% of air) is the most abundant gas, but its molecules do not absorb infrared radiation — being plentiful is not the same as being a greenhouse gas.

question: Which of the following methods can be used to remove temporary hardness from water?
solution:
This question tests water hardness and how temporary hardness is removed.

Temporary hardness comes from dissolved calcium and magnesium hydrogencarbonates, Ca(HCO3)2 and Mg(HCO3)2. These dissolve in water as it passes through limestone.

  1. When the water is boiled, the hydrogencarbonates decompose.
  2. They form insoluble carbonates, which appear as a white solid (the "fur" inside a kettle):
Ca(HCO3)2→CaCO3(s)+H2O+CO2
  1. The solid is then filtered off, leaving soft water. That is why boiling removes temporary hardness.

Permanent hardness comes from calcium and magnesium sulphates and chlorides; boiling cannot remove it. It is removed with washing soda (sodium carbonate) or by ion exchange.

Why the other options are wrong: filtration removes suspended solid particles, not salts that are dissolved; sedimentation just lets heavy particles settle to the bottom; chlorination kills germs but does not remove hardness.

question: What is Faraday's constant?
solution:
This question tests Faraday's constant, the charge carried by one mole of electrons.

  1. One mole of electrons contains Avogadro's number of electrons: 6.022 × 1023.
  2. One electron carries a charge of 1.602 × 10−19 C.
  3. Multiply to get the charge of one mole of electrons:
6.022×1023×1.602×10−19=96485 C/mol

So Faraday's constant is about 96,485 C/mol. In electrolysis it links the quantity of electricity passed with the amount of substance deposited or liberated: one mole of electrons (96,485 C) deposits one mole of a singly charged ion, or half a mole of a doubly charged ion.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) 6.022 × 1023 mol−1 is Avogadro's constant — a count of particles, not a charge.
  • (b) 3.00 × 108 m/s is the speed of light.
  • (c) 9.81 m/s2 is the acceleration due to gravity.

question: A gas occupies a volume of 1.5 liters at a pressure of 2 atmospheres. If the pressure is increased to 4 atmospheres while the temperature remains constant, what will be the new volume of the gas?
solution:
This question tests Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional.

So the product of pressure and volume stays the same:

P1V1=P2V2
  1. Write down what we know: P1 = 2 atm, V1 = 1.5 L, P2 = 4 atm.
  2. Rearrange for the new volume:
V2=P1V1P2=2×1.54=0.75 L

Check by sense: the pressure doubled (2 atm to 4 atm), so the volume must halve (1.5 L to 0.75 L). ✔

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) 6 L would mean the volume grew as pressure grew, which is the opposite of Boyle's law.
  • (b) 1.5 L would mean the volume did not change at all despite doubling the pressure.
  • (d) 3 L would mean doubling the volume when the pressure doubled.

question: Stainless steel is an alloy made up of
solution:
This question tests the composition of alloys, using stainless steel as the example.

Stainless steel is mostly iron with a large amount of chromium (about 10–20%), and usually some nickel too.

  1. Iron gives the strength.
  2. Chromium reacts with oxygen in the air to form a very thin, invisible layer of chromium(III) oxide, Cr2O3, on the surface.
  3. This layer seals the metal off from air and water, so the iron underneath cannot rust. That is why stainless steel is used for cutlery, sinks and surgical instruments.

So the correct pair is iron and chromium — option (c).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Iron and zinc describes galvanised iron (zinc-coated iron); zinc is also the metal alloyed with copper to make brass.
  • (b) Copper and tin make bronze, which contains no iron at all.
  • (d) Iron and carbon is ordinary carbon steel (with a little carbon, up to about 2%), and it still rusts.

question: What is the state of matter in which particles are widely spaced and move freely with high kinetic energy?
solution:
This question tests the states of matter and how the particles behave in each one.

  1. Solid: fixed shape and fixed volume; particles are packed tightly and can only vibrate.
  2. Liquid: fixed volume but takes the shape of its container; particles are close but can slide past one another.
  3. Gas: no fixed shape or volume; particles are widely spaced, move quickly and randomly with high kinetic energy, and spread out to fill the whole container.

The description — widely spaced particles moving freely with high kinetic energy — is exactly the gas state, so the answer is (d).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Liquid particles are still close together and move only by sliding over each other.
  • (b) Solid particles are tightly packed and cannot move about freely.
  • (c) Plasma also has widely spaced particles, but it is a special case: a gas that has been ionised (electrons stripped off) at extremely high temperatures, as in stars, lightning and neon tubes. Ordinary widely spaced particles with high kinetic energy describe a gas.

question:
Identify the reducing agent in the following reaction:
Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu
solution:
This question tests redox: identifying the reducing agent in a displacement reaction.

Remember OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain.

  1. Zinc atoms lose electrons and become zinc ions:
Zn(s)→Zn2++2e−
  1. Copper ions gain those electrons and become copper metal:
Cu2++2e−→Cu(s)
  1. Zinc is oxidised (its oxidation number goes from 0 to +2); copper is reduced (+2 to 0).
  2. The substance that is oxidised is the reducing agent, because by handing over electrons it causes the other substance to be reduced. That is zinc, option (b).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Cu is the product of reduction — the result of being reduced, not the agent doing the reducing.
  • (c) ZnSO4 contains the Zn2+ that was formed, so it is the oxidation product, not an agent.
  • (d) CuSO4 is the substance that takes the electrons, so it is the oxidising agent.

question:
Balance the following redox reaction:
Fe2O3 + CO → Fe + CO2
solution:
This question tests balancing an equation by counting atoms on each side.

We start with: Fe2O3 + CO → Fe + CO2

  1. Iron: there are 2 Fe atoms in each Fe2O3, so we need 2Fe on the right.
  2. Carbon: each CO gives one CO2, so the number of CO and CO2 molecules must be the same. Call that number x.
  3. Oxygen: on the left we have 3 (from Fe2O3) + x (from CO). On the right we have 2x (two O in each CO2). So: 3+x=2x which gives x = 3.
  4. So we put 3 in front of CO and 3 in front of CO2:
Fe2O3+3CO→2Fe+3CO2

Check every atom: Fe 2 = 2; O 3 + 3 = 6 and 3 × 2 = 6; C 3 = 3. Balanced.

This is also a redox change: iron goes from +3 to 0 (reduced) and carbon in CO goes from +2 to +4 (oxidised).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Fe2O3 + CO → 2Fe + 2CO2: carbon is not balanced (1 on the left, 2 on the right).
  • (b) 2Fe2O3 + 3CO → 4Fe + 3CO2: oxygen is not balanced (9 on the left, 6 on the right).
  • (c) Fe2O3 + 2CO → 2Fe + 2CO2: oxygen is not balanced (5 on the left, 4 on the right).

question: What is the trend for ionization energy across a period in the periodic table?
solution:
This question tests the periodic trend in ionisation energy.

Ionisation energy is the energy needed to pull the outermost electron away from a neutral atom in the gas state.

  1. Going across a period from left to right, each new element has one more proton in the nucleus.
  2. The extra electrons go into the same shell, so they do not shield each other much.
  3. So the pull of the nucleus on the outer electrons gets stronger, the atom gets smaller, and the outer electron is held more tightly.
  4. More energy is therefore needed to remove it, so ionisation energy increases from left to right.

Example across Period 2: Li < Be < B < C < N < O < F < Ne (with small wiggles at B and O, but the general trend is upwards).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (b) Remains constant and (c) varies randomly are both false: the change is regular and predictable.
  • (d) Decreases from left to right is the reverse of the truth. Ionisation energy decreases down a group, because extra shells shield the outer electron and it sits further from the nucleus.

question: Which type of chemical combination involves the transfer of electrons from one atom to another, resulting in the formation of oppositely charged ions?
solution:
This question tests the types of chemical bonding, specifically bonding by transfer of electrons.

  1. A metal atom has few outer electrons. It loses them and becomes a positively charged ion (cation).
  2. A non-metal atom needs electrons. It gains them and becomes a negatively charged ion (anion).
  3. The two opposite charges attract each other very strongly, and billions of these ions pack together in a giant lattice held by electrostatic attraction. This is ionic bonding.
Na→Na++e− Cl+e−→Cl−

Sodium chloride is the classic example. Ionic compounds have high melting points, dissolve in water and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (b) Hydrogen bonding is a fairly weak attraction between molecules (when hydrogen is joined to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine). Nothing is transferred.
  • (c) Covalent bonding is the sharing of electron pairs between atoms, as in H2 or CH4.
  • (d) Metallic bonding is positive metal ions held together by a "sea" of delocalised electrons — the electrons are shared by all the atoms, not transferred to one atom.

question: Which of the following alkanes has a straight-chain structure?
solution:
This question tests the shapes of alkane chains — straight-chain versus branched.

A straight chain means every carbon is joined in one continuous line, with no side branches. Alkanes obey the general formula:

CnH2n+2
  1. Pentane, C5H12: five carbons in one line, CH3–CH2–CH2–CH2–CH3. No branches. Straight chain. ✔
  2. Check the formula with n = 5: 2(5) + 2 = 12, so C5H12 is a true alkane.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Cyclopentane, C5H10: the carbons form a closed ring, not a straight line, and its formula is CnH2n — it is a cycloalkane, not a straight-chain alkane.
  • (b) Isobutane, C4H10: a branched alkane, with three CH3 groups on one central carbon.
  • (c) 2-methylpropane, C4H10: this is just the systematic name for the same branched compound as (b), so it is also branched.

question: What is the product of the electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride (NaCl) using inert electrodes?

option.a: Hydrogen gas at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode
option.b: Hydrogen gas at the cathode and oxygen gas at the anode
option.c: Sodium metal at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode
option.d: Sodium metal at the cathode and oxygen gas at the anode

solution:
Idea tested: the products of the electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride (brine) using inert electrodes.

In brine the important ions are Na+, H+, Cl− and OH−. At the cathode, H+ ions are easier to reduce than Na+ ions, so hydrogen gas is produced:

2H++2e−→H2

At the anode, Cl− ions lose electrons in preference to OH− ions in concentrated brine, so chlorine gas is produced:

2Cl−→Cl2+2e−

So the products are hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode — option a.

Why the other options are wrong: sodium metal is not produced from aqueous NaCl (that needs molten NaCl), and oxygen is not the main anode product for concentrated brine.

question: When an acidic solution is diluted, what happens to its pH?

option.a: It depends on the specific acid

solution:
This question tests pH and what happens when we add water to an acid.

pH is a measure of how concentrated the hydrogen ions are:

pH=−log[H+]

More H+ means a smaller pH (more acidic). Diluting an acid lowers its H+ concentration, so the pH increases.

  1. Start with 10 cm3 of 0.01 mol/dm3 HCl: [H+]=0.01=10−2, so pH = 2.
  2. Add water to make the volume 100 cm3 — that is 10 times more dilute, so the concentration drops 10 times: [H+]=10−3, so pH = 3.
  3. The pH went up from 2 to 3, so the acid became less acidic (closer to neutral).

Adding water can never turn the acid into a base: the pH rises towards 7 but stays below 7 at room temperature.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (b) Decreases would mean the solution became more acidic after adding water, which is the opposite of what happens.
  • (c) Remains the same is false because the H+ ions are now spread through a bigger volume.
  • (a) Depends on the specific acid is false for the direction of the change: any acid, strong or weak, has a lower H+ concentration after dilution, so its pH always rises.

question: Which of the following factors does NOT affect the rate of a chemical reaction?
solution:
This question tests the factors that change the rate of a reaction.

For a reaction to happen, particles must collide, and they must collide with enough energy (the activation energy) to break the bonds that need breaking.

  1. Concentration: more particles in the same space means more collisions per second, so the reaction is faster.
  2. Temperature: hotter particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent and more energetic — faster.
  3. Catalyst: it lowers the activation energy, so a bigger fraction of collisions succeed — faster.
  4. Surface area: powder reacts faster than a big lump because more surface is exposed to the other reactant.

The molecular weight of the products tells you nothing about how quickly the reactants collide. The products do not even exist at the start of the reaction, so they cannot influence its speed. That is why (c) is the factor that does not affect the rate.

Why the other options are wrong: (a), (b) and (d) are all standard factors that speed up or slow down a reaction, as explained above.

question: Which organic compound is responsible for the characteristic aroma of fruits?
solution:
This question tests the smell of the different organic families, and specifically the esters.

Esters are made when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol — a reaction called esterification:

CH3COOH+C2H5OH→CH3COOC2H5+H2O

Many esters have sweet, fruity smells — for example, the flavours of banana, pineapple and apple. That is why esters are used in perfumes, sweets and fruit flavourings.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Alkanes have little or no smell of their own; petrol smells are mostly other compounds.
  • (b) Alkynes are hydrocarbons with triple bonds; they are not the fruity aroma compounds.
  • (d) Amines very often smell like fish or ammonia, which is not a fruit aroma.

question: What is the molar mass of water (H2O)?
solution:
This question tests how to work out a molar mass from the formula.

The molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole (g/mol). You get it by adding up the relative atomic masses of all the atoms in the formula.

Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

M=2×1+1×16=18 g/mol
  1. Hydrogen: 2 atoms × 1 g/mol = 2 g/mol
  2. Oxygen: 1 atom × 16 g/mol = 16 g/mol
  3. Total: 2 + 16 = 18 g/mol

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (b) 22 g/mol is close to the molar volume of a gas at s.t.p. (22.4 dm3), which is a volume, not a mass.
  • (c) 16 g/mol is the mass of the oxygen atom alone — it leaves out the two hydrogens.
  • (d) 12 g/mol is the relative atomic mass of carbon, which is not in water at all.

question: What is the chemical formula of rust, which is formed on the surface of iron in the presence of oxygen and moisture?
solution:
This question tests rusting, which is the corrosion of iron, and the formula of rust.

Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, written Fe2O3·xH2O. In its simple form it is Fe2O3, which is the keyed answer. It is the reddish-brown flaky coating you see on old iron.

  1. Rusting needs both oxygen and water; salt or acid makes it happen faster.
  2. Iron atoms lose electrons and are oxidised to Fe3+, while oxygen is reduced.
  3. Overall: 4Fe+3O2+xH2O→2Fe2O3·xH2O
  4. Because rust flakes off, fresh iron is exposed and the metal keeps wasting away. Painting, oiling or galvanising (coating with zinc) keeps out air and water and prevents rust.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Fe3O4 is magnetite, a different iron oxide formed at high temperature (for example when iron burns in oxygen); it is not ordinary rust.
  • (b) FeO is iron(II) oxide, a black solid, not the reddish-brown rust.
  • (c) Fe(OH)3 is iron(III) hydroxide, a brown gelatinous solid that can form as an intermediate, but rust itself is the hydrated oxide.

question: How many pi (π) bonds are there in an alkene with six carbon atoms?
solution:
This question tests sigma and pi bonds in alkenes.

  • A single bond is one sigma (σ) bond.
  • A double bond is one sigma bond plus one pi (π) bond.
  • A triple bond is one sigma bond plus two pi bonds.

An alkene has the general formula CnH2n and contains one carbon-to-carbon double bond. For six carbon atoms the alkene is hexene, C6H12.

C6H12,one C=C=1σ+1π

So there is exactly 1 pi bond — option (a).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (b) 6 would mean one pi bond for every carbon atom, but a pi bond needs a double bond between two carbons.
  • (c) 5 is the number of carbon-to-carbon single bonds in a six-carbon chain (C–C), not the number of pi bonds.
  • (d) 3 would require three double bonds (a triene, C6H8), which is no longer a simple alkene.

question: What is the principal ore of iron, from which iron is extracted?
solution:
This question tests ores of iron and how iron is extracted.

The principal ore of iron is haematite, iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3. It contains about 70% iron by mass, which is why it is the ore most used by industry.

  1. Haematite is roasted and then fed into the blast furnace with coke and limestone.
  2. The coke burns to carbon monoxide, which reduces the iron oxide:
Fe2O3+3CO→2Fe+3CO2
  1. Limestone removes sandy impurities as slag, and molten iron collects at the bottom of the furnace.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Calcite is calcium carbonate, CaCO3 — the limestone added to the furnace to remove impurities, not a source of iron.
  • (b) Bauxite is the ore of aluminium (hydrated Al2O3).
  • (c) Magnetite, Fe3O4, is also an iron ore, but haematite is the principal one.

question: Which group does calcium belong to in the periodic table?
solution:
This question tests the groups of the periodic table.

Calcium is in Group 2, the second column of the periodic table. Its atoms have two electrons in their outer shell, so calcium loses both to form Ca2+:

Ca→Ca2++2e−

Group 2 metals are called the alkaline earth metals: beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium. Their oxides and hydroxides are alkaline, which is where the name comes from. Calcium compounds include limestone (CaCO3), quicklime (CaO) and slaked lime (Ca(OH)2).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (b) Halogens are Group 17 (F, Cl, Br, I) — non-metals that gain one electron.
  • (c) Alkali metals are Group 1 (Li, Na, K) — they have only one outer electron and are more reactive than calcium.
  • (d) Noble gases are Group 18 (He, Ne, Ar) — unreactive gases with full outer shells.

question: Which of the following is the main constituent of natural gas?
solution:
Idea tested: the composition of natural gas.

Natural gas is mainly methane, CH4. It usually contains about 70–90% methane, with small amounts of ethane, propane and butane.

Pentane and heptane are hydrocarbons found in crude oil and petrol fractions, not the main gas in natural gas. Ethanol is an alcohol and is not a natural-gas constituent.

Therefore the answer is methane — option d.

question: What is the main source of carbon monoxide (CO) in urban areas?
solution:
This question tests air pollution by carbon monoxide and where it comes from.

Carbon monoxide (CO) forms when a carbon-containing fuel burns with too little oxygen — incomplete combustion:

2C+O2→2CO
  1. In towns and cities the commonest fuel burners are cars, buses, motorcycles and generators using petrol and diesel.
  2. Their engines often do not have enough oxygen for complete burning, so the exhaust contains CO.
  3. Idling traffic and traffic jams make it worse — which is why CO levels are highest along busy roads.

So vehicle emissions are the main urban source, option (b).

Why CO is dangerous: it is colourless and odourless, and it sticks to haemoglobin in the blood about 200 times more strongly than oxygen does, so the blood cannot carry enough oxygen. That is why car exhaust fumes can kill in a closed garage.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) Volcanic eruptions release some CO, but they are natural and not a city source.
  • (c) Forest fires do produce CO, but they are occasional and usually far from city centres.
  • (d) Industrial processes also give off CO, but in urban areas vehicles are the biggest single source.

question: What is the empirical formula of a compound containing 40.00% carbon, 6.67% hydrogen, and 53.33% oxygen by mass?
solution:
This question tests how to find an empirical formula from percentage composition.

The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms in a compound.

  1. Imagine 100 g of the compound. Then the masses are: 40.00 g C, 6.67 g H and 53.33 g O.
  2. Convert each mass to moles by dividing by the relative atomic mass:
C:40.0012=3.33 mol H:6.671=6.67 mol O:53.3316=3.33 mol
  1. Divide every answer by the smallest (3.33):
C:3.333.33=1,H:6.673.33=2,O:3.333.33=1
  1. So the simplest ratio is C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1, giving CH2O.

Why the other options are wrong: C4H8O4, C2H4O2 and C3H6O3 all have the same ratio of 1 : 2 : 1, so they are all multiples of the empirical formula — these would be molecular formulae. The empirical formula must be the simplest one, CH2O (the empirical formula of methanoic acid, formaldehyde and glucose, C6H12O6).

question: Which separation technique is used to separate different pigments in a mixture based on their affinity for a stationary phase and a mobile phase?
solution:
This question tests chromatography, a separation technique that uses two phases.

  1. The stationary phase does not move — for example the water held in the fibres of chromatography paper, or a layer of silica on a plate.
  2. The mobile phase moves — a solvent that creeps up the paper or is pushed through the column.
  3. Each component of the mixture moves between the two phases. A component that dissolves well in the mobile phase travels far; one that sticks strongly to the stationary phase travels only a short way.
  4. Because different pigments have different affinities, they travel different distances and separate into coloured spots or bands.

This is exactly the description in the question, so the answer is chromatography. It is used to separate the dyes in ink, the colourings in food, and to test whether a substance is pure.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (b) Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper.
  • (c) Decantation means gently pouring a liquid off a settled solid.
  • (d) Distillation separates liquids with different boiling points by boiling and condensing them.

question: What is the common name for ethanoic acid?
solution:
This question tests the common names of carboxylic acids.

Ethanoic acid has the formula CH3COOH. Its common name is acetic acid, and it is the acid that gives vinegar its sour taste (vinegar is roughly 5% ethanoic acid in water).

CH3COOH⇌CH3COO−+H+

It is a weak acid, so it only partly ionises in water. It is used in vinegar, as a preservative, and to make esters (which give fruit flavours).

Why the other options are wrong:
