Fructose is a simple sugar (a monosaccharide) found in fruits and honey. Its molecular formula is C6H12O6.

Now compare the two forms:

C6H12O6=C6(H2O)6

because 6 × H2O gives H12O6. So x = 6 and y = 6, meaning fructose has six carbon atoms.

Why the other options are wrong: x = 3 would be a three-carbon sugar such as glyceraldehyde, C3H6O3. x = 5 (a pentose) is the sugar found in nucleic acids, such as ribose, C5H10O5. x = 12 belongs to a twelve-carbon sugar such as sucrose, C12H22O11, which is made of two six-carbon sugars joined together. Fructose itself is a six-carbon sugar.

The correct option is d.

question: If a gold bar and a silver bar are tied together firmly and left for years, some of the gold particles will be found in the silver bar due to
solution:
This question tests diffusion in solids.

All particles — atoms, ions and molecules — are in constant random motion, and they move from where they are crowded towards where they are less crowded until they are evenly spread. That process is diffusion.

In a solid the particles are packed tightly, so movement is very slow, but it does happen over years. When a gold bar and a silver bar are pressed firmly together, gold atoms slowly wander into the silver lattice and silver atoms wander into the gold. This has been shown in experiments where thin plates of different metals were clamped together and, after a long time, each metal was found inside the other. It is also the reason a gold ring left on a silver chain for years can leave a mark.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Brownian movement is the random jiggling of tiny visible particles (such as smoke or pollen grains) suspended in a gas or liquid, caused by collisions with molecules. It does not describe atoms swapping places inside a solid metal.
  • displacement is a chemical reaction in which a more reactive element pushes a less reactive one out of its compound, for example zinc displacing copper from copper(II) sulphate. No compound is involved here.
  • osmosis is the movement of solvent molecules through a semi-permeable membrane from a dilute to a concentrated solution. There is no membrane and no solvent in two solid metal bars.

The correct option is b.

question: A metal that can be found in the free state in nature is
solution:
Idea tested: the reactivity series and which metals occur uncombined (native) in nature.

Metals high in the reactivity series, such as sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium and aluminium, react readily with oxygen and water. They are therefore found combined in compounds, never as the free metal.

Silver is a noble metal. It is very unreactive and does not combine readily with oxygen or water, so it can be found in the earth's crust in the free (native) state — option a. Gold and platinum behave similarly.

Why the other options are wrong: zinc occurs as zinc blende (ZnS) or calamine (ZnCO3); iron occurs as haematite (Fe2O3) and magnetite (Fe3O4); sodium is too reactive to exist free in nature.

question: Which of the following has the highest boiling point?
solution:
This question tests how hydrogen bonding and chain length affect boiling point.

Boiling point rises when the forces between molecules are stronger and when the molecules are bigger (more electrons means stronger van der Waals forces).

Look at the four substances:

  • a: ethanol, CH3CH2OH — can hydrogen bond, small molecule, b.p. about 78 °C.
  • d: propan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2OH — can hydrogen bond and has one extra CH2 group, b.p. about 97 °C.
  • b: 1-chloropropane, CH3CH2CH2Cl — no O–H, so no hydrogen bonding; only dipole–dipole forces, b.p. about 46 °C.
  • c: hexane, C6H14 — non-polar, only van der Waals forces, b.p. about 69 °C.

Hydrogen bonding lifts the alcohols well above the other two. Between ethanol and propanol, the longer chain of propanol gives stronger van der Waals forces on top of the hydrogen bonds, so propanol boils higher:

46<69<78<97

So propan-1-ol has the highest boiling point.

Why the other options are wrong: hexane has the most carbon atoms, but without hydrogen bonding its boiling point is still below both alcohols. 1-Chloropropane has a polar bond but no O–H, so its dipole attractions are much weaker than hydrogen bonds. Ethanol hydrogen bonds too, but its shorter chain makes it boil 19 °C lower than propanol.

The correct option is d.

question: From the graph, it can be inferred that

option.a: the solubility of X and Y is the same at all temperature
option.b: the solubility of X, Y and Z is temperature dependent
option.c: solubility of Z increases as temperature increases
option.d: solubility of Y increases steadily as temperature increases

solution:
This question tests reading a solubility–temperature graph.

The graph plots solubility (g per 100 g of water) against temperature. Each line tells the story of one substance.

  • Y is a straight line that starts at about 20 g at 0 °C and climbs steadily to about 70 g at 60 °C. The steady upward slope means the solubility of Y increases steadily as the temperature rises.
  • X is a curve. It starts lower than Y but rises more steeply and crosses Y at roughly 58 °C, so X is less soluble than Y when cold but more soluble when hot.
  • Z is a horizontal line at about 45 g. A flat line means the solubility of Z hardly changes with temperature at all.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (a) X and Y are only equal at the single temperature where the lines cross; at every other temperature they are different.
  • (b) this is false for the set as a whole, because Z’s solubility is constant, so it is not temperature dependent.
  • (c) Z’s line is flat, so its solubility stays the same as temperature rises; it does not increase.

The statement that matches the graph is that the solubility of Y increases steadily with temperature, so the correct option is d.

question: The gas that is commonly used to demonstrate the fountain experiment is
solution:
This question tests the fountain experiment and the solubility of gases.

In the fountain experiment, a round-bottomed flask is filled with a gas that dissolves very readily in water. A little water is squirted in (often with a dropper), and the gas at once dissolves in it. This leaves far fewer gas particles in the flask, so the pressure inside drops and becomes much lower than the pressure of the air outside.

The outside air then pushes the water up the tube and into the flask, making a fountain. If an indicator is in the water, the colour change shows the solution formed.

Hydrogen chloride is ideal for this because it is extremely soluble: about 450 volumes of HCl gas dissolve in one volume of water. The tiny amount of water squirted in dissolves a huge amount of gas, creating the sudden low pressure needed for a good fountain, and the solution formed is hydrochloric acid.

Why the other options are wrong: hydrogen sulphide is only slightly soluble and is also a poisonous gas with a bad smell, so it gives no dramatic fountain. Dinitrogen(I) oxide (N2O) and nitrogen(II) oxide (NO) are almost insoluble in water, so the pressure inside the flask would hardly fall and no fountain would form.

The correct option is a.

question: Which of the following statements is false about hard water?

option.a: Helps animals to build strong teeth
option.b: Cannot be supplied in pipes made of leads
option.d: Helps animals to build strong bones.

solution:
This question asks which statement about hard water is false.

Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions (as hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV), sulphate or chloride). These ions make it hard for soap to lather, because they form an insoluble scum.

Now test each statement:

  • (a) Helps animals build strong teeth — true. Calcium and magnesium are needed for teeth.
  • (d) Helps animals build strong bones — true, for the same reason; calcium is the main mineral in bone.
  • (c) Tastes better than soft water — generally accepted as true: the dissolved minerals give hard water a fuller taste, and many people prefer it.
  • (b) Cannot be supplied in pipes made of lead — this is the false statement. Hard water can be carried in lead pipes. When hard water flows through a lead pipe, the dissolved hydrogen carbonate reacts with the lead to deposit a thin, insoluble coating of lead carbonate and calcium carbonate scale on the inside of the pipe. That coating seals the lead off from the water, so very little lead dissolves into it.

Soft water is the dangerous one: it has no such scale-forming minerals and is slightly acidic, so it slowly dissolves lead and can cause lead poisoning.

Since the question asks for the false statement, the correct option is b.

question:
The empirical mass of C6H12O6 is 

[H =1, C = 12, O = 16]
solution:
This question tests the difference between empirical formula and molecular formula.

The molecular formula gives the actual number of each kind of atom in a molecule. The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of those atoms.

Step 1: find the simplest ratio. For C6H12O6 all three numbers can be divided by 6:

C6H12O6÷6=CH2O

So the empirical formula is CH2O.

Step 2: calculate the empirical mass. Using C = 12, H = 1, O = 16:

12+(2×1)+16=30

So the empirical mass is 30.

As a check, the molecular mass of C6H12O6 is 6 × 30 = 180, which is the mass of glucose and fructose.

Why the other options are wrong: 180 is the molecular mass, not the empirical mass. 90 is half of 180 and comes from dividing the formula only partly (a C3H6O3 unit), which is still not the simplest ratio. 45 is half of 90, so it is not obtained from CH2O at all.

The correct option is d.

question: The nitrogenous compound in dead materials in the soil is converted to
solution:
This question tests the first stage of the nitrogen cycle in the soil, called ammonification.

Dead plants, animals, manure and other waste contain nitrogen locked up in proteins and other complex organic compounds. Certain bacteria and fungi (the decomposers) break these compounds down and release the nitrogen as ammonia, NH3:

organic nitrogen compounds→NH3

This is why a heap of rotting material smells of ammonia. The ammonia partly dissolves in soil water, taking up a hydrogen ion to form ammonium ions, NH4+, which plants can absorb.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • trioxonitrate(V), NO3−, is formed in the next stage, nitrification, when nitrifying bacteria such as Nitrobacter oxidise nitrite to nitrate. It is not the direct product of decay.
  • ammonium salts come about only after the ammonia has dissolved and reacted with acids in the soil; the compound released straight from the dead material is ammonia itself.
  • dioxonitrate(III), NO2−, is the intermediate of nitrification, made by Nitrosomonas from ammonia. It comes later, not first.

The correct option is a.

question:
CH3C ≡ CCH(CH3)2

The IUPAC nomenclature of the compound above is
solution:
This question tests IUPAC naming of an alkyne.

The structure is CH3–C≡C–CH(CH3)–CH3. Follow the rules in order.

Step 1: find the longest chain that contains the triple bond. Going straight through the triple bond gives five carbons: C–C≡C–C–C. So the parent name is based on pent, with the ending -yne for the triple bond.

Step 2: number the chain so the triple bond gets the lowest number. Numbering from the left end, the triple bond starts at carbon 2:

C1−C2≡C3−C4−C5

Numbering from the other end would put the triple bond at carbon 3, which is higher, so we keep 2. The parent is pent-2-yne.

Step 3: name the branch. A –CH3 group is attached to carbon 4, so it is a 4-methyl group.

Step 4: put the parts together. 4-methyl + pent-2-yne = 4-methylpent-2-yne.

Why the other options are wrong: "3-ethylbut-2-yne" and "2-ethylbut-2-yne" use a butane chain of only four carbons, which would leave a methyl group hanging off a chain-end carbon; the longest chain rule forbids that, so but-2-yne is the wrong parent. "2-methylpent-2-yne" puts the methyl on carbon 2, but carbon 2 already carries the triple bond and has no room for a branch; in this molecule the branch is on carbon 4.

The correct option is b.

question: In the laboratory preparation of oxygen using potassium trioxochlorate(V), tetraoxomanganate (VII), usually not recommended in modern laboratory because

option.a: it forms explosive mixture with carbonaceous materials

solution:
This question tests the laboratory preparation of oxygen from potassium trioxochlorate(V) (potassium chlorate, KClO3).

Oxygen can be made by heating potassium chlorate with a little manganese(IV) oxide as a catalyst:

2KClO3→2KCl+3O2

The trouble is that potassium chlorate is a very strong oxidising agent. On its own it does not explode simply from being heated gently — but if it touches anything that can burn easily (carbonaceous material such as dust, cork, rubber tubing, filter paper or grease), the mixture becomes extremely sensitive and can explode violently when warmed or rubbed. Laboratories have therefore stopped using this method and prefer safer ones, such as dropping hydrogen peroxide onto manganese(IV) oxide:

2H2O2→2H2O+O2

Why the other options are wrong: the salt is not explosive by itself when handled cleanly (option b), so that is an overstatement. It does not react with the manganese(IV) oxide catalyst (option c) — the catalyst is unchanged and only speeds up decomposition. "It is hazardous" (option d) is true in a vague way, but it does not give the specific reason, which is the dangerous explosive mixture formed with carbonaceous material.

The correct option is a.

question: Rust on the surface of a metal sheet contains
solution:
This question tests what rust is made of.

Rust is the reddish-brown coat that forms on iron when iron meets oxygen and water (moisture) at the same time.

Iron loses electrons and changes to iron(III) oxide, and that oxide then holds some water molecules:

4Fe+3O2+xH2O→2Fe2O3·xH2O

So rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, which is option B.

  • Iron(III) trioxocarbonate(IV) is a carbonate salt, Fe2(CO3)3. It is not rust.
  • Hydrated iron(II) oxide would contain iron with a charge of +2, but in rust the iron is in the +3 state.
  • Iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)3, is an hydroxide, while rust is an oxide.

question: The organic compounds that give positive iodoform test is
solution:
This question tests the iodoform test, which is a test for the group CH3CO– or the group CH3CH(OH)–.

When such a group is warmed with iodine and sodium hydroxide, a yellow precipitate of iodoform (CHI3) is formed.

Propan-2-ol is CH3–CH(OH)–CH3. The carbon that carries the –OH group is joined to a CH3 group, so the test works in two steps:

  1. The iodine and alkali first oxidise the alcohol to propanone (acetone): CH3CH(OH)CH3+[O]→CH3COCH3+H2O
  2. Propanone now has the CH3CO– group, so it reacts with iodine: CH3COCH3+3I2+4NaOH→CHI3+CH3COONa+3NaI+3H2O

The yellow solid shows a positive result, so option A is correct.

  • Butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid. It has no CH3CO– group, so it gives no iodoform.
  • Methanol would only be oxidised to methanal, HCHO, which has no CH3 group.
  • Propan-1-ol would be oxidised to propanal, CH3CH2CHO, which has no CH3CO– group either.

question: The bleaching action of chlorine is by
solution:
This question tests how chlorine bleaches coloured materials.

Dry chlorine does not bleach. It needs moisture, because chlorine must first react with water:

  1. Chlorine reacts with water to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid: Cl2+H2O→HCl+HClO
  2. Hypochlorous acid is unstable. It breaks down (decomposes) and gives off a very reactive oxygen atom, called nascent oxygen: HClO→HCl+[O]
  3. This nascent oxygen attacks the coloured dye and oxidises it to a colourless compound. That is why the colour disappears.

The colour is destroyed when the HClO decomposes, so among the options given, option A is the correct one.

  • Reduction means gaining electrons. The dye is not bleached by gaining electrons; it is oxidised.
  • Displacement means a more reactive element pushing a less reactive element out of its compound. That is not what happens here.
  • Hydrolysis means splitting a compound with water. Chlorine does react with water, but the bleaching itself is done by the product of the decomposition of HClO.

question: The bond type between copper(ii) ion and water molecule is
solution:
This question tests the dative (coordinate) covalent bond in complex ions.

When copper(II) ions dissolve in water, each ion attracts water molecules and a complex ion is formed:

Cu2++6H2O→[Cu(H2O)6]2+

Look at the oxygen atom in a water molecule. It has two lone pairs of electrons that it is not using for bonding.

The copper(II) ion has empty orbitals that can accept a pair of electrons. So the oxygen atom donates one whole lone pair into an empty orbital of the copper ion.

A bond in which both shared electrons come from only one atom is called a dative bond (also called a coordinate or coordinate covalent bond). Option A is correct.

  • Covalent means the two atoms each contribute one electron to the shared pair. Here only oxygen donates.
  • Ionic means electrons are completely transferred to form separate ions.
  • Metallic means positive metal ions held in a sea of delocalised electrons, which is how copper metal is held together, not how Cu2+ joins water.

question:
C2H4  + xO2 → yCO2 + zH2O

In the equation above, the values of x,y and z respectively are
solution:
This question tests balancing a combustion equation by counting atoms.

The unbalanced equation is:

C2H4+xO2→yCO2+zH2O

Step 1: balance carbon. There are 2 carbon atoms on the left, so there must be 2 on the right:

2=y⇒y=2

Step 2: balance hydrogen. There are 4 hydrogen atoms on the left and 2 in each water molecule on the right:

4=2z⇒z=2

Step 3: balance oxygen. On the right we now have 2(2) oxygen atoms in the CO2 plus 2 in the water:

2x=2y+z=2(2)+2=6 x=3

So x = 3, y = 2 and z = 2, which is option A:

C2H4+3O2→2CO2+2H2O
  • 3, 2 and 1 would leave 4 oxygen atoms on the right but 6 on the left.
  • 2, 1 and 2 gives only 1 CO2, so carbon is not balanced.
  • 2, 3 and 1 does not balance oxygen or hydrogen.

question:
3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) ⇌  Fe3O4(s)  + 4H2(g)

In the equation above, the equilibrium constant, kc is
solution:
This question tests how to write an equilibrium constant Kc.

The rule is simple: put the products on top and the reactants below, each raised to the power of its balancing number. But substances that are pure solids or pure liquids are left out, because their concentration does not change.

The equation is:

3Fe(s)+4H2O(g)⇌Fe3O4(s)+4H2(g)
  • Fe(s) is a solid, so it is dropped.
  • Fe3O4(s) is a solid, so it is dropped too.
  • H2(g) is a gas and there are 4 of them, so the top is [H2]4.
  • H2O(g) is a gas and there are 4 of them, so the bottom is [H2O]4.

Therefore:

Kc=[H2]4[H2O]4

This is option D.

  • Option A puts the solids into the expression and uses no powers, which is wrong.
  • Option B leaves out the water and the hydrogen completely.
  • Option C includes the solids Fe and Fe3O4, which must not appear.

question:
N2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2NO(g)  ΔH = - 220kJ/mol

In the reaction above, the entropy change at 1000C is
solution:
This question tests the entropy change of the surroundings when a reaction gives out heat.

The reaction is exothermic: ΔH = –220 kJ/mol. Heat leaves the system and warms the surroundings, so the surroundings become more disordered and their entropy goes up.

The formula is:

ΔSsurr=−ΔHT

Step 1: change the temperature to kelvin. The temperature given is 100 °C (the small 0 after the number is the degree sign), so:

T=100+273=373K

Step 2: put in the values. The minus sign in the formula cancels the minus sign of ΔH:

ΔSsurr=−−220373=+0.59kJ/K/mol

So the entropy change is +0.59 kJ/K/mol, option A. The plus sign makes sense because the surroundings gain heat and become more disordered.

  • –0.59 is the answer you get if you forget that a negative ΔH makes the surroundings' entropy positive.
  • –1.69 and +1.69 do not come from dividing by 373 K; they use a wrong temperature, so they are wrong.

question: The mass in grams of K2SO4 in 100cm3 of 0.15 moldm−3 is [K = 39, S = 32, O = 16]
solution:
This question tests how to find the mass of a substance in a solution when its concentration and volume are given.

Step 1: find the molar mass of K2SO4 using K = 39, S = 32, O = 16.

M=(2×39)+32+(4×16)=78+32+64=174g/mol

Step 2: find the number of moles. 100 cm3 is the same as 0.1 dm3:

n=C×V=0.15×1001000=0.15×0.1=0.015mol

Step 3: change moles to mass:

mass=n×M=0.015×174=2.61g

The mass is 2.61 g, option C.

  • 15 and 1.5 come from multiplying the concentration by the volume in cm3 and forgetting the molar mass.
  • 26.1 g would be the mass in a full 1000 cm3 (1 dm3), not in 100 cm3.

question: A condition necessary for the rusting of iron to occur is
solution:
This question tests the conditions that iron needs before it can rust.

Rusting is the reaction of iron with oxygen and water. Both must be present at the same time, because iron cannot rust in perfectly dry air or in water that contains no dissolved oxygen.

Air is a mixture of gases and about one-fifth of it is oxygen, so air supplies the oxygen that iron needs:

4Fe+3O2+2H2O→2Fe2O3·H2O

So air is a necessary condition, and option C is correct.

  • Smoke is a mixture of tiny solid particles and gases from burning. It is not needed for rusting.
  • Smog is smoky fog found in polluted cities. It can speed up corrosion, but it is not a necessary condition.
  • Sand is silicon(IV) oxide and other minerals. It plays no part in rusting.

question: The process by which sea water is turned into drinking water is
solution:
Idea tested: methods of treating water, especially removing dissolved salts from sea water.

Sea water contains a lot of dissolved salts, mainly sodium chloride. Drinking water must be low in salt. The process that removes these dissolved salts is called desalination.

Common desalination methods include reverse osmosis (pushing water through a membrane that traps the salt ions) and distillation (evaporating the water and condensing the pure vapour).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • Chlorination adds chlorine to kill germs; it does not remove dissolved salt.
  • Filtration removes solid particles suspended in water, not salts that are dissolved.
  • Coagulation clumps tiny suspended particles so they can settle or be filtered out; it does not remove dissolved salts.

So the correct answer is desalination — option c.

question: The waste that is biodegradable is
solution:
This question tests the meaning of biodegradable waste.

Biodegradable means the waste can be broken down by living things such as bacteria and fungi into simple harmless substances. Such waste rots away naturally.

Sewage is mostly human waste, food remains and other organic matter. Microorganisms feed on it and decompose it, so sewage is biodegradable. Option D is correct.

  • Plastics are long-chain polymers that bacteria cannot digest, so they stay in the environment for many years. They are non-biodegradable.
  • Metal scraps are elements; they can corrode slowly, but they are not decomposed by microorganisms.
  • Lead compounds are inorganic and poisonous; they are not broken down by living organisms.

This is why sewage is treated in ponds and tanks where bacteria are allowed to feed on it, while plastics and metals must be recycled.

question: The IUPAC nomenclature of the compound with the formula (CH3)2CHCH(CH3)2 is
solution:
This question tests how to name a branched alkane using IUPAC rules.

This compound is (CH3)2CHCH(CH3)2. Writing every carbon out makes the skeleton clear:

CH3–CH(CH3)–CH(CH3)–CH3

Step 1: find the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms. The longest chain has 4 carbon atoms, so the parent name is butane.

Step 2: number the chain from the end that gives the branches the smallest numbers. Both ends give 2 and 3, so the branches sit on carbon 2 and carbon 3.

Step 3: name the branches. Each branch is a one-carbon group, that is a methyl group, and there are two of them, so we write “dimethyl”.

Putting it together:

2,3-dimethylbutane

That is option C.

  • 2-methylpentane would have a 5-carbon chain with only one methyl branch, so it is a different compound.
  • 1,2,3,4-tetramethylethane is not a proper name: an ethane chain has only two carbons and cannot carry four methyl groups.
  • 1,2,3,4-tetramethylbutane would contain 8 carbon atoms, but this compound has only 6.

question: The gas liberated when an aqueous solution of (NH4)2CO3 is warmed with NaOHaq is
solution:
This question tests the reaction between an ammonium salt and an alkali when heated.

Ammonium carbonate contains the ammonium ion, NH4+. When it is warmed with sodium hydroxide solution, the hydroxide takes the hydrogen from the ammonium ion and ammonia gas is set free:

(NH4)2CO3+2NaOH→Na2CO3+2NH3+2H2O

The gas formed is ammonia, NH3, so option A is correct.

You can recognise ammonia easily: it has a sharp, choking smell, it turns damp red litmus paper blue, and it turns damp universal indicator paper green or blue.

  • H2 is given off when a reactive metal reacts with an acid, not here.
  • N2 is not produced when an ammonium salt is warmed with alkali.
  • CO2 is given off when a carbonate reacts with an acid. Warming with an alkali does not free the carbon dioxide as a gas; the carbonate simply stays as sodium carbonate.

question: Solid particles dispersed in liquid medium are called
solution:
This question tests the names of the different kinds of mixture called colloids.

A colloid is a mixture in which tiny particles of one substance are spread through another substance. The name we use depends on the state of the particles and the state of the medium they are spread in.

  • Sol: solid particles spread in a liquid, such as paint, ink or muddy water.
  • Emulsion: liquid droplets spread in a liquid, such as milk or mayonnaise.
  • Aerosol: solid or liquid particles spread in a gas, such as smoke or a spray.
  • Fog: tiny liquid water droplets spread in air, which is one kind of aerosol.

The question says solid particles in a liquid medium, so the answer is a sol. Option D is correct.

The other three options fail because an aerosol and a fog both have a gas as the medium, while an emulsion has liquid particles instead of solid particles.

question: When methyl orange is used in acid-base titration, the colour of the mixture of the end point is
solution:
This question tests the colour change of methyl orange in a titration.

Methyl orange is an indicator, which is a weak dye that changes colour as the pH changes. Its two colours are:

  • Red in acid (pH below about 3.1).
  • Yellow in alkali (pH above about 4.4).
  • Orange in between, when the solution is close to neutral.

When you add acid to a base, the pH falls during the titration. The colour stays yellow while the solution is alkaline. At the end point, the last drop of acid neutralises the base and the indicator passes through its in-between colour, which is orange. That is neither the pure acid colour nor the pure alkali colour.

So the end point colour is orange, option C.

  • Red would mean there is excess acid, which is after the end point.
  • Pink is the colour of phenolphthalein in alkali, not a methyl orange colour.
  • Yellow would mean the solution is still alkaline, before the end point.

question: To produce ethyl propanoate, propanoic acid will react with
solution:
This question tests esterification, the reaction that makes an ester from an acid and an alcohol.

The general reaction is:

carboxylicacid+alcohol⇌ester+water

One molecule of acid reacts with one molecule of alcohol, so the mole ratio is 1 : 1.

To make ethyl propanoate, we need the acid part to have 3 carbons (propanoate) and the alcohol part to have 2 carbons (ethyl).

C2H5COOH+C2H5OH⇌C2H5COOC2H5+H2O

Propanoic acid (C2H5COOH) plus 1 mole of ethanol therefore gives ethyl propanoate and water. Option B is correct.

  • 2 moles of ethanol is more alcohol than needed; only one molecule of alcohol joins the ester, and the extra ethanol is simply left over.
  • 1 mole of propanoic acid is already the acid we started with; an acid cannot make an ester with itself in this way.
  • 2 moles of propanoic acid would not give an ethyl group in the ester, because the alcohol supplies the alkyl group.

question: An example of a dibasic acid is
solution:
This question tests the meaning of a dibasic acid.

A basic acid is one that can give up a certain number of hydrogen ions (H+) from each molecule. “Dibasic” means it can give up two hydrogen ions per molecule.

Look at tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid:

H2SO4→2H++SO42−

Each molecule of H2SO4 releases two H+ ions, so it is dibasic, and option D is correct.

  • HCl has only one hydrogen atom, so it gives one H+ and is monobasic.
  • HNO3 also has only one replaceable hydrogen, so it is monobasic.
  • CH3COOH has three hydrogen atoms, but only the one in the –COOH group is acidic; the other three are firmly held in the methyl group. So it is monobasic.

A quick check: dibasic acids can neutralise two moles of a base such as NaOH for every one mole of acid.

question: Which of these compounds is not an isomer of pentan-1-ol, C5H11OH ?
solution:
Idea tested: recognising structural isomers — compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements.

Pentan-1-ol has the formula C5H12O: a chain of 5 carbon atoms with an –OH group.

Check each option:

  • 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol: 5 carbons (3 in the chain + 2 methyl groups), C5H12O → an isomer.
  • Pentan-2-ol: 5 carbons with the –OH on carbon 2, C5H12O → an isomer.
  • 2,2-dimethylbutan-1-ol: 4 + 2 = 6 carbons, C6H14O → not an isomer of pentan-1-ol.
  • Ethoxypropane: an ether with 5 carbons (C2H5–O–C3H7), C5H12O → an isomer.

Only 2,2-dimethylbutan-1-ol has a different molecular formula, so it is not an isomer — option c.

question: The process of extraction of iron in the blast furnace involves
solution:
This question tests the chemical change that happens in the blast furnace.

In the blast furnace, iron is extracted from haematite, which is mainly iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3.

Carbon (coke) burns to make carbon dioxide, and the carbon dioxide then reacts with more hot coke to make carbon monoxide:

C+O2→CO2 CO2+C→2CO

The carbon monoxide then takes oxygen away from the iron oxide:

Fe2O3+3CO→2Fe+3CO2

The iron oxide loses oxygen. Losing oxygen is one definition of reduction, so the process is reduction and option B is correct.

  • Electrolysis is the use of electric current to break down a compound. It is used for very reactive metals such as aluminium, not for iron in the blast furnace.
  • Oxidation is the opposite of what happens to the iron oxide: it would mean the oxide gains oxygen or loses electrons.
  • Hydration means adding water to a substance, which has nothing to do with extracting iron from its ore.

question: What is the solubility of the salt if 0.4mole of it dissolves in 250cm3 of water?
solution:
This question tests how to express the solubility of a substance in moles per cubic decimetre.

Solubility in mol/dm3 means the number of moles that would dissolve in 1 dm3 (that is, 1000 cm3) of the solvent.

We are told that 0.4 mole dissolves in 250 cm3. First work out how much 1 cm3 would hold, then scale up to 1000 cm3:

solubility=0.4mol250cm3×1000cm3 =0.4×1000250=0.4×4=1.6mol/dm3

So the solubility is 1.6 mol/dm3, option A.

  • 0.1 mol/dm3 comes from dividing by 4 instead of multiplying by 4, which makes the answer four times too small.
  • 2.5 mol/dm3 comes from dividing 250 by 100, which has no meaning in this calculation.
  • 1.0 mol/dm3 does not follow from the numbers either; the correct scaling factor is 4, not 2.5.

question: Which of the following will shift the equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g)  ⇌ 2NH3(g) (ΔH= - ve) to the right?
solution:
This question tests Le Chatelier's principle: when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that opposes the change.

The reaction is:

N2(g)+3H2(g)⇌2NH3(g)ΔH<0

The forward reaction is exothermic because ΔH is negative.

Look at each choice:

  • Removing ammonia as it forms lowers the concentration of a product. The system responds by making more ammonia, so the equilibrium moves to the right. This is correct, option B.
  • Increasing temperature adds heat. The system opposes this by taking in heat, which means favouring the endothermic direction, that is the backward reaction. So the equilibrium moves left.
  • Decreasing pressure favours the side with more gas molecules, because that side needs more room. There are 4 molecules on the left and 2 on the right, so lowering the pressure moves the equilibrium to the left, not the right.
  • Adding a catalyst makes both the forward and backward reactions faster by the same amount. It helps the system reach equilibrium sooner but does not change the position of equilibrium.

question: Which of the following is an alkaline earth metal?
solution:
This question tests the names of the groups in the periodic table.

The alkaline earth metals are the elements of Group 2: beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium.

Magnesium is in Group 2, so magnesium is the alkaline earth metal. Option D is correct.

  • Aluminium is in Group 3 (Group 13 in the modern numbering), a metal but not an alkaline earth metal.
  • Sodium is in Group 1 and is an alkali metal.
  • Potassium is also in Group 1 and is an alkali metal.

A useful reminder: Group 1 metals are called alkali metals, while Group 2 metals are called alkaline earth metals. Their oxides dissolve in water to give alkaline solutions.

question: The oxidation of secondary alcohols yields
solution:
This question tests what happens when the three classes of alcohol are oxidised.

The class of an alcohol depends on how many carbon groups are joined to the carbon that carries the –OH group.

  • Primary alcohol: the carbon with –OH is joined to one carbon group and two hydrogens. It is oxidised first to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid.
  • Secondary alcohol: the carbon with –OH is joined to two carbon groups and one hydrogen.
  • Tertiary alcohol: the carbon with –OH is joined to three carbon groups and no hydrogen.

When a secondary alcohol such as propan-2-ol is oxidised, the hydrogen on the middle carbon is removed and a double bond to oxygen is formed:

CH3CH(OH)CH3→CH3COCH3+2[H]

The product is propanone, which belongs to the family of alkanones (ketones). Option A is correct.

  • Alkanals are aldehydes, and they come from primary alcohols, not secondary ones.
  • Alkanoic acids come from primary alcohols after a second oxidation step.
  • Alkenes are made by removing water from an alcohol, which is dehydration, not oxidation.

question: Which indicator is most suitable for the titration of a weak acid and a strong base?
solution:
This question tests how to choose the right indicator for a titration.

You choose an indicator whose colour change happens at the pH of the end point.

When a weak acid is titrated with a strong base, the salt formed is made from a weak acid and a strong base. Such a salt reacts with water to give an alkaline solution, so at the end point the pH is above 7, usually around 8 to 9.

Phenolphthalein is colourless below about pH 8.3 and pink above about pH 10. Its colour change therefore falls in the alkaline region, which matches the end point:

8.3≤pH≤10.0

So phenolphthalein is the best choice, option D.

  • Methyl orange changes from red to yellow around pH 3.1 to 4.4, which is acidic. It is used for strong acid against weak base titrations.
  • Methyl red changes around pH 4.4 to 6.2, also too acidic for this titration.
  • Litmus changes over a wide range of about pH 5 to 8 and the colour change is gradual, so the end point would be hard to see sharply.

question: Which of the following is the physical property of chlorine?

option.a: It turns damp litmus paper red
option.d: It reacts with hydrogen to form HCl

solution:
This question tests the difference between a physical property and a chemical property.

A physical property can be observed or measured without the substance changing into a new substance. Examples are colour, smell, state, density and melting point.

A chemical property describes how the substance reacts and forms new substances.

Chlorine is a greenish-yellow gas. We can see the colour and the gas state with our eyes and nose, and chlorine is still chlorine afterwards. So this is a physical property, option C.

  • Turning damp litmus paper red: chlorine reacts with the water in the paper to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid, which are new substances. That is chemical.
  • Being a bleaching agent: chlorine oxidises the dye and destroys its colour, forming a new compound. That is chemical.
  • Reacting with hydrogen to form HCl: a new compound, hydrogen chloride, is made. That is clearly chemical.

question: Which of the following is the property of an ideal gas?

option.a: There are strong forces of attraction between the molecule
option.b: Collisions between molecules are perfectly elastic
option.c: The gas can be liquefied at low temperatures
option.d: The molecules have a significant volume

solution:
This question tests the assumptions of the kinetic theory for an ideal gas.

Ideal gases are a model. In this model we assume:

  • Gas molecules are in constant random motion.
  • The forces of attraction between the molecules are negligible, so there are none worth speaking of.
  • The volume of the molecules themselves is tiny compared with the volume of the container.
  • Collisions between molecules, and with the walls, are perfectly elastic, meaning no kinetic energy is lost.

Because no energy is lost in a collision, the molecules simply exchange momentum and keep moving. This is exactly what option B says, so B is correct.

  • Strong forces of attraction is the opposite of the assumption. Real gases have weak forces; ideal gases are taken to have none.
  • Can be liquefied at low temperatures is a property of real gases. An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so it would never condense.
  • Significant molecular volume is wrong: in the ideal model the molecules are treated as points with negligible volume.

question: The bombardment of Nitrogen-14 with alpha particles to produce oxygen-17 with a proton is an example of
solution:
This question tests the meaning of artificial transmutation.

Transmutation means changing one element into a different element by changing its nucleus. When this is done by bombarding a nucleus with particles in the laboratory, it is called artificial transmutation.

Rutherford's famous experiment bombarded nitrogen-14 with alpha particles and produced oxygen-17 plus a proton:

N714+He24→O817+H11

Check that the numbers balance:

mass:14+4=18=17+1 charge:7+2=9=8+1

The element has changed from nitrogen to oxygen, so this is transmutation, and it was done by bombardment in the laboratory. Option D is correct.

  • Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus such as uranium into two smaller nuclei.
  • Natural radioactivity happens by itself in unstable elements, without any bombardment.
  • Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei, for example hydrogen nuclei forming helium in the sun.

question: Which of the following is the correct electronic configuration for the Iron (III) ion (Fe3+? [Fe = 26]
solution:
This question tests how electrons are arranged in a transition metal ion.

Iron has atomic number 26, so a neutral iron atom has 26 electrons:

Fe:1s22s22p63s23p64s23d6

Count the electrons: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 = 26. Good.

To make the Fe3+ ion, remove three electrons. In the first row of the transition series the 4s electrons are lost first, because they are further from the nucleus and higher in energy. So both 4s electrons go, and then one electron is removed from the 3d subshell:

Fe3+:1s22s22p63s23p63d5

Count again: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 5 = 23 electrons, which is 26 – 3. That is option C.

  • Option A still has the 4s2 electrons, so it is the neutral Fe atom with 26 electrons.
  • Option B has 24 electrons (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6), which is Fe2+, not Fe3+.
  • Option D has left out the 2s2 electrons and has only 22 electrons, so it is wrong.

question: A sample of gas has a volume of 2.0dm3 at 270C. What will be its volume at 1270C, if the pressure remains constant?
solution:
This question tests Charles's law, which says that the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature when the pressure is constant.

V1T1=V2T2

Step 1: change both temperatures to kelvin by adding 273.

T1=27+273=300K T2=127+273=400K

Step 2: rearrange for V2 and put in the values.

V2=V1T2T1=2.0×400300 V2=800300=2.67dm3

So the new volume is 2.67 dm3, option A. This makes sense: the gas is heated, so it expands.

  • 9.40 dm3 comes from using the Celsius numbers directly, 2.0 × 127/27, which is wrong because gas laws need kelvin.
  • 3.00 dm3 comes from an arithmetic slip in the ratio.
  • 1.50 dm3 comes from turning the ratio upside down, 2.0 × 300/400. Heating a gas cannot make it shrink.

question: In an electrolytic cell, the cathode is the electrode where
solution:
This question tests the definition of the cathode in an electrolytic cell.

In electrolysis the cell uses electrical energy to drive a chemical change. The battery pushes electrons into one electrode and pulls them out of the other.

At the cathode, electrons are supplied to the ions, so positive ions (cations) move there and gain electrons. Gaining electrons is called reduction. Option B is correct.

A simple memory aid is RED CAT: REDuction happens at the CAThode. And AN OX: OXidation happens at the ANode.

For example, when copper(II) sulphate solution is electrolysed, copper ions gain electrons at the cathode:

Cu2++2e−→Cu
  • Anions are discharged at the anode, because negative ions are attracted to the positive electrode.
  • Electrons are lost at the anode during oxidation, not gained at the cathode.
  • Oxidation occurs at the anode, which is the opposite electrode.

question: The process of heating an ore strongly in a limited supply of air to remove volatile impurities is called
solution:
Idea tested: the difference between calcination and combustion.

Calcination is the process of heating an ore strongly in a limited supply of air (or in the absence of air) to remove volatile impurities or to decompose carbonates. For example, heating limestone:

CaCO3(s)→CaO(s)+CO2(g)

Combustion, on the other hand, is burning a substance in oxygen to release heat and light. Since the question describes heating an ore in a limited supply of air to remove impurities, the correct term is calcination — option c.

Why the other options are wrong: destructive distillation is heating a substance without air to break it into useful products (e.g., coal); combustion is burning with oxygen; oxidation is a reaction in which a substance loses electrons or gains oxygen.

question: A solution with a pH of 2 is how many times more acidic that a solution with a pH of 4?
solution:
This question tests the fact that pH is a logarithmic scale.

The pH of a solution is linked to its hydrogen ion concentration by:

pH=−log⁡[H+]

This means each step of one pH unit means the hydrogen ion concentration changes by a factor of 10.

Step 1: write the concentration for each solution.

pH=2⇒[H+]=1×10−2mol/dm3 pH=4⇒[H+]=1×10−4mol/dm3

Step 2: divide one by the other to see how many times bigger the first is.

10−210−4=10−2+4=102=100

So a pH 2 solution is 100 times more acidic, option B.

  • 2 times comes from simply subtracting the pH numbers, which ignores that the scale is logarithmic.
  • 10 times would be right for a difference of only one pH unit.
  • 1000 times would need a difference of three pH units.

question: Which of the following metals can be extracted by electrolysis?
solution:
This question tests which metals are obtained by electrolysis and which by chemical reduction.

The method used to extract a metal depends on how reactive it is. Reactive metals hold on to their compounds very tightly, so carbon cannot pull the oxygen away from them. These metals must be extracted by passing electricity through their molten compounds.

Aluminium is high up in the reactivity series. Its oxide, Al2O3, is very stable, so aluminium is extracted by electrolysis in the Hall–Héroult process:

2Al2O3→4Al+3O2

The alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite to lower the melting point. Pure aluminium collects at the cathode. Option C is correct.

  • Iron is extracted in the blast furnace by reduction with carbon monoxide.
  • Copper is obtained by heating its ore with carbon, or by reduction of copper compounds.
  • Lead is extracted by reducing lead(II) oxide with carbon or carbon monoxide.

All three of these metals are lower than aluminium in the reactivity series, so carbon is enough to reduce them.

question: Which of the following is the property of a covalent compound?
solution:
This question tests the typical properties of simple covalent (molecular) compounds.

In a covalent compound, atoms share electrons and form small molecules. The forces holding the atoms inside each molecule are strong, but the forces between one molecule and another are weak.

Because the molecules are usually uncharged and often non-polar, they mix readily with other non-polar substances. This is the rule “like dissolves like”. For example, iodine and grease dissolve in benzene or in tetrachloromethane but hardly at all in water. So option A is correct.

  • Conducts electricity when molten: conduction needs free-moving charged particles. Covalent molecules have no ions and no free electrons, so they do not conduct. Molten ionic compounds do conduct.
  • High melting point: only a little energy is needed to separate the weakly attracted molecules, so simple covalent compounds have low melting and boiling points. High melting points are shown by ionic and giant covalent substances such as diamond.
  • Exists only as solids: many covalent compounds are liquids or gases at room temperature, such as water, ethanol, carbon dioxide and oxygen.

question: The most electropositive elements are found in
solution:
This question tests the meaning of electropositivity and the trend across the periodic table.

Electropositive describes how easily an atom loses electrons to form a positive ion. Metals are electropositive; non-metals are electronegative, which means they attract electrons instead.

Group 1 elements (lithium, sodium, potassium and the rest) each have exactly one electron in their outermost shell. That single electron is well shielded from the nucleus and easy to remove, so these atoms form 1+ ions very readily.

The ease of losing electrons can be judged from the first ionisation energy:

Na(g)→Na+(g)+e−

The lower this energy, the more electropositive the element. Group 1 has the lowest values of any group and the value falls further as you go down the group. So Group 1 is the most electropositive group, and option C is correct.

  • Group 17 contains the halogens, which are the most electronegative elements; they gain electrons.
  • Group 18 contains the noble gases, which have full outer shells and do not easily lose or gain electrons.
  • Group 2 elements are also metals, but they lose two electrons and are less electropositive than Group 1.

question: The bond formed between two elements with a large difference in electronegativity is
solution:
This question tests the link between electronegativity difference and the type of bond formed.

Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to pull the shared electrons in a bond towards itself.

When two atoms have similar electronegativity, the electrons are shared almost equally and a covalent bond forms.

When the difference is large, the stronger atom pulls the electron(s) completely away from the weaker one:

  • The atom that loses electrons becomes a positive ion (cation).
  • The atom that gains electrons becomes a negative ion (anion).

The two oppositely charged ions then attract each other strongly, and this attraction is the ionic bond. A good example is sodium chloride:

Na→Na++e−andCl+e−→Cl−

So a large difference in electronegativity gives an ionic bond, option A.

  • Covalent bonds form when the difference is small, so the electrons are shared.
  • Metallic bonding happens between metal atoms, which release electrons into a shared sea of electrons.
  • Dative is a special covalent bond in which one atom donates both electrons; it still involves sharing, not complete transfer.

question: The bond angle in a linear molecule like BeCl2 is
solution:
This question tests how the shape of a molecule is predicted using electron pair repulsion.

Electron pairs in the outer shell of the central atom repel one another and arrange themselves as far apart as possible. This idea is called VSEPR theory.

Look at beryllium chloride, BeCl2. The central beryllium atom is joined to two chlorine atoms by two single bonds, and it has no lone pairs left.

With only two bonding pairs around the central atom, the best way to keep them apart is to put them on opposite sides of the beryllium, making a straight line:

Cl—Be—Cl

Such a molecule is linear, and the angle between the two bonds is 180°. Option C is correct.

  • 90° is found in molecules with more electron pairs, such as an octahedral arrangement.
  • 120° is found in a trigonal planar molecule such as BF3, which has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs.
  • 104° is close to the bond angle in water, where two lone pairs push the two O–H bonds closer together.

question: The IUPAC name for CH3CH2COOCH3 is
solution:
This question tests how to name an ester.

The formula CH3CH2COOCH3 has the ester group –COO– in the middle. An ester is made from an acid and an alcohol, and its name is written in two parts: alkyl alkanoate.

Step 1: identify the part that came from the alcohol. It is the group joined to the single-bonded oxygen, here –CH3. One carbon means methyl.

Step 2: identify the part that came from the acid. It is the group joined to the carbonyl carbon, here CH3CH2CO–, which has 3 carbon atoms. Three carbons means propanoate.

CH3CH2COOCH3=methylpropanoate

Step 3: combine them, alkyl first, and we get methyl propanoate, option B.

  • Propyl methanoate would be HCOOCH2CH2CH3, with one carbon on the acid side and three on the alcohol side. Our compound is the other way round.
  • Methyl ethanoate would be CH3COOCH3, which has only 2 carbons on the acid side.
  • Ethyl ethanoate would be CH3COOCH2CH3, with an ethyl group and only 2 carbons on the acid side.

question: Which of the following is an example of an endothermic process?
solution:
This question tests the difference between endothermic and exothermic changes.

  • Exothermic: heat is released to the surroundings, so the surroundings get warmer. ΔH is negative.
  • Endothermic: heat is taken in from the surroundings, so the surroundings get colder. ΔH is positive.

When ammonium chloride dissolves in water, two things happen. Energy is needed to break the ionic lattice apart, and some energy is released when water molecules cluster around the ions. For NH4Cl the energy needed to break the lattice is greater than the energy released, so the extra energy is taken from the water. The solution becomes cold.

ΔHsolution=latticeenergy+hydrationenergy>0

So dissolving NH4Cl is endothermic, option B.

  • Rusting of iron releases heat as iron combines with oxygen, so it is exothermic.
  • Neutralisation of HCl and NaOH releases heat; the mixture warms up, so it is exothermic.
  • Combustion of methane gives out a large amount of heat and light, so it is strongly exothermic.

question: The process of cracking is used in the petroleum industry to

option.b: convert long chain alkanes into shorter ones
option.d: Increase the boiling point of lubricants

solution:
This question tests the purpose of cracking in the petroleum industry.

Crude oil contains many hydrocarbons with very long chains. These heavy fractions are not in great demand, while short-chain alkanes used as petrol and alkenes used to make plastics are needed in large amounts.

Cracking breaks a long-chain alkane into a shorter alkane plus an alkene, usually by heating it strongly, often with a catalyst:

C10H22→C8H18+C2H4

So cracking turns long-chain alkanes into shorter ones, option B. The shorter products are more useful as fuels and as raw materials for making plastics.

  • Separating crude oil into fractions is fractional distillation, which is a physical separation based on boiling points. Cracking is a chemical change.
  • Removing impurities from petrol is done by treating and refining the fuel, not by cracking.
  • Increasing the boiling point of lubricants is the opposite of what cracking does: breaking big molecules into smaller ones lowers the boiling point.

question: Which of the following is an example of a mixture?
solution:
A mixture is formed when two or more substances are put together without chemical combination, so each part keeps its own properties and can be separated by physical means. Blood is a mixture: it contains red cells, white cells, plasma, water and dissolved salts, and the parts can be separated by centrifuging or filtering.

Common salt (sodium chloride), sand (silicon(IV) oxide) and washing soda (hydrated sodium trioxocarbonate(IV)) each have a fixed formula and a fixed composition by mass, so they are pure substances (compounds), not mixtures.

That is why only blood fits the definition of a mixture.

question:
Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in calcium trioxonitrate (V)
[Ca = 40, N = 14, O = 16]
solution:
We want the percentage by mass of nitrogen in calcium trioxonitrate(V), Ca(NO3)2.

Find the molar mass first: Ca = 40; two nitrate groups give N = 2 × 14 = 28 and O = 6 × 16 = 96. Total = 40 + 28 + 96 = 164 g mol-1.

So 28 g of nitrogen is present in every 164 g of the salt:

% N = (28 ÷ 164) × 100 = 17.07% ≈ 17.1%

Option 8.5% comes from using only one nitrogen atom (14 ÷ 164 × 100), while 13.1% and 27.6% come from other wrong ratios. The correct answer is 17.1%.

question: The droplets of water observed around a bottle of milk taken out of the refrigerator is due to the fact that the?

option.a: water vapour in the air around the bottle gains some energy from the bottle
option.b: temperature of the milk drops as it loses heat into the surroundings
option.c: saturated vapour pressure of the milk is equal to the atmospheric pressure
option.d: water vapour in the air around the bottle loses some of its energy to the bottle

solution:
This question is about condensation, a change of state. When the milk bottle leaves the refrigerator its surface is cold. Water vapour in the warm air around the bottle touches the cold glass and loses energy to the bottle. The vapour molecules slow down, come closer together and change into liquid droplets on the bottle.

So the bottle gains energy and the vapour loses it — option A says the opposite and is wrong. Option B only says the milk cools down, which does not explain the droplets. Option C wrongly compares the vapour pressure of milk with atmospheric pressure.

The droplets appear because water vapour in the air loses some of its energy to the bottle.

question: The volume of a given gas is V cm3 at a pressure P mm Hg. what is the new volume of the gas if the pressure is reduced to half at constant temperature?
solution:
This is an application of Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure, so P1V1=P2V2.

Here the new pressure is half the old pressure, P/2. Substituting:

P × V = (P/2) × V2, giving V2 = 2V cm3.

This makes sense: when the pressure is halved, the gas particles hit the walls only half as often, so the gas spreads out to twice its volume.

V/2 is wrong because it describes doubling the pressure instead. V and 4V are also wrong, since 4V would need the pressure to fall to one quarter.

question: Moving from left to right across a period, the general rise in the first ionization energy can be attributed to the?
solution:
First ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms.

Moving across a period, one proton is added to the nucleus at each step (nuclear charge increases), while the extra electrons enter the same outermost shell. The inner electrons therefore shield the outer electrons by almost the same amount all across the period.

With a stronger pull from the nucleus and little change in screening, the outer electrons are held more tightly and are harder to remove, so the ionisation energy generally rises.

Options A and C are wrong because nuclear charge increases, not decreases, and shielding hardly changes. Option D is wrong because stronger shielding would make electrons easier to remove, lowering the value.

question: How many unpaired electron(s) are there in the nitrogen sub-levels?
solution:
Nitrogen has atomic number 7, so its electronic configuration is 1s2 2s2 2p3.

The 2p sub-level has three orbitals (2px, 2py, 2pz). By Hund's rule, electrons occupy orbitals singly before any pairing starts, so each p orbital receives one electron: 2px1 2py1 2pz1.

All three of these electrons are unpaired, so the answer is 3. The 1s and 2s electrons are already paired and do not count.

Choosing 1 or 2 would mean pairing electrons in one p orbital before the others each have one, which Hund's rule forbids. "None" is wrong because the p electrons are clearly unpaired.

question: The stability of the noble gases is due to the fact that they?

option.a: have no electron in their outermost shells
option.b: have duplet or octet electron configurations
option.c: belong to group zero of the periodic table

solution:
Noble gases (group 0 or 18) are very unreactive because their atoms already have a complete outer shell — a duplet (2 electrons) in helium, or an octet (8 electrons) in neon, argon, krypton and xenon.

Since their outer shells are full, they have no need to gain, lose or share electrons, so they hardly form compounds.

Option A is wrong because they do have electrons in the outermost shell — two or eight. Option C only describes their position in the periodic table and does not explain the stability. Option D is a physical property (they are gases with low boiling points) and is not the reason for stability.

The stable duplet/octet arrangement is the real cause, so option B is correct.

question: The maximum number of electrons in the L shell of an atom is?
solution:
Shells are filled in the order K, L, M, N. The maximum number of electrons a shell can hold is given by 2n2, where n is the number of the shell.

The K shell has n = 1, so it holds 2(1)2 = 2 electrons.
The L shell is the second shell, n = 2, so it holds 2(2)2 = 8 electrons.

Option A (2) is the capacity of the K shell. The values 18 and 32 are the maxima for the M shell (n = 3) and the N shell (n = 4).

Therefore the L shell of an atom can hold a maximum of 8 electrons.

question: Elements in the same period in the periodic table have the same?
solution:
A period is a horizontal row of the periodic table. All the elements in one period are built up by filling the same principal shell, so they have the same number of electron shells. For example, sodium and argon both have three shells.

Option B is wrong because the atomic number always increases from left to right, so it cannot be the same.

Chemical properties depend on the number of outer-shell electrons. These change across a period but stay the same down a group, so option C is wrong.

Physical properties also change gradually across a period — melting point, for instance — so option D is wrong. Similar chemical properties are shared by elements in the same group, not the same period.

question:
12D + 13T → 24He + 01n + energy
The reaction above illustrates?
solution:
The equation shows two light nuclei joining to form a heavier one, which is nuclear fusion:

H2+H3→He4+n1+energy

Deuterium and tritium combine to give helium-4, a neutron and a large amount of energy.

Check the balance: mass numbers 2 + 3 = 5, and 4 + 1 = 5; atomic numbers 1 + 1 = 2, and 2 + 0 = 2.

Alpha decay (A) is the emission of a helium nucleus from one heavy nucleus, artificial transmutation (B) is the bombardment of one nucleus to change it into another, and fission (D) is the splitting of a heavy nucleus. Only fusion describes two light nuclei combining.

question: A noble gas with a high power of fog penetration used in aerodrome beacons is?
solution:
This question tests the uses of the noble gases. Krypton gives a very bright, penetrating light when electricity is passed through it, so it is used in high-intensity lamps such as aerodrome (airport) beacons and fog lamps, where the light must cut through fog.

Neon gives the familiar orange-red glow of advertising signs but does not penetrate fog well. Argon is used to fill electric light bulbs and to provide an inert atmosphere in welding. Helium is used in balloons and as a coolant because it is very light and unreactive.

Only krypton has the strong fog-penetrating property needed in aerodrome beacons, so option A is the correct answer.

question: Permanent hardness of water can be removed by?
solution:
Permanent hardness is caused by dissolved calcium and magnesium sulphates and chlorides, which are not removed by boiling. It is removed by adding caustic soda (sodium hydroxide), which supplies hydroxide ions. These combine with the hardness-causing ions, especially Mg2+, to form insoluble hydroxides, while calcium ions are thrown down as calcium trioxocarbonate(IV). The precipitate is then filtered off, leaving soft water.

Boiling (D) removes only temporary hardness, caused by hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV) salts. Filtration (A) removes only suspended solid particles. Adding slaked lime (B) is used in Clark's process for temporary hardness and is much less effective for permanent hardness.

Hence caustic soda is the correct answer.

question: Substance employed as drying agents are usually?
solution:
Hygroscopic substances absorb moisture from the air without dissolving in it, so they are used as drying agents — for example concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, calcium chloride and silica gel. They take water vapour out of the gas or air being dried.

Amphoteric substances (A) can react with both acids and bases; that has nothing to do with drying. Efflorescent substances (C) lose their water of crystallisation to the air, which is the opposite behaviour, so they cannot dry anything. Being acidic (D) is not a requirement, because some of the best drying agents, such as calcium chloride, are salts.

Only "hygroscopic" correctly describes a drying agent, so option B is right.

question:
Calculate the solubility in mol dm-3 of 40g of CuSO4 dissolved in 100g of water at 120°C?
[Cu = 64, S = 32, O = 16]
solution:
Solubility in mol dm-3 is the number of moles of solute dissolved in 1 dm3 (1000 cm3) of solution.

Molar mass of CuSO4 = 64 + 32 + (4 × 16) = 160 g mol-1.
Moles of CuSO4 = 40 ÷ 160 = 0.25 mol.
The solvent is 100 g of water, which is about 100 cm3 = 0.1 dm3.

Concentration = 0.25 mol ÷ 0.1 dm3 = 2.50 mol dm-3.

Option 0.25 is just the number of moles (not divided by volume), 0.40 comes from a wrong mass-to-volume ratio, and 4.00 comes from using an incorrect molar mass. The correct answer is 2.50.

question: Coffee stains can best be removed by?

option.c: a solution of borax in water

solution:
Coffee contains coloured substances (tannins) that dissolve in water and cling to the fabric. A solution of borax in water is mildly alkaline and acts as a cleansing agent: it dissolves the stain and lifts it out of the cloth so that it can be rinsed away.

Kerosene (A) and turpentine (B) are organic solvents used for grease, oil paint and ink stains, not for coffee. Ammonia solution (D) is used for grease and some fruit stains but is not the recommended treatment for coffee.

The question asks for the best method, and borax solution is the standard treatment for coffee stains, so option C is correct.

question: Carbon (II) oxide is considered dangerous if inhaled mainly because it?

option.a: can cause injury to the nervous system
option.b: competes with oxygen in the blood
option.c: competes with carbon (IV) oxide in the blood

solution:
This question is about the harmful effect of carbon(II) oxide, CO. Haemoglobin in the blood normally combines with oxygen and carries it round the body. Carbon(II) oxide combines with haemoglobin far more strongly, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, so it competes with oxygen for the haemoglobin and blocks it.

The blood then carries less oxygen, the body is starved of oxygen, and this can quickly kill a person in a closed room.

Option C is wrong because it is oxygen, not carbon(IV) oxide, that is displaced. Option A is wrong because CO does not directly injure the nervous system, and option D is wrong because CO is not a lung carcinogen.

Hence option B is correct.

question: The acid that is used to remove rust is?
solution:
Rust is mainly hydrated iron(III) oxide, which is a basic oxide. It reacts with an acid to form a soluble salt and water, so the rust layer dissolves and can be washed away.

Hydrochloric acid is the acid normally used — dilute hydrochloric acid is the common rust remover sold for cleaning metal surfaces. The reaction is:

Fe2O3 + 6HCl → 2FeCl3 + 3H2O

Boric acid (A) is far too weak to dissolve rust. Trioxonitrate(V) acid (C) is a strong oxidising acid that attacks the iron itself, and tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid (D) is also corrosive and less suitable.

Therefore option B is correct.

question: Calculate the volume of 0.5 mol dm-3 H2SO4 that is neutralized by 25 cm3 of 0.1 mol dm-3 NaOH?
solution:
This is a titration calculation. The balanced equation is:

H2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2H2O

So 1 mole of the acid neutralises 2 moles of the base.

Moles of NaOH = 0.1 × 25/1000 = 0.0025 mol.
Moles of H2SO4 used = 0.0025 ÷ 2 = 0.00125 mol.
Volume = moles ÷ concentration = 0.00125 ÷ 0.5 = 0.0025 dm3 = 2.5 cm3.

Option 5.0 cm3 is obtained when the 1:2 mole ratio is ignored. Options 0.4 and 0.1 cm3 come from other arithmetic slips. The correct answer is 2.5 cm3.

question: The colour of methyl orange in alkaline medium is?
solution:
Methyl orange is an acid–base indicator used in titration. It is red in acidic solution, orange at about the neutral point, and yellow in alkaline solution.

The colour change happens because the indicator molecule changes its structure when hydrogen ions are removed by an alkali, which changes the way it absorbs light.

Pink is the colour of phenolphthalein in alkaline solution, not methyl orange, so option B is wrong. Orange is seen only near the neutral point (C), and red is the acid colour (D).

This is why methyl orange is suitable for titrations of strong acids with weak bases, where the end point is acidic. In an alkaline medium the colour is yellow, option A.

question: Which of the following salts is slightly soluble in water?
solution:
Apply the solubility rules. All sodium salts are soluble in water, so Na2CO3 (C) dissolves freely.

Silver chloride, AgCl (A), and lead(II) chloride, PbCl2 (D), are insoluble in cold water; they form white precipitates when their ions are mixed.

Calcium tetraoxosulphate(VI), CaSO4 (B), is only slightly soluble — it dissolves to a very small extent (about 0.2 g per 100 g of water). This is why it is one of the main causes of permanent hardness of water.

So the salt that is only slightly soluble is calcium tetraoxosulphate(VI), option B.

question:
6AgNO3(aq) + PH3(g) + 3H2O(l) → 6Ag(s) + H3PO3(g) + 6HNO3(aq)
In the above reaction, the reducing agent is?
solution:
In a redox reaction, the reducing agent is the substance that is itself oxidised — it gives up electrons, reduces the other substance, and its oxidation number increases.

In phosphine, PH3, hydrogen is +1, so phosphorus is −3. In H3PO3, phosphorus is +3. Since phosphorus changes from −3 to +3, PH3 is oxidised and is therefore the reducing agent.

At the same time silver in AgNO3 falls from +1 to 0, so AgNO3 is the oxidising agent (D is wrong). Water and the nitric acid formed are not the species oxidised.

So the reducing agent is PH3(g), option C.

question: The IUPAC nomenclature of the compound LiAlH4 is?
solution:
This question tests the IUPAC nomenclature of inorganic (coordination) compounds. LiAlH4 contains the complex anion [AlH4]−, in which four hydride ions (H−) are attached to aluminium.

The rule is: name the ligands first with a prefix — "tetrahydrido" — then the central metal as "aluminate". The oxidation state of aluminium goes in Roman numerals in brackets. Each hydrogen is −1, so aluminium must be +3 to give an overall charge of −1: hence (III). The cation is named first as "lithium".

Putting this together: lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III).

Options B and C have the words in the wrong order, and D is the trivial name, not the IUPAC name.

question: Iron can be protected from corrosion by coating the surface with?
solution:
Iron rusts when it is in contact with moist air. Coating it with zinc protects it in two ways:

  • the zinc layer keeps air and water away from the iron;
  • even if the coating is scratched, zinc is more reactive than iron, so zinc is oxidised first and protects the iron (sacrificial protection).

Gold and silver (A and B) would also cover the surface, but they are very expensive and, being less reactive than iron, cannot protect it sacrificially. Copper (C) is dearer than zinc and offers no sacrificial protection.

Galvanising with zinc is therefore the practical and correct answer, option D.

question:
What quantity of aluminum is deposited when a current of 10A is passed through a solution of an aluminum salt for 1930s?
[Al = 27, F = 96500 C mol -1]
solution:
Use the two electrolysis formulae. First find the charge passed:

Q=It=10A×1930s=19300C

For aluminium, Al3+ + 3e− → Al, so 3 moles of electrons deposit 1 mole (27 g) of aluminium.

Moles of electrons = 19300 ÷ 96500 = 0.20 mol.
Moles of Al = 0.20 ÷ 3 = 0.0667 mol.
Mass = 0.0667 × 27 = 1.8 g.

Option 0.2 g mistakes the moles of electrons for mass, 5.4 g comes from forgetting to divide by 3, and 14.2 g comes from other slips. The answer is 1.8 g, option B.

question: In which of the following is the entropy change positive?

option.b: Reaction between an acid and a base
option.c: Addition of concentrated acid to water
option.d: Dissolution of sodium metal in water

solution:
Entropy is a measure of disorder or randomness. A positive entropy change means the products are more disordered than the reactants — usually more moles of gas are produced.

When ammonium chloride is heated it dissociates:

NH4Cl(s) → NH3(g) + HCl(g)

One mole of an ordered solid gives two moles of gas, so disorder increases greatly and ΔS is positive.

In an acid–base reaction, ions combine to form water, so order increases and ΔS is negative. Adding concentrated acid to water and dissolving sodium in water both involve hydration, which orders water molecules around the ions, so these do not give a clear increase in disorder.

Hence option A is the correct answer.

question: If a reaction is exothermic and there is a great disorder, it means that?

option.b: the reaction is in a state of equilibrium
option.c: there will be a large increase in free energy
option.d: there will be a large decrease in free energy

solution:
The free energy change is given by:

ΔG=ΔH−TΔS

"Exothermic" means heat is released, so ΔH is negative. "Great disorder" means entropy increases, so ΔS is positive; therefore −TΔS is also negative at a positive temperature. Adding two negative terms gives a large negative ΔG.

A large negative ΔG means a large amount of free energy is released and the reaction is spontaneous.

Options A and B are wrong because such a reaction is neither static nor at equilibrium — it moves forward. Option C is wrong because free energy decreases, not increases.

So there will be a large decrease in free energy, option D.

question: In the preparation of oxygen by heating KClO3 in the presence of MnO2, only moderate heat is needed because the catalyst acts by?

option.a: lowering the pressure of the reaction
option.b: increasing the surface area of the reactant
option.c: increase the rate of the reaction
option.d: lowering the energy barrier of the reaction

solution:
A catalyst speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy — the energy barrier that reactant particles must overcome before they can react.

With MnO2 present, potassium trioxochlorate(V) breaks down to give oxygen at a much lower temperature, so only moderate heating is needed:

2KClO3 → 2KCl + 3O2

The catalyst does not change the pressure (A). It is not a reactant, so it does not increase surface area (B). It does increase the rate, but that is an effect, not the way it works (C).

Option D correctly explains the mechanism: the catalyst lowers the energy barrier, so more particles have enough energy to react.

question: The graph above demonstrate the effect of?

option.a: surface area on the rate of reaction
option.b: catalyst on the rate of reaction
option.d: concentration on the rate of reaction

solution:
The graph plots the volume of gas produced against time for the same reaction carried out with reactants of different particle size — for example, powdered and lump calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) reacting with dilute acid.

Smaller particles expose a larger surface area to the acid, so the reaction is faster: that curve rises steeply and levels off sooner. Both curves finally reach the same maximum volume because the same amount of reactant is used.

A catalyst (B) would also speed up the reaction, but the curves would be labelled "with catalyst" and "without catalyst". Pressure (C) and concentration (D) change the rate and often the final volume of gas as well.

So the graph demonstrates the effect of surface area on the rate of reaction, option A.

question:
2H2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2H2O(g) ΔH = -ve
what happens to the equilibrium constant of the reaction above if the temperature is increased?
solution:
The reaction 2H2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2H2O(g) has a negative ΔH, so the forward reaction is exothermic and the reverse reaction is endothermic.

According to Le Chatelier's principle, raising the temperature favours the endothermic change, so the equilibrium shifts to the left, giving more hydrogen and oxygen and less water vapour.

The equilibrium constant is K = [H2O]2 ÷ ([H2]2[O2]). The numerator becomes smaller and the denominator larger, so K decreases.

It is not unaffected (A), it does not become zero (B), and it certainly does not increase (D). The answer is option C.

question: To a solution of an unknown compound, a little dilute tetraoxosulphate (VI) acid was added with some freshly prepared iron (II) tetraoxosulphate (VI) solution. The brown ring observed after the addition of a stream of concentrated tetraoxosulphate (VI) acid confirmed the presence of?
solution:
This is the brown ring test for trioxonitrate(V) ions, NO3−. The unknown solution is mixed with freshly prepared iron(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI) solution and dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid. Concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid is then poured gently down the side of the tube.

The nitrate is reduced to nitrogen(II) oxide, which combines with Fe2+ to form the brown complex [Fe(H2O)5NO]2+, seen as a brown ring where the two liquids meet.

Chloride would give a white precipitate with silver trioxonitrate(V), sulphite would liberate sulphur(IV) oxide, and trioxocarbonate(IV) would give carbon(IV) oxide. Only NO3− gives the brown ring, so option D is correct.

question: Which of the following is used in rocket fuels?
solution:
Trioxonitrate(V) acid (nitric acid, HNO3) is a powerful oxidising agent. In rocket fuels it acts as the oxidiser: it supplies oxygen rapidly so that the fuel burns fiercely and produces a large thrust. Nitric acid is used in this way in some space rockets.

Ethanoic acid (B) is a weak organic acid, tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid (C) is not used as a rocket oxidiser, and hydrochloric acid (D) is not a strong enough oxidiser for propulsion.

Hence HNO3 is the correct answer, option A. The question also reminds us of one of the important uses of nitric acid in industry.

question: A constituent common to bronze and solder is?
solution:
This question tests knowledge of alloys.

  • Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.
  • Solder is an alloy of tin and lead (commonly about 60% tin and 40% lead).

The element common to both alloys is therefore tin.

Lead is found only in solder, copper only in bronze, and silver is not a normal constituent of either alloy. Remember also that brass is copper and zinc, while steel is iron with a little carbon.

So the correct answer is tin, option D.

question: When iron is exposed to moist air, it gradually rusts. This is due to the formation of?
solution:
Rusting is the corrosion of iron in the presence of oxygen and water. The iron is oxidised from iron(0) to iron(III), and the product is hydrated iron(III) oxide, roughly Fe2O3·xH2O — the reddish-brown flaky solid called rust.

Water of crystallisation is part of rust, so the anhydrous oxides (B and C) are wrong. Iron(II) oxide (D) is not the final product; any iron(II) first formed is quickly oxidised further to iron(III).

Rust is therefore hydrated iron(III) oxide, option A. Its flaky nature is why rust does not protect the metal underneath, unlike the tough oxide layer on aluminium.

question: A compound gives an orange-red color to non-luminous flame. This compound is likely to contain?
solution:
A flame test identifies metal ions by the colour they give to a non-luminous (Bunsen) flame. The heat excites electrons in the metal ions; as the electrons fall back to lower levels they emit light of a characteristic colour.

Calcium ions, Ca2+, give a brick-red or orange-red flame, which matches the observation, so option B is correct.

Sodium ions give a persistent golden-yellow flame (A). Iron ions, Fe2+ and Fe3+, give no useful characteristic flame colour — only faint sparks — so C and D are wrong. Potassium would give lilac and copper blue-green.

The test must be done with a clean nichrome or platinum wire.

question: Stainless steel is used for making?
solution:
Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with chromium (about 18%) and nickel (about 8%), plus a little carbon. The chromium forms a thin, tough layer of chromium(III) oxide on the surface that prevents rust and corrosion, so the steel stays hard and shiny.

Because it is strong, hard, and resists corrosion and wear even at high temperatures, it is used for cutting tools, surgical instruments, kitchen utensils and machine parts — hence option B.

Magnets (A) are made from iron, steel or special alloys such as alnico. Coins and medals (C) are usually made from cupronickel or bronze. Moving parts of clocks (D) need special non-magnetic alloys.

question: The residual solids from the fractional distillation of petroleum are used as?

option.b: raw materials for the cracking process

solution:
Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into fractions such as petrol, kerosene, diesel and lubricating oil. The residue left at the bottom of the fractionating column is a thick, dark solid called petroleum coke or bitumen (asphalt).
