Because it is waterproof and resists chemical attack, it is used for coating pipes (and for surfacing roads).

It is not used as a raw material for cracking (B); cracking is applied to heavier liquid fractions such as gas oil to obtain petrol. It cannot be used as tractor fuel (C), which is diesel, nor as jet fuel (D), which is a kerosene-type fraction.

Therefore option A is correct.

question: The IUPAC nomenclature of the compound above is?
solution:
To name an alkane by IUPAC rules, find the longest continuous carbon chain and number it so that the branch gets the lowest possible number.

Here the longest chain contains eight carbon atoms, so the parent name is octane (not heptane). The branch is an ethyl group, C2H5, and counting from the end nearest the branch places it on carbon 4. The full name is therefore 4-ethyloctane.

Option B, 5-ethyloctane, uses the wrong numbering direction, which gives a higher number. Options C and D wrongly take the longest chain as seven carbons, but a straight chain of eight carbons is longer.

question: Which of the following is used as fuel in miners' lamp?
solution:
The miners' safety lamp (Davy lamp) burns a fuel gas to give light and to warn miners of flammable gases in the mine. Ethyne (acetylene, C2H2) is the fuel used in such lamps; it burns with a very hot, bright flame and is also used in oxy-acetylene welding.

Ethyne is an alkyne with a carbon–carbon triple bond, C≡C, and a high percentage of carbon, which makes its flame bright.

Ethane (D) and ethene (C) are hydrocarbons used as fuels and for making plastics, not in miners' lamps. Ethanal (A) is an aldehyde and is not used as a lamp fuel.

Hence the correct answer is ethyne, option B.

question: Which of the following organic compounds is very soluble in water?
solution:
Solubility in water depends on the ability to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

Ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, has a carboxyl group (−COOH). Its O–H and C=O parts form hydrogen bonds with water, so it mixes with water in all proportions and is very soluble.

Ethyne (B) and ethene (C) are hydrocarbons with no polar group, so they are almost insoluble in water. Ethyl ethanoate (D) has an ester group but no O–H bond, so it is only slightly soluble.

The general rule is "like dissolves like": polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents such as water. So the very soluble compound is CH3COOH, option A.

question: Benzene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of nickel catalyst at 180°C to give?
solution:
Benzene, C6H6, is an aromatic compound with a ring of six carbon atoms and delocalised electrons.

When benzene is heated with hydrogen and a nickel catalyst at about 180 °C, three molecules of hydrogen are added across the ring, so the aromatic ring becomes a fully saturated six-membered ring:

C6H6 + 3H2 → C6H12

The product is cyclohexane, option D.

Xylene (A) and toluene (B) are formed by substitution of methyl groups onto the ring, not by adding hydrogen. Cyclopentane (C) has only five carbon atoms, so it cannot come from a six-carbon ring. This addition reaction shows that benzene can behave like an unsaturated compound.

question:
What is the concentration of a solution containing 2g of NaOH in 100cm3 of solution?
[Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1]
solution:
The idea tested here is molar concentration — the number of moles of solute dissolved in 1 dm3 (1 litre) of solution.

Step 1: molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol-1.

Step 2: moles in 2 g = 2 ÷ 40 = 0.05 mol.

Step 3: volume = 100 cm3 = 100 ÷ 1000 = 0.1 dm3.

Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 0.05 ÷ 0.1 = 0.50 mol dm-3, so option B is correct.

Option C (0.05) is only the number of moles, not yet divided by the volume. Options A and D come from using a wrong molar mass or forgetting to convert cm3 to dm3. Always divide moles by the volume in dm3.

question: Which of the following properties is NOT peculiar to matter?

option.a: kinetic energy of particles increase from solid to gas
option.b: Random motion of particles increases from liquid to gas
option.c: Orderliness of particles increases from gas to liquid
option.d: Random motion of particles increases from gas to solid

solution:
This question tests the kinetic theory of matter — how the particles of solids, liquids and gases are arranged and how they move.

In a solid the particles are closely packed and only vibrate; in a liquid they are less ordered and slide over one another; in a gas they are far apart and move rapidly and randomly. Therefore:

  • kinetic energy does increase from solid to gas — true;
  • random motion increases from liquid to gas — true;
  • orderliness increases from gas to liquid — true, because cooling packs the particles into a more regular pattern.

Option D is false: when a gas changes to a solid, the random motion of its particles decreases greatly; it does not increase. That statement is therefore NOT peculiar to matter, which makes D the answer.

question: From the diagram above, an ideal gas can be represented by
solution:
This question tests the behaviour of an ideal gas using a graph of the product PV plotted against pressure P.

For an ideal gas, Boyle's law says that at constant temperature PV=constant. So however the pressure is changed, the product PV stays the same, and the graph must be a horizontal straight line — that is line N (option B).

Lines M, K and L slope or bend upwards: real gases behave like this at high pressure because their particles attract one another and occupy space of their own, so PV is not perfectly constant. Only N shows the constant value required of an ideal gas, so N is the correct representation.

question: Which of the following questions is correct about the periodic table?

option.a: The non-metallic properties of the elements tend to decrease across each period
option.b: The valence electrons of the elements increase progressively across the period
option.c: Elements in the same group have the same number of electron shells
option.d: Elements in the same period have the number of valence electrons

solution:
This question tests periodic trends across a period and down a group.

Moving from left to right across a period, one proton and one electron are added at each step, so the number of valence electrons increases progressively. In Period 3, for example: Na = 1, Mg = 2, Al = 3, Si = 4, P = 5, S = 6, Cl = 7, Ar = 8. Option B is correct.

  • A is wrong: non-metallic character increases across a period; it does not decrease.
  • C is wrong: a group shares the same number of valence electrons (and similar chemistry), but the number of electron shells increases down the group.
  • D is wrong: a period shares the same number of shells, not the same number of valence electrons.

question: The relative atomic mass of a naturally occurring lithium consisting of 90% 73Li and 6310% Li is
solution:
This question tests how the relative atomic mass is obtained from isotopic abundance. It is the weighted average of the masses of the isotopes, allowing for how much of each one is present.

Calculation:

  • 90% of 7Li: 90 × 7 = 630
  • 10% of 6Li: 10 × 6 = 60
  • total = 690
  • divide by 100: 690 ÷ 100 = 6.9

So the relative atomic mass is 6.9 (option A). It lies between 6 and 7 and is closer to 7 because the isotope of mass 7 is 90% abundant. Option B (7.1) comes from reversing the percentages, while C and D come from arithmetic slips.

question: An isotope has an atomic number of 15 and a mass number of 31. The number of protons it contain is
solution:
This question tests the meaning of atomic number and mass number.

  • The atomic number (proton number) is the number of protons in the nucleus. Here it is 15, so the atom contains 15 protons — option B.
  • The mass number is the total of protons and neutrons, so the number of neutrons = 31 − 15 = 16.

Isotopes of one element always have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so the 15 protons fix the identity of the element. Option A (16) is the neutron number, not the proton number; C (46) is the sum of mass number and atomic number; D (31) is the mass number itself. Only the atomic number gives protons directly.

question: The molecular lattice of iodine is held together by
solution:
This question tests the forces that hold a molecular lattice together, using iodine as the example.

Solid iodine is built from separate I2 molecules. Inside each molecule the two atoms are joined by a strong covalent bond, but the molecules themselves are packed into a lattice held only by weak van der Waals (intermolecular) forces. Option D is correct.

These forces are weak, which explains why iodine has a low melting point, sublimes easily and forms soft crystals. A dative bond would need a lone pair donated to an acceptor, a metallic bond needs a lattice of cations in a sea of electrons, and hydrogen bonding needs hydrogen attached to N, O or F — none of these occurs between iodine molecules, so A, B and C are wrong.

question: The arrangement of particles in crystal lattices can be studied using
solution:
This question tests the technique used to study the arrangement of particles in a crystal lattice.

Crystal structures are studied by X-ray crystallography: a narrow beam of X-rays is passed through the crystal and is diffracted by the regularly spaced layers of particles. The diffraction pattern obtained gives the distances between the particles and their positions, so the three-dimensional lattice can be worked out. Option A is correct.

X-rays work because their wavelength is about the same as the spacing between particles in a crystal (about 10-10 m). Gamma rays have far too short a wavelength to give useful diffraction, while alpha and beta rays are streams of particles that would be absorbed or scattered instead of producing a diffraction pattern.

question: From the diagram above, find the amount of solute deposited when 200 cm3 of the solution is cooled from 55°C to 40°C.
solution:
This question tests reading a solubility curve and using it to work out the amount of solute crystallised when a solution is cooled.

From the graph, the number of moles of solute in 1000 cm3 (1 dm3) of saturated solution is:

  • at 55°C: about 7 moles;
  • at 40°C: about 6 moles.

So cooling deposits 7 − 6 = 1 mole from every 1000 cm3 of solution.

For 200 cm3: 1 × (200 ÷ 1000) = 0.20 mole, option B.

Option C (0.01) and D (0.02) come from dividing by 10 000 or 10 instead of 5, and option A (0.10) from using 100 cm3. Always scale the graph difference to the actual volume given.

question: The importance of sodium aluminate (III) in the treatment of water is to
solution:
This question tests the use of sodium aluminate(III) in the treatment of water.

Raw water carries tiny suspended particles of clay and dirt that do not settle because they repel one another. Sodium aluminate reacts with the alkalinity of the water to form a gelatinous precipitate of aluminium hydroxide. This sticky precipitate traps the fine particles and drags them down as larger, heavier clumps — a process called coagulation (or flocculation). Option A is correct.

Germs are killed by chlorination, not by aluminate; acidity is corrected with lime or dilute acid; and iodine and fluoride are the substances linked with goitre and tooth decay. So options B, C and D each describe a different water-treatment step, not the work of sodium aluminate.

question: What type of bond exits between an element X with atomic number 12 and Y with atomic number 17?
solution:
This question tests how the type of bond formed depends on electronic configuration.

X has atomic number 12: 2, 8, 2 — a metal with two outer electrons. Y has atomic number 17: 2, 8, 7 — a non-metal needing one more electron for a stable octet.

X loses its two valence electrons to become X2+, and two Y atoms each gain one electron to become Y-. The oppositely charged ions then attract strongly, giving the compound XY2. This complete transfer of electrons forms an electrovalent (ionic) bond, so option A is correct.

Covalent bonding involves sharing between non-metals, a dative bond needs a lone pair donated to an acceptor, and metallic bonding needs a lattice of cations in a sea of electrons; none of these fits here.

question: Hardness of water is mainly due to the presence of

option.d: calcium chloride or sodium chloride salts

solution:
This question tests the causes of hardness of water.

Water is hard when it contains dissolved calcium or magnesium salts. These ions react with soap to form an insoluble scum instead of a lather. The main culprits are:

  • calcium or magnesium hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV) — causes temporary hardness, removed by boiling;
  • calcium or magnesium tetraoxosulphate(VI) and the chlorides — cause permanent hardness, removed by ion exchange or washing soda.

Option B names calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) and calcium tetraoxosulphate(VI), so it is correct. Hydroxides are added to soften water, not to harden it, and sodium salts do not cause hardness at all — so A, C and D are wrong.

question: A suitable solvent for iodine and naphthalene is
solution:
This question tests the rule 'like dissolves like'.

Iodine and naphthalene are non-polar molecular solids held together by weak van der Waals forces. They dissolve readily in non-polar solvents whose molecules also interact by weak dispersion forces. Benzene, C6H6, is non-polar, so it dissolves both — option D.

Water is strongly polar and hydrogen bonded, so iodine and naphthalene hardly dissolve in it, and ethanol is also polar, so it is a poor solvent for these solids. Carbon(IV) sulphide is non-polar as well, but it is extremely volatile, flammable and poisonous; benzene is therefore the safer, preferred laboratory solvent and gives a clear brown iodine solution.

question: Which of the following noble gases is commonly found in the atmosphere?
solution:
This question tests knowledge of the composition of the atmosphere and the noble gases.

Dry air contains about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon, and small amounts of carbon(IV) oxide and the other noble gases. Argon is by far the commonest noble gas in air, so option D is correct. It is obtained industrially by the fractional distillation of liquid air.

Neon, helium, krypton and xenon occur only in traces, and helium is mostly extracted from natural gas. Argon is used to fill electric bulbs and to provide an inert atmosphere in welding because it is so unreactive. Options A, B and C are therefore not the noble gas commonly found in the atmosphere.

question:
N2O4(g) ↔ 2NO2(g) ΔH = +ve
In the reaction above, an increase in temperature will

option.a: increase the value of the equilibrium constant
option.b: decreases the value of the equilibrium constant
option.d: shift the equilibrium to the left

solution:
This question tests Le Chatelier's principle applied to an endothermic equilibrium.

The forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH is positive), so heat is absorbed when N2O4 breaks into NO2. Raising the temperature adds heat, and the system opposes the change by shifting in the endothermic direction — to the right, producing more NO2.

The equilibrium constant is the ratio of product to reactant concentrations: K=[NO2]2[N2O4]. More NO2 and less N2O4 means a larger K, so option A is correct.

B is the opposite of the truth, C is wrong because reactant production falls, and D is wrong because the equilibrium shifts right, not left.

question:
CH3COOH(aq) + OH-(aq) ↔ CH3COO-(aq) + H2O(l)
In the reaction above ,CH3COO-(aq) is
solution:
This question tests the Brønsted–Lowry idea of acids and bases.

A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton (H+) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. In the equation, ethanoic acid donates a proton to the hydroxide ion:

CH3COOH + OH- ↔ CH3COO- + H2O

After donating its proton, CH3COOH becomes CH3COO-. The particle left behind after an acid has lost a proton is its conjugate base, so option A is correct. By the same reasoning, OH- is the base and H2O is its conjugate acid.

CH3COO- cannot be an acid here because it has no proton to donate, and it is not a base or a conjugate acid in this reaction, so B, C and D are wrong.

question: How many cations will be produced from a solution of potassium aluminium tetraoxosulphate (VI)?
solution:
This question tests the dissociation of a salt in water and the meaning of cations.

Potassium aluminium tetraoxosulphate(VI) has the formula KAl(SO4)2. In water it breaks up completely into its ions:

KAl(SO4)2 → K+ + Al3+ + 2SO42-

Cations are the positively charged ions, so only K+ and Al3+ qualify: that is 2 cations, option D.

The two tetraoxosulphate(VI) ions are anions, so they are not counted. Option B (4) is the total number of ions produced, while options A (3) and C (1) come from counting charges or only one cation — both are mistakes.

question: Which of the following is NOT an alkali?
solution:
This question tests the difference between a base and an alkali.

An alkali is a base that is soluble in water, producing hydroxide ions. Sodium hydroxide, calcium hydroxide and ammonia (which dissolves to form ammonium hydroxide) all dissolve and turn red litmus blue, so they are alkalis.

Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2, is only very slightly soluble in water, so it is a base but not an alkali — option B. Its low solubility is actually useful in the medicine 'milk of magnesia', where it neutralises excess stomach acid gently.

Options A, C and D all dissolve to give alkaline solutions, so none of them is the exception the question asks for.

question: An effect of thermal pollution on water bodies is that the

option.c: level of oxides of nitrogen increase

solution:
This question tests the effect of thermal pollution on water bodies.

Thermal pollution happens when factories or power stations discharge hot cooling water into rivers, lakes or seas. Gases dissolve less in warm water than in cold water, so the amount of dissolved oxygen falls — option D.

Fish and other aquatic animals then find it hard to breathe and may die, and the warmer water also speeds up their metabolism, so they need even more oxygen. The volume of the water does not change, and heating does not create chemical waste or oxides of nitrogen. Options A, B and C are therefore incorrect. This shows how human activity can upset the balance of an ecosystem.

question: Which of the following is a deliquescent compound?
solution:
This question tests the terms deliquescent, hygroscopic and efflorescent.

  • A deliquescent substance absorbs so much water vapour from the air that it dissolves in it and forms a solution. Calcium chloride, CaCl2, does this, so option B is correct. It is used to keep containers dry.
  • A hygroscopic substance absorbs moisture but does not dissolve in it.
  • An efflorescent substance loses its water of crystallisation to the air; washing soda, Na2CO3.10H2O, is the classic example, so option D is the opposite case.

Sodium nitrate is soluble but does not liquefy in air, and copper(II) oxide is insoluble in water, so A and C are wrong.

question: A chemical reaction which the hydration energy is greater than the lattice energy is referred to as
solution:
This question tests the energy changes that occur when an ionic solid dissolves.

Two energy terms oppose each other:

  • lattice energy — the energy needed to pull the ions apart (endothermic, absorbs heat);
  • hydration energy — the energy released when water molecules surround the ions (exothermic, gives out heat).

The net heat change is the difference between them. If the hydration energy is greater than the lattice energy, more heat is released than absorbed, the solution becomes warmer and the process is exothermic — option C.

The opposite case, where lattice energy is larger, gives an endothermic dissolution as with ammonium nitrate. The statement says nothing about the reaction being reversible or spontaneous, so A and D do not follow.

question: The function of zinc electrode in a galvanic cells is that it
solution:
This question tests the electrodes of a galvanic (voltaic) cell.

In a simple cell such as zinc and copper dipped in dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, zinc is the more reactive metal. At the zinc electrode, zinc atoms lose electrons and pass into solution:

Zn → Zn2+ + 2e- (oxidation)

So zinc is the negative electrode (anode) and its function is to produce electrons that flow through the external wire to the copper cathode. Option C is correct.

Option A is wrong because oxidation, not reduction, occurs at zinc; reduction happens at the copper electrode. Option B is wrong because zinc is negative, not positive. Option D is wrong because zinc gives out electrons instead of using them up.

question:
CH4(g) + Cl2(g) → CH3 Cl(s) + HCl(g)
The major factor that influence the rate of the reaction above is
solution:
This question tests the rate of a photochemical (light-catalysed) reaction.

Methane reacts with chlorine by free-radical substitution. The Cl–Cl bond must first be broken into two chlorine radicals, and the energy for this comes from ultraviolet light:

Cl2 → 2Cl•

Once the radicals form, the chain reaction quickly produces chloromethane and hydrogen chloride. In the dark the mixture hardly reacts even though the gases are in contact, so light is the controlling factor — option D.

Temperature and concentration affect rates in general, but they cannot start this particular reaction at room temperature. No catalyst is used here; light supplies the energy that a catalyst normally would.

question: The condition required for corrosion to take place is the presence of
solution:
This question tests the conditions needed for rusting, the corrosion of iron.

Rusting is an electrochemical process that needs both oxygen and water — option D. Iron at the surface loses electrons to form Fe2+, and the oxygen dissolved in the film of water gains those electrons:

2Fe + O2 + 2H2O → 2Fe(OH)2, later oxidised to hydrated iron(III) oxide (rust).

Carbon(IV) oxide and acids only speed the process up; they are not essential. Iron stays bright in boiled, air-free water and in dry air, which proves the point. Options A, B and C all wrongly make carbon(IV) oxide a necessity.

question: The diagram above best illustrates the effect of decrease in
solution:
This question tests how the concentration of the reactants affects the rate of a reaction.

The graph plots rate of reaction against time. The curve is steepest at the start and flattens out later, meaning the rate is high at first and then steadily falls.

That is exactly what happens when concentration falls: as the reactants are used up, there are fewer particles per unit volume, so effective collisions between them become less frequent and the rate drops. Option A — a decrease in concentration — is therefore the effect illustrated.

A decrease in temperature or in surface area would also lower the rate, but neither changes gradually as the reaction proceeds in the way shown. The steady fall with time is the signature of decreasing concentration.

question:
MnO4(aq)- + Y + 5Fe(aq)2+ → Mn(aq)2+ + 5Fe(aq)3+ + 4H2O(l)
In the equation above, Y is
solution:
This question tests balancing a redox equation by the ion–electron method.

Permanganate is reduced in acid solution: manganese goes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons. Iron is oxidised from Fe2+ to Fe3+, losing 1 electron each. To equalise the electrons, 1 MnO4- needs 5Fe2+.

Balancing oxygen requires 4H2O on the right, which in turn requires 8H+ on the left:

MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe2+ → Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O

Checking charge: left = −1 + 8 + 10 = +17; right = 2 + 15 = +17. It balances, so Y is 8H+ (option D). Options A, B and C leave the charges unequal.

question:
Given that M is the mass of a substance deposited during electrolysis and Q is the quantity of electricity consumed, then Faraday's first law can be written as
[Electrochemical equivalent]
solution:
This question tests Faraday's first law of electrolysis.

The law states that the mass of a substance deposited at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity that passes through the electrolyte: M ∝ Q. Putting in a constant gives

M = EQ

where E is the electrochemical equivalent (the mass deposited by one coulomb) and Q is the quantity of electricity in coulombs. So option B is correct.

Because M = EQ, options A (M = E/Q) and C (M = Q/E) are wrong: they divide instead of multiplying, yet doubling Q must double the mass, not halve it. Option D (M = E/2Q) is also wrong. Check the units: E is in grams per coulomb and Q in coulombs, so EQ gives grams.

question: The impurities formed during the laboratory preparation of chlorine gas are removed by
solution:
This question tests the purification of chlorine prepared in the laboratory.

Chlorine is made by heating manganese(IV) oxide with concentrated hydrochloric acid. The gas collected is impure: it carries over hydrogen chloride gas and water vapour.

The hydrogen chloride is removed by passing the gas through water, because HCl is extremely soluble in water while chlorine is only slightly soluble — option A. The moist gas is then dried by passing it through concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid and collected by downward delivery, since it is denser than air.

Ammonia would react with the chlorine, and more HCl would add to the impurity, so B and D are wrong; the concentrated acid is a drying agent, not a scrubber for HCl.

question: The effect of the presence of impurities such as carbon and sulphur on iron is that they
solution:
This question tests the effect of impurities on the properties of iron.

Pure iron is soft, malleable and ductile with a high melting point (about 1535°C). When impurities such as carbon and sulphur are present, they sit between the iron atoms and disturb the regular packing, so the atoms cannot lie as closely together and the forces holding them weaken. As a result the melting point is lowered — option D. This is why pig iron, with about 4% carbon, melts at a lower temperature and is easier to melt in the blast furnace.

The impurities also make iron hard and brittle; they do not raise its tensile strength or make it more malleable and ductile, so A, B and C are wrong.

question: A few drops of concentrated HNO3 is added to an unknown solution and boiled for a while. If this produces a brown solution, the cation present is likely to be
solution:
This is a test for iron(III) ions, Fe3+, using concentrated trioxonitrate(V) acid.

Concentrated HNO3 is a strong oxidising agent. When a few drops are added and the mixture is boiled, any iron present is oxidised to the +3 state, and iron(III) salts give a characteristic yellow-brown to reddish-brown solution. That brown colour shows the cation is Fe3+, so option C is correct.

Lead(II) salts are colourless, copper(II) salts are blue-green, and iron(II) salts are pale green. Option D is close, but Fe2+ would be oxidised to Fe3+ by the hot concentrated acid, and it is the Fe3+ formed that gives the brown colour seen.

question: The bleaching action of chlorine gas is effective due to the presence of
solution:
This question tests the bleaching action of chlorine.

Dry chlorine does not bleach. Bleaching needs moisture (water), so option B is correct. Chlorine reacts with water to form hydrochloric acid and a weak acid that supplies oxygen:

Cl2 + H2O → HCl + HOCl

The hypochlorous acid then breaks down to give nascent oxygen, which oxidises the coloured dye molecule to a colourless product:

HOCl → HCl + [O]

Hydrogen chloride, air and oxygen alone cannot do this, so options A, C and D are wrong. The bleaching is permanent because the colouring matter is destroyed, not merely covered up.

question: In the laboratory preparation of oxygen, dried oxygen is usually collected over
solution:
This question tests the collection of a dry gas in the laboratory.

Oxygen prepared from potassium trioxonitrate(V) or hydrogen peroxide is first dried by passing it through a drying agent such as calcium chloride. The dried gas must then be collected without picking up water again, so it cannot be collected over water.

It is therefore collected over mercury, a dense liquid metal that neither dissolves nor reacts with oxygen and keeps the gas dry — option B. Mercury is used in the same way for gases that dissolve in water.

Acids are not used as collecting liquids, and calcium chloride is a drying agent, not a liquid to collect a gas over, so C and D are wrong. Water would make the dried oxygen moist again, so that method is unsuitable here.

question: The property of concentrated H2SO4 that makes it suitable for preparing HNO3 is its
solution:
This question tests the preparation of trioxonitrate(V) acid and the reason a non-volatile acid is used.

Nitric acid is made by heating a nitrate such as potassium trioxonitrate(V) with concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid:

KNO3 + H2SO4 → KHSO4 + HNO3

Concentrated H2SO4 is used because it has a very high boiling point (about 338°C), while HNO3 is volatile (boiling point about 83°C). The more volatile acid therefore distils off and is collected, leaving the sulphuric acid behind — option A.

Its density, oxidising power and dehydrating power are genuine properties, but they are not the reason for this preparation, so B, C and D are wrong.

question: Bronze is preferred to copper in the making of medals because it
solution:
This question tests the properties of alloys, using bronze.

Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin (about 90% copper and 10% tin). Atoms of different sizes are introduced into the copper lattice, and these distort the layers so that they cannot slide over one another easily. The result is a metal that is harder and stronger than pure copper — option A. Bronze also resists corrosion and casts well, so a medal keeps its shape and shine for a long time.

Pure copper is soft and wears away quickly, so it is less suitable. Bronze is not lighter than copper, its use has nothing to do with low temperatures, and a low tensile strength would be a disadvantage, not a reason for preference.

question: The constituents of baking powder that makes the dough to rise is
solution:
This question tests the chemistry of baking powder.

Baking powder contains sodium hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV), NaHCO3, together with a mild acid such as cream of tartar. When the dough is mixed and warmed, the acid reacts with the hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV):

NaHCO3 + H+ → Na+ + H2O + CO2

The carbon(IV) oxide produced is trapped by the stretchy gluten in the dough, forming bubbles that make the dough rise and become light and spongy. Option A is therefore correct.

Sodium hydroxide and sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) are too strongly alkaline and leave a soapy taste, and sodium chloride gives off no gas at all, so B, C and D are wrong.

question: The ability of carbon to form long chains is referred to as
solution:
This question tests catenation, a special property of carbon.

Carbon atoms can join to one another by strong covalent bonds to form long chains and rings of almost any length, and they can also form double and triple bonds. This self-linking is called catenation, so option C is correct. It explains why there are millions of organic compounds — alkanes, alkenes, alkanols, sugars and polymers.

Alkylation is the transfer of an alkyl group from one molecule to another, and acylation is the introduction of an acyl group; both are reactions, not self-linking. Carbonation means treating a substance with carbon(IV) oxide, as in fizzy drinks. None of these describes the long-chain ability tested here.

question: Which of the following compounds will undergo polymerization reaction?
solution:
This question tests the conditions for addition polymerisation.

Ethene, C2H4, has a carbon–carbon double bond. Under heat, pressure and a catalyst the double bond opens and thousands of ethene molecules join into one long chain:

nCH2=CH2 → (–CH2–CH2–)n

This is addition polymerisation, giving poly(ethene), or polythene, used for bags and buckets. Option A is correct.

Ethane (C2H6), ethanol (C2H5OH) and propanoic acid (C2H5COOH) are saturated — they have no double bond that can open, so they cannot polymerise in this way. Options B, C and D are therefore wrong.

question:
An organic compound has an empirical formula CH2O and vapour density of 45.
What is the molecular formula?
[C = 12, H = 1, O = 16]
solution:
This question tests how to find a molecular formula from an empirical formula and a vapour density.

First find the relative molecular mass: it is twice the vapour density.

Mr = 2 × 45 = 90

The mass of the empirical formula CH2O is 12 + (2 × 1) + 16 = 30.

Number of units, n = 90 ÷ 30 = 3.

Molecular formula = (CH2O)3 = C3H6O3, option C.

Option D, C2H4O2, has Mr = 60, and options A and B have Mr values of 60 and 46 — none of them equals 90. Remember that vapour density is measured relative to hydrogen, hence the factor of 2.

question:
At 25 °C and with zymase as catalyst,
C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 + energy
The reaction represented by the equation above is useful in the production of
solution:
This question tests the fermentation of glucose to produce an alkanol.

The equation shows one glucose molecule breaking down into two molecules of C2H5OH and two molecules of carbon(IV) oxide, with energy released:

C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2

The enzyme zymase, found in yeast, catalyses the reaction at about 25°C. The product C2H5OH is ethanol, so option D is correct. This process is used to make alcoholic drinks and, after distillation, industrial spirit and fuel.

Methanol, propanol and butanol contain one, three and four carbon atoms respectively, so none of them can be the product of this breakdown of a six-carbon sugar.

question: The number of isomers that can be obtained from C4H10 is
solution:
This question tests structural isomerism in alkanes.

Isomers have the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms. C4H10 has only two possible carbon skeletons:

  • a straight chain of four carbons — butane, CH3CH2CH2CH3;
  • a chain of three carbons with one branch — 2-methylpropane (isobutane), CH3CH(CH3)CH3.

So there are 2 isomers, option D. Putting the methyl group on an end carbon simply gives back the straight chain, and moving it along the chain gives the same molecule again. Options A (3) and B (4) belong to larger alkanes: C5H12 already has three isomers.

question: Which of the following methods can be used to obtain pure water from a mixture of sand, water and methanoic acid?

option.a: neutralization with NaOH followed by filtration
option.b: neutralization with NaOH followed by distillation

solution:
The idea tested is choosing a separation method by looking at the properties of each part of the mixture.

  • Sand does not dissolve, so filter paper holds it back during filtration.
  • The filtrate is water mixed with methanoic acid, two miscible liquids with different boiling points, so distillation separates them: water vapour rises first, condenses in the condenser and is collected as pure water while the acid stays in the flask.

So filtration followed by distillation is correct.

Neutralising with sodium hydroxide (option a) only turns the acid into sodium methanoate and still leaves it dissolved; filtration alone cannot remove a dissolved acid; fractional distillation alone cannot deal with the sand, which would block the apparatus.

question:
How many atoms are present in 6.0g of magnesium?
[Mg = 24, NA = 6.02 × 1023 mol-1]
solution:
This question tests the mole concept and Avogadro's constant.

Step 1 — moles of magnesium: n=mM=6.024=0.25 mol

Step 2 — number of atoms: one mole contains 6.02 × 1023 atoms, so

0.25 × 6.02 × 1023 = 1.505 × 1023 ≈ 1.51 × 1023 atoms, option c.

Option d (3.02 × 1023) comes from using 0.5 mol, as if the mass were 12 g; options a and b arise from using 1022 instead of 1023, which makes the answers ten times too small.

question: 50 cm3 of gas was collected over water at 10°C and 765 mm Hg. Calculate the volume of the gas at s.t.p. if the saturated vapour pressure of water at 10°C is 5mm Hg
solution:
The idea tested is the combined gas law, corrected for the water vapour collected with the gas.

Gas collected over water is wet, so the total pressure is shared between the gas and the vapour:

Pgas = 765 − 5 = 760 mmHg

Using P1V1T1=P2V2T2 with s.t.p. = 760 mmHg and 273 K:

V2 = 50 × (760 ÷ 760) × (273 ÷ 283) = 48.23 cm3, option d.

The other values come from forgetting to subtract the saturated vapour pressure, or from using the wrong temperature ratio.

question: An increase in the pressure exerted on gas at a constant temperature results in

option.a: a decrease in the number of effective collisions
option.c: an increase in the average intermolecular distance

solution:
This tests Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.

P1V1=P2V2

In particle terms, squeezing a gas brings the particles closer together, so they strike the walls more often per unit area and the pressure rises. Working backwards, if you increase the pressure on a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, the volume must fall, so option b is correct.

Option a is wrong: collisions per unit area increase, not decrease. Option c is wrong because the average distance between molecules becomes smaller, not larger. Option d is wrong because volume falls instead of rising.

question:
2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2 O(g)
In the reaction above, what volume of hydrogen would be left over when 300 cm3 of oxygen and 1000 cm3 of hydrogen are exploded in a sealed tube?
solution:
This tests Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes: gases react in simple whole-number volume ratios given by the balanced equation.

2H2(g) + O2(g) → 2H2O(g)

The equation shows that 2 volumes of hydrogen react with 1 volume of oxygen. Hydrogen needed for 300 cm3 of oxygen = 2 × 300 = 600 cm3.

Hydrogen supplied = 1000 cm3, so hydrogen left over = 1000 − 600 = 400 cm3, option b. Oxygen is the limiting reactant and is used up completely.

Option c (600 cm3) is the hydrogen used, not the leftover; option a (200 cm3) comes from a wrong 1:1 ratio; option d (700 cm3) comes from simply subtracting 300 from 1000.

question:
l . Evaporation. ll. Sublimation. lll. Diffusion. IV. Brownian motion.
Which of the above can correctly be listed as evidences for the particulate nature of matter?
solution:
The idea tested is evidence that matter is made of tiny particles in constant motion.

  • Evaporation: fast-moving surface particles escape as vapour, leaving the liquid behind.
  • Sublimation: particles of a solid escape straight into the gas phase, as with iodine or ammonium chloride.
  • Diffusion: particles of one substance spread and mix with those of another, e.g. bromine vapour spreading through air.
  • Brownian motion: tiny smoke or pollen grains jiggle because invisible particles bombard them unevenly.

All four are correct, so option d is right. Options a, b and c each leave out some of the evidence.

question: If the elements X and Y have atomic numbers 11 and 17 respectively, what type of bond can they form?
solution:
The idea tested is predicting the type of bond from electronic configurations.

X (atomic number 11) is sodium: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1. Losing its single outer electron gives a stable Na+ with the neon configuration.

Y (atomic number 17) is chlorine: 2, 8, 7. Gaining one electron completes its outer shell as Cl−.

The electron is transferred from the metal to the non-metal, and the oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly, giving an ionic (electrovalent) bond in NaCl — option c.

Covalent bonding (b) needs two non-metals sharing electrons; a dative bond (a) needs a lone pair donated to an acceptor; metallic bonding (d) needs a lattice of positive ions in a sea of electrons.

question: A hydrogen atom which has lost an electron contains

option.d: one proton, one electron and one neutron

solution:
This tests the structure of the atom.

An ordinary hydrogen atom (protium) is written 11H. It has one proton and one electron, and no neutron in its nucleus.

Removing the electron leaves only the nucleus, so the H+ ion contains one proton only — option a.

Option b is impossible because protium has no neutron to leave behind. Option c wrongly adds a neutron. Option d describes a particle that has lost nothing, and it also needs a neutron that hydrogen-1 does not have. Isotopes such as deuterium do contain one neutron, but the atom in the question is ordinary hydrogen.

question: The electronic configuration of Mg 2+ is
solution:
The idea tested is writing the electronic configuration of an ion from that of the neutral atom.

Magnesium has atomic number 12, so a neutral Mg atom is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2, that is 2, 8, 2.

Mg2+ has lost the two electrons of the outermost 3s shell, so 12 − 2 = 10 electrons remain:

1s2 2s2 2p6, which is option b. This is the stable configuration of neon.

Option a (…3s2 3p2) is silicon, option c (…3s2) is the neutral magnesium atom still holding its outer electrons, and option d (2, 6) has too few electrons and does not belong to magnesium at all.

question: Group VII elements are
solution:
This tests the trends in Group VII, the halogens — fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine.

Each halogen atom has seven outer electrons, one short of a noble-gas arrangement. That strong pull for an extra electron makes them good oxidizing agents: they accept electrons and are themselves reduced, for example

Cl2 + 2e− → 2Cl−

so option b is correct.

The other options are wrong: halogens exist as diatomic molecules (F2, Cl2, Br2, I2), not monoatomic; they are highly electronegative, not electropositive; and they gain rather than donate electrons.

question: Which of the following is used to study the arrangement of particles in crystal lattices?
solution:
This tests how the internal arrangement of particles in a crystal is studied.

The spacing between particles in a crystal lattice is of the same order as the wavelength of X-rays, about 10−10 m. When X-rays strike a crystal, the layers of particles act like a diffraction grating, and the pattern of diffracted beams reveals where the particles sit. This is X-ray crystallography; the Bragg equation nλ=2dsinθ links the angles to the spacing, so option d is correct.

Alpha and beta particles are charged and are absorbed or deflected, not diffracted in a useful way, and gamma rays are far too penetrating with too short a wavelength.

question:
I. It has a varied composition from one place to another. ll. it constituents can be separated by physical means
lll. It contains unreactive noble gases
which of the above shows that air is a mixture?
solution:
The idea tested is the difference between a mixture and a compound, using air as the example.

  • I: air varies in composition from place to place — a city has more carbon(IV) oxide than a forest — while a compound has a fixed formula everywhere.
  • II: the parts of air can be separated by physical means, such as fractional distillation of liquid air, with no chemical reaction.
  • III: air contains unreactive noble gases such as argon, simply mixed in and taking no part in chemical combination.

All three show that air is a mixture, so option d is correct. Options a, b and c each leave out one valid piece of evidence.

question: The chemicals used to soften hard water involves the addition of

option.a: insoluble sodium compounds which form soluble solutions of calcium and magnesium
option.b: soluble sodium compounds which form soluble solutions of calcium and magnesium ions
option.c: soluble sodium compounds which form insoluble precipitates of calcium and magnesium ions
option.d: insoluble precipitates of calcium and magnesium ions

solution:
The idea tested is the chemical softening of hard water.

Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions. Softening removes them.

Soluble sodium compounds are added, for example washing soda (Na2CO3) or slaked lime with soda. The trioxocarbonate(IV) or hydroxide ions they supply combine with Ca2+ and Mg2+ to form insoluble precipitates — calcium carbonate, magnesium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide — which settle out and are filtered off. Hence option c is correct.

Option a is wrong because the sodium compound must be soluble to release the reacting ions; option b keeps the hardness ions in solution; option d names no reagent at all.

question: Chlorination of water for town supply is carried out to
solution:
This tests the treatment of water for town supply.

Chlorine is added in small amounts as a disinfectant. It dissolves to give chlorine water containing the strong oxidizing agent hydrochlorous acid:

Cl2 + H2O → HCl + HOCl

HOCl attacks the cell walls and enzymes of bacteria and viruses, killing them and preventing water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. So chlorination removes germs — option b.

Option a is wrong because colour is removed by coagulation with alum and filtration through activated charcoal. Option c is wrong because chlorination leaves a slight chlorine taste. Option d is wrong because odour is removed by aeration and activated charcoal.

question: The solubilites of different solutes in a given solvent can be compared by

option.a: plotting their solubility curves on separete axes
option.b: plotting their solubility curves on the same axes
option.c: plotting some of the solubility curves on the x-axis and others on the y-axis
option.d: plotting their solubility curves on the x-axis only

solution:
This tests how solubility data are presented and compared.

A solubility curve is a graph of solubility, usually in g per 100 g of water or in mol dm−3, against temperature. To compare two or more solutes in the same solvent, their curves must be drawn on the same axes and to the same scale, so that at any temperature you can read off which solute is more soluble and how steeply its solubility changes. That is option b.

Option a is wrong because curves on separate axes cannot be compared by eye. Option c confuses the axes: temperature is the independent variable and always goes on the x-axis, while solubility goes on the y-axis. Option d is meaningless, since a curve cannot be drawn on an x-axis alone.

question:
Potassium trioxochlorate (V)has a solubility of 1.5 mol dm -3 at 45 °C.On cooling this solution to a temperature of 20 °C, the solubility was found to be 0.5 mol dm -3. What mass of KCIO 3 was crystalized out?
[K = 39, Cl = 35.5 O =16]
solution:
This tests solubility and crystallisation calculations.

Solubility falls by 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 mol dm−3 when the solution cools from 45 °C to 20 °C, so 1.0 mole of potassium trioxochlorate(V) crystallises from each dm3.

Molar mass of KClO3 = 39 + 35.5 + (3 × 16) = 122.5 g mol−1

Mass crystallised = 1.0 mol × 122.5 g mol−1 = 122.5 g, option d.

Option c (12.25 g) is ten times too small, option a (1.00 g) confuses moles with grams, and option b (10.00 g) does not follow from the data at all.

question: Which of the following pollutants is associated with brain damage?
solution:
The idea tested is the health effects of common air pollutants.

Carbon(II) oxide is colourless, odourless and combines with haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, forming carboxyhaemoglobin. This blocks the transport of oxygen to the brain and other organs. Small amounts cause headache, dizziness and confusion, and larger amounts cause unconsciousness, brain damage and death — hence option a.

Radioactive fallout (b) mainly causes cancers and genetic damage. Biodegradable waste (c) pollutes water by using up dissolved oxygen and killing fish. Sulphur(IV) oxide (d) irritates the respiratory tract and helps form acid rain; it is not associated with brain damage.

question: Which of the following will produce a solution with pH less than 7 at equivalent point?
solution:
The idea tested is the pH at the equivalence point of an acid–base titration.

The pH at equivalence depends on the salt formed. A strong acid with a weak base gives a salt that hydrolyses to an acidic solution, so the pH is less than 7.

In option c, HCl is a strong acid while Mg(OH)2 is a weak base, being only slightly soluble and only partly ionised. The salt MgCl2 contains the small, highly charged Mg2+ ion, which hydrolyses water and releases H+, so the solution is acidic.

Options a, b and d each pair a strong acid with a strong base (NaOH or KOH), giving salts of very weak conjugate acids, so those solutions are neutral with pH about 7.

question: The number of hydroxonium ions produced by one molecule of an acid in aqueous solution is its
solution:
This tests the meaning of basicity.

The basicity of an acid is the number of replaceable hydrogen atoms, that is the number of hydroxonium ions, H3O+, that one molecule of the acid can produce in water.

  • HCl is monobasic: HCl + H2O → H3O+ + Cl−
  • H2SO4 is dibasic and gives two H3O+ ions
  • H3PO4 is tribasic

Acid strength (b) measures how far an acid ionises, not how many protons it can give. pH (c) measures hydrogen ion concentration, and concentration (d) is the amount of acid per unit volume of solution.

question: During a titration experiment, 0.05 moles of carbon (lV) oxide is liberated. What is the volume of gas liberated?
solution:
The idea tested is the molar volume of a gas.

At s.t.p., one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm3, that is 22 400 cm3.

Volume = moles × molar volume
= 0.05 mol × 22.4 dm3 mol−1 = 1.12 dm3, option d.

Option a (22.40 dm3) is the volume of one whole mole, option b (11.20 dm3) the volume of 0.5 mole, and option c (2.24 dm3) the volume of 0.1 mole. Each simply uses the wrong number of moles.

question: A major factor considered in selecting a suitable method for preparing a simple salt is its
solution:
This tests how the method for preparing a salt is chosen.

The deciding factor is the solubility of the salt in water.

  • A soluble salt of a very reactive metal, such as a sodium, potassium or ammonium salt, is prepared by titration, because the reaction with an acid has no visible end point.
  • A soluble salt of an insoluble base or carbonate, e.g. copper(II) tetraoxosulphate(VI), is made by adding excess solid to the acid, then filtering off the excess.
  • An insoluble salt, e.g. barium tetraoxosulphate(VI), is made by precipitation, mixing two solutions.

Melting point, crystalline form and reactivity with acids do not decide the general method, so a, b and c are wrong.

question: The oxidation number of boron in NaBH 4 is
solution:
This tests how oxidation numbers are worked out.

Rules used: the oxidation numbers in a neutral compound add up to zero; sodium in its compounds is always +1; hydrogen combined with a metal such as boron is a hydride, H−, so each hydrogen is −1.

Let the oxidation number of boron be x:

(+1) + x + 4(−1) = 0

+1 + x − 4 = 0, so x = +3, option d.

The negative values arise from wrongly treating hydrogen as +1 in a hydride, or from forgetting that the whole compound is neutral. Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) therefore contains boron in the +3 state.

question:
2Na2O2(s) + 2H2O(l) → 4NaOH(s) + O2(g)
The substance that is oxidized in the reaction above is
solution:
This question tests oxidation and reduction seen as changes in oxidation number. Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number; reduction is a decrease.

  • In sodium peroxide, Na2O2, sodium is +1, so each oxygen is -1.
  • In NaOH, oxygen is -2; in O2, oxygen is 0.
  • In water, H2O, oxygen is -2 and stays -2 in NaOH, so water is not oxidised.

The oxygen in Na2O2 changes from -1 to 0 in O2 (oxidation) and from -1 to -2 in NaOH (reduction). Therefore the substance oxidised is Na2O2, option A.

question:
What number of moles of Cu 2+ will be deposited by 360 coulombs of electricity?
[f = 96500 C mol -1]
solution:
This tests Faraday's laws of electrolysis.

Step 1 — moles of electrons:

n(e−)=QF=36096500=3.73×10−3 mol

Step 2 — electrode reaction: Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu. Two moles of electrons deposit one mole of copper, so divide by 2:

n(Cu) = 3.73 × 10−3 ÷ 2 = 1.87 × 10−3 mol, option b.

Option d (3.73 × 10−3 mol) is the commonest error because it forgets the two electrons needed by copper(II); options a and c divide by the wrong number of electrons.

question:
A metal M displaces zinc from ZnCl solution
This shows that

option.a: electrons flow from zinc to M
option.b: M is more electropositive than zinc
option.c: M is more electonegative than zinc
option.d: zinc is more electropositive than M

solution:
The idea tested is the reactivity (activity) series of metals.

A metal higher in the series is more electropositive: it loses electrons more readily and so displaces a less electropositive metal from a solution of its salt.

Here M pushes zinc out of zinc chloride:

M + ZnCl2 → MCl2 + Zn

Zinc ions gain electrons and are reduced to zinc metal, while atoms of M lose electrons and are oxidised. Since M can reduce Zn2+, it must be more electropositive than zinc — option b.

Electrons pass from M to zinc, not from zinc to M, so a is wrong. A more electronegative metal (c) holds its electrons tightly and could not displace zinc, and d states the opposite of the truth.

question:
CO(g) + H2O(g) → CO2(g) + H2(g)
Calculate the standard heat change of the reaction above, if the standard enthalpies of formation of CO2(g), H2O(g) and CO(g) in kJ mol-1 are -394, -242 and -110 respectively.
solution:
The idea tested is Hess's law using standard enthalpies of formation.

For any reaction:

ΔHr = Σ ΔHf(products) − Σ ΔHf(reactants)

Products: CO2 (−394) and H2 (0, because it is an element). Reactants: CO (−110) and H2O (−242).

ΔH = (−394 + 0) − (−110 − 242)
= −394 + 352 = −42 kJ mol−1

So option d is right and the reaction is exothermic. Option c has the correct size but the wrong sign, while options a and b (262) come from combining the values with wrong signs, for example −394 − 110 + 242 = −262.

question: An increase in entropy can best be illustrated by
solution:
The idea tested is entropy, a measure of the disorder or randomness of a system.

Entropy increases when particles become more spread out and more free to move, because there are then more ways of arranging them.

When two different gases are mixed, the molecules of each gas spread through the other and fill the larger total volume, giving many more possible arrangements. Disorder, and therefore entropy, increases, so ΔS is positive — option a.

Freezing of water, condensation of a vapour and solidifying of candle wax all change a liquid or a gas into a more ordered solid with particles fixed in position. In each of those cases entropy falls rather than rises.

question: The highest rate of production of carbon (lV) oxide can be achieved using

option.a: 0.05 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> HCl and 5g powdered CaCO<sub>3</sub>
option.b: 0.05 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> HCl and 5g lump CaCO<sub>3</sub>
option.c: 0.10 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> HCl and 5g powdered CaCO<sub>3</sub>
option.d: 0.025 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> HCl and 5g powdered CaCO<sub>3</sub>

solution:
This tests the factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction.

CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2

The rate depends on how often acid particles collide with the solid surface.

  • Concentration: a higher acid concentration means more acid particles per unit volume, so more collisions each second.
  • Surface area: powdered calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) exposes a much larger surface to the acid than lumps of the same mass.

Option c has both the highest concentration (0.10 mol dm−3) and powdered solid, so carbon(IV) oxide is produced fastest. Options a, b and d use weaker acid or lump calcium carbonate and are therefore slower.

question: A piece of filter paper moistened with lead (ll) ethanoate solution turns black when the paper is dropped into a gas likely to be
solution:
The idea tested is the test for hydrogen sulphide gas.

Lead(II) ethanoate solution reacts with hydrogen sulphide to give a black precipitate of lead(II) sulphide:

Pb(CH3COO)2 + H2S → PbS (black) + 2CH3COOH

A filter paper moistened with the solution therefore turns black in the presence of H2S, so option d is correct. This is the standard test used when a sulphide is treated with dilute acid.

Sulphur(IV) oxide, hydrogen chloride and the other gases do not form a black lead compound, so they leave the paper unchanged or give only a faint colouration.

question: Which of the following gases has a characteristic pungent smell, turns red litmus paper blue and forms dense white fumes with hydrogen chloride gas?
solution:
This tests the identification of ammonia gas.

The gas described is NH3, option d. Ammonia:

  • has a sharp, pungent, choking smell;
  • is the only common alkaline gas, so it turns moist red litmus paper blue;
  • reacts with hydrogen chloride to form dense white fumes of ammonium chloride: NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl.

Nitrogen (a) and dinitrogen(I) oxide (b) are colourless, neutral gases that give none of these reactions. Chlorine (c) is pungent and bleaches moist litmus, but it is acidic rather than alkaline and gives no white fumes with hydrogen chloride.

question: Commercial bleaching can be carried out using
solution:
This tests bleaching agents studied under the halogens and sulphur compounds.

Two different mechanisms are used in industry.

  • Chlorine bleaches by oxidation. In water it forms hydrochlorous acid, HOCl, which releases oxygen that destroys the coloured part of the dye, leaving a colourless compound.
  • Sulphur(IV) oxide bleaches by reduction. It adds hydrogen to the coloured substance and reduces it to a colourless compound.

So chlorine and sulphur(IV) oxide are the commercial bleaching agents — option c. Sulphur(IV) oxide with ammonia (a) and ammonia with chlorine (d) simply form salts, while hydrogen sulphide (b) is a poisonous reducing gas that blackens lead salts and is not used for bleaching.

question: Mineral acids are usually added to commercial hydrogen peroxide to

option.d: reduce it to water and oxygen

solution:
This tests the storage and stability of hydrogen peroxide.

Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly at room temperature:

2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2

The decomposition is catalysed by light, dust, rough surfaces and traces of metal ions such as Cu2+, Fe3+ and Mn2+. Commercial hydrogen peroxide is therefore kept in dark plastic bottles, and a little mineral acid, such as dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, is added. The acid lowers the pH and stops metal ions from catalysing the breakdown, so it minimises decomposition — option c. Sodium stannate or acetanilide may also be added as stabilisers.

Options a, b and d are wrong: the acid does not oxidise, decompose or reduce the peroxide.

question: Which of the following compounds will burn with a brick-red colour in a non-luminous Bunsen flame?
solution:
This tests the flame test used to identify metal ions.

When a compound of a metal is heated in a non-luminous Bunsen flame, outer electrons absorb energy and then fall back to lower levels, giving out light of a characteristic colour.

  • LiCl gives a crimson flame
  • NaCl gives a golden yellow flame
  • CaCl2 gives a brick-red flame
  • MgCl2 gives no characteristic colour

So calcium chloride is the answer, option c, the colour coming from the calcium ion. Option a is a common confusion because lithium is also red, but lithium is crimson rather than brick-red.

question: The purest form of iron which contains only about 0.1% carbon is
solution:
The idea tested is the types of commercial iron and their carbon content.

  • Pig iron: about 3–4 % carbon plus silicon, sulphur and phosphorus; hard and brittle, taken straight from the blast furnace.
  • Cast iron: about 2–4 % carbon; hard but brittle, used for engine blocks and manhole covers.
  • Wrought iron: the purest commercial form, containing only about 0.1 % carbon; soft, malleable, ductile and slow to rust, used for chains and ornamental work.

Steel is also made, with 0.1–1.5 % carbon. Iron pyrite (d) is not a form of iron but the ore FeS2.

Therefore the correct answer is b, wrought iron.

question: A common characteristic between zinc and the other transition elements is the ability to
solution:
This tests the characteristic properties of transition elements and the special position of zinc.

Most transition metals show variable oxidation states and form coloured ions because of partly filled 3d orbitals, and many act as catalysts. Zinc is an exception: it has a completely filled d10 shell, so it shows only the +2 state, its compounds are white or colourless, and it is not a useful catalyst.

What zinc does share with the other transition elements is the ability to form complex ions, for example [Zn(NH3)4]2+ and the zincate ion [Zn(OH)4]2−. That makes option b correct, while a, c and d describe the true transition metals but not zinc.

question: Which of the following metals is the least reactive?
solution:
This tests the reactivity series of metals.

The metals in the question lie towards the bottom of the series. In order of decreasing reactivity:

Pb > Sn > Hg > Au

Gold is at the very bottom, so it is the least reactive — option d. Its atoms hold electrons very tightly, and it is not oxidised by air or by dilute acids, which is why gold occurs in nature uncombined and is used for jewellery and coins.

Lead and tin (a and b) are more reactive and tarnish slowly in air; tin is used to coat steel in tin plate. Mercury (c) is quite unreactive, but it still reacts with nitric acid and forms amalgams, so it is not as unreactive as gold.

question: Geometric isomerism can exist in
solution:
The idea tested is geometric (cis–trans) isomerism.

Geometric isomerism needs restricted rotation, that is a C=C double bond, and two different groups on each of the doubly bonded carbons. The groups can then lie on the same side (cis) or on opposite sides (trans).

Hex-3-ene, CH3CH2CH=CHCH2CH3, satisfies this: each double-bond carbon carries one H and one C2H5 group, so cis and trans forms exist — option a.

Hexane (b) is saturated and has no C=C. Prop-1-ene (c) and 3-methylbut-1-ene (d) each have a terminal CH2= carbon with two identical hydrogen atoms, so no cis–trans forms are possible.

question: Alkanals can be distinguished from alkanones by the reaction with
solution:
This tests the tests used to distinguish alkanals (aldehydes) from alkanones (ketones).

An alkanal has a hydrogen atom on the carbonyl carbon, next to the C=O group, so it is easily oxidised. An alkanone has two alkyl groups there and is not oxidised by mild reagents.

Fehling's solution is a blue solution of copper(II) ions in alkali. On warming with an alkanal, the alkanal is oxidised to an alkanoic acid while the blue Cu2+ is reduced to a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide. An alkanone gives no such change, so option d is correct.

The other reagents do not separate them: Sudan III stains fats, starch iodide paper detects oxidizing agents such as chlorine, and lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III) reduces both alkanals and alkanones to alkanols.

question: The isomers of C3H8O ARE
solution:
This tests isomerism among alkanols.

Propanol has the molecular formula C3H8O, and isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures. The −OH group can sit at different positions along the chain:

  • propan-1-ol: CH3CH2CH2OH, with −OH on an end carbon
  • propan-2-ol: CH3CH(OH)CH3, with −OH on the middle carbon

These are position isomers, so option a is correct.

Option b simply names the same compound twice. Option c is wrong because propanone is C3H6O, a ketone with two hydrogen atoms fewer, so it is not an isomer of propanol.

question: Carbohydrates are large molecules with the molecular formula Cx(H2O)y. In which of the following pairs is x not equal to y?
solution:
This tests the general formula of carbohydrates, Cx(H2O)y.

For a pair to answer the question, x must differ from y in both compounds.

  • Glucose C6H12O6: x = 6, y = 6, so x = y. The same is true of fructose and galactose.
  • Sucrose C12H22O11: x = 12, y = 11, so x ≠ y.
  • Maltose C12H22O11: x = 12, y = 11, so x ≠ y.
  • Starch (C6H10O5)n: x = 6n, y = 5n, so x ≠ y.

Only maltose and starch both have x ≠ y, so option b is the answer. Options a, c and d each contain one sugar in which x = y.

question: The presence of an impurity in substance will cause the melting point to
solution:
Idea tested: the effect of an impurity on the melting point of a solid.

A pure solid has a sharp, fixed melting point because all its particles sit in the same regular lattice and need the same amount of energy to break free. An impurity introduces particles of a different size, which distort the lattice and weaken some of the forces holding it together. Less heat energy is therefore needed before the solid collapses into a liquid, so the melting point is lowered.

  • be zero – wrong; ordinary solids do not melt at 0 °C.
  • increase – wrong; impurities raise the boiling point but lower the melting point.
  • be stable – wrong; the melting point falls and also becomes less sharp.

Correct option: B (reduce).

question: What volume of carbon (ll) oxide is produced by reacting excess carbon with 10 dm3 of oxygen?
solution:
Idea tested: Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes.

Write the balanced equation for burning carbon in a limited supply of oxygen:
2C+O2→2CO

Gases react in simple whole-number volume ratios at the same temperature and pressure. One volume of oxygen gives two volumes of carbon(II) oxide:

  • Volume of CO = 2 × volume of O2
  • Volume of CO = 2 × 10 dm3 = 20 dm3

Carbon is in excess, so oxygen is the limiting reactant and all of it is used. The 10 dm3 option ignores the 1 : 2 ratio, 5 dm3 halves it wrongly, and 15 dm3 comes from no valid ratio. Correct option: B (20 dm3).

question: The radioisotope used in industrial radiography for the rapid checking of faults in welds and casting is
solution:
Idea tested: industrial uses of radioisotopes.

Industrial radiography uses penetrating radiation to photograph the inside of metal welds, castings and pipelines so that hidden cracks or air bubbles can be seen without cutting the metal open. Cobalt-60 is chosen because it gives out very energetic gamma rays that pass through thick steel and expose a photographic film placed behind the object.

  • Carbon-14 is a weak beta emitter used to date once-living materials.
  • Phosphorus-32 is a beta emitter used as a tracer in plants and medicine.
  • Iodine-131 is used to check and treat the thyroid gland.

Only cobalt-60 has the highly penetrating gamma radiation needed for rapid fault-checking of welds. Correct option: C (cobalt-60).

question: The shape of the carbon (lV) oxide molecule is
solution:
Idea tested: molecular shape from electron-pair repulsion (VSEPR).

In carbon(IV) oxide the central carbon atom is joined to each oxygen by a double bond:
O=C=O

Carbon uses two electron pairs for bonding and has no lone pairs, so the two double bonds push as far apart as possible, giving a bond angle of 180° and a linear molecule, O=C=O.

  • Angular and pyramidal shapes need lone pairs on the central atom, as in H2O and NH3.
  • Tetrahedral needs four single bonds, as in methane, CH4.

Carbon(IV) oxide has only two bonding directions, so it is linear. Correct option: B (linear).

question: Which of the following molecules is held together by hydrogen bond?
solution:
Idea tested: conditions for hydrogen bonding.

A hydrogen bond forms when hydrogen is covalently bonded to a very electronegative atom (F, O or N) that also has lone pairs. The bond is strongly polar, so the hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the lone pair on F, O or N of a neighbouring molecule.

In HF, fluorine is the most electronegative element, so the H–F bond is very polar and strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds hold the molecules together. This explains its unusually high boiling point for such a small molecule.

  • CH4 is non-polar, so only weak van der Waals forces act.
  • HBr is polar but Br is not electronegative enough; only dipole–dipole forces act.
  • H2SO4 is held mainly by strong covalent bonds and readily loses its acidic hydrogen; HF is the classic hydrogen-bonded molecule.

Correct option: D (HF).

question: The bond formed between two elements with electron configurations 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 and 1s2 2s2 2p4 is
solution:
Idea tested: predicting bond type from electron configuration.

Element 1: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 has 12 electrons – magnesium, a metal with 2 outer electrons that it easily loses to form Mg2+.
Element 2: 1s2 2s2 2p4 has 8 electrons – oxygen, a non-metal needing 2 electrons to complete its outer shell.

Magnesium transfers its two outer electrons to oxygen, giving Mg2+ and O2−. The oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly, so the bond is electrovalent (ionic), as in MgO.

  • Covalent bonds involve sharing between two non-metals.
  • Dative bonds need a lone pair donated to an acceptor atom.
  • Metallic bonding occurs only between metal atoms.

Correct option: D (ionic).

question: The constituent of air that acts as a diluent is
solution:
Idea tested: the composition and function of the gases in air.

Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.03% carbon(IV) oxide and small amounts of noble gases and water vapour. Nitrogen is the most abundant gas and is almost unreactive; it merely dilutes the oxygen so that burning, rusting and breathing go on at a moderate, safe rate instead of violently.

  • Oxygen is the active gas that supports combustion and respiration – it is the gas being diluted, not the diluent.
  • Carbon(IV) oxide is present in only about 0.03%, far too little to be the main diluent, though it does slow down burning.
  • Noble gases are inert but exist only in traces.

Because of its large proportion and low reactivity, nitrogen is the diluent of air. Correct option: A (nitrogen).

question: Steam changes the colour of anhydrous cobalt (ll) chloride from
solution:
Idea tested: the chemical test for water using cobalt(II) chloride.

Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue. When steam or water touches it, it takes up water of crystallisation to form the hydrated salt:

CoCl2(s)+6H2O(l)→CoCl2·6H2O(s)

The hydrated salt is pink, so the colour change on adding water is blue to pink. Heating reverses the change, giving blue again, which is why the salt is a reversible test for water. The white-to-blue colour change belongs to anhydrous copper(II) sulphate, and blue-to-white is what happens on heating, not on adding water. Correct option: C (blue to pink).

question: An example of a hygroscopic substance is
solution:
Idea tested: hygroscopic, deliquescent and efflorescent substances.

A hygroscopic substance absorbs water vapour from the air but does not dissolve in the water it absorbs; it simply becomes damp while remaining a solid. Copper(II) oxide, CuO, is such a substance: it takes up moisture from the atmosphere without turning into a solution, so it can be used where a dry, non-dissolving solid is wanted.

  • CaCl2 and MgCl2 absorb so much water that they dissolve in it – they are deliquescent, not merely hygroscopic.
  • NaOH is also deliquescent and absorbs carbon(IV) oxide as well, so it is not a simple hygroscopic example.

Only CuO absorbs moisture without dissolving, making it the hygroscopic example. Correct option: A (CuO).

question: The solvent used for removing grease stain is
solution:
Idea tested: choosing a solvent to remove a grease stain.

Grease is a fat or oil, and fats are esters that are attacked by alkalis. Ammonia solution is alkaline, so it reacts with the grease in a saponification reaction, turning the fat into soluble soap-like products that are easily washed away with water. It also emulsifies the oily film so that it lifts off the fabric.

  • Turpentine is a solvent for paints, varnish and tar, not the best for grease.
  • Ethanol dissolves inks, dyes and some resins.
  • Borax solution is a mild alkaline laundry booster but too weak for a heavy grease stain.

Because grease is a fat, the alkaline ammonia solution is the correct stain remover. Correct option: B (ammonia solution).

question: In a water body, too much sewage leads to

option.a: a decrease in the temperature of the water which cause in death of aquatic animals
option.b: an increase in the number of aquatic animals in the water
option.c: an increase in the bacterial population which reduces the level of oxygen in the water
option.d: a decrease in the bacterial population which increases the level of oxygen in the water

solution:
Idea tested: the effect of sewage pollution on a water body.

Sewage is rich in organic matter and mineral nutrients. When it is discharged into a river or pond in large amounts, bacteria and other micro-organisms feed on it and multiply rapidly. These bacteria decompose the organic waste aerobically, using up the dissolved oxygen in the water. The resulting oxygen shortage (high biochemical oxygen demand) kills fish and other aquatic animals, and the water becomes foul and cloudy.

  • A rise in aquatic animal numbers is wrong; they die from lack of oxygen.
  • Bacterial numbers increase, not decrease, and oxygen falls rather than rises.
  • The temperature change is slight and not the cause of death.

Correct option: C (more bacteria, less oxygen).

question: 10.0 dm3 of water was added to 2.0 mol dm-3 of 2.5dm3 solution of HCl. What is the concentration of the final solution in mol dm-3?
solution:
Idea tested: dilution of a solution and molar concentration.

When water is added, the amount (moles) of HCl stays the same but the volume increases, so the concentration falls.

Step 1: moles of HCl = concentration × volume = 2.0 mol dm−3 × 2.5 dm3 = 5.0 mol.

Step 2: final volume = 2.5 dm3 + 10.0 dm3 = 12.5 dm3.

Step 3: new concentration = 5.0 mol ÷ 12.5 dm3 = 0.4 mol dm−3.

0.5 comes from dividing by 10 dm3 only, 8.0 from multiplying the figures, and 2.0 ignores the added water. Correct option: A (0.4).

question: Three drops of a 1.0 mol dm-3 solution of HCl was added to 20 cm3 of a solution of pH 6.4. The pH of the resulting solution will be

option.a: close to that of pure water

solution:
Idea tested: the pH scale and the effect of adding an acid.

pH measures the concentration of hydrogen ions: the more H+ present, the lower the pH. The solution already has pH 6.4, so it is slightly acidic but very dilute.

Adding three drops of 1.0 mol dm−3 HCl introduces extra hydrogen ions into the 20 cm3 of solution. The H+ concentration therefore rises, so the pH must fall to a value less than 6.4.

  • Close to that of pure water (pH 7) is wrong because the solution was already below 7 and becomes more acidic, not neutral.
  • Greater than 6.4 would mean the solution became less acidic, which adding acid cannot do.
  • Unaltered is wrong because the acid adds new H+ ions.

Correct option: B (less than 6.4).

question: Which of the following substances is not a salt?
solution:
Idea tested: recognising a salt and distinguishing it from an oxide.

A salt is formed when the replaceable hydrogen of an acid is wholly or partly replaced by a metal or ammonium ion. Its name has two parts: a metal (or ammonium) cation and an acid radical anion.

  • Sodium hydrogentrioxosulphate(IV) is NaHSO3, an acid salt of trioxosulphate(IV) acid.
  • Sodium trioxocarbonate(IV) is Na2CO3, a normal salt of trioxocarbonate(IV) acid.
  • Zinc chloride is ZnCl2, a salt of hydrochloric acid.

Aluminium oxide, Al2O3, contains only aluminium and oxygen. It is an amphoteric oxide – it can react with both acids and alkalis – but it is not a salt because there is no acid radical in it. Correct option: A (aluminium oxide).

question: An insoluble salt can be prepared by

option.a: the reaction of trioxocarbonate (V) with an acid
option.c: the action of dilute acid on an insoluble base
option.d: the reaction of metals with an acid

solution:
Idea tested: methods of preparing salts, especially insoluble salts.

An insoluble salt is prepared by double decomposition (precipitation). Two soluble salts are mixed in solution; their ions exchange partners and form a new salt that is insoluble, which appears as a precipitate. It is then filtered, washed with distilled water and dried between filter papers. Example:

AgNO3(aq)+NaCl(aq)→AgCl(s)↓+NaNO3(aq)

The other three methods (acid with a trioxocarbonate(IV), acid with an insoluble base, metal with acid) all produce soluble salts such as NaCl, CuSO4 or ZnCl2 that stay in solution. Correct option: B (double decomposition).

question:
2H2O (l) + 2F2(g) → 4HF(aq) + O2(g).
In the reaction above, the substance that is being reduced is
solution:
Idea tested: identifying oxidation and reduction by electron transfer.

Reduction is gain of electrons, shown by a fall in oxidation number. In the reaction

2H2O+2F2→4HF+O2

fluorine in F2 has oxidation number 0; in HF it is −1. Each fluorine atom has gained one electron, so F2 is reduced (and acts as the oxidising agent). Meanwhile oxygen goes from −2 in water to 0 in O2, so water is oxidised.

  • O2 is the product of oxidation, not the substance reduced.
  • H2O is oxidised, the opposite change.
  • HF is the product; its fluorine is already at −1.

Correct option: C (F2).

question: In an electrochemical cell, polarization is caused by
solution:
Idea tested: polarization in an electrochemical (galvanic) cell.

In a simple cell such as the zinc–copper cell, hydrogen gas is liberated at the positive electrode as the reaction proceeds. The tiny bubbles form a layer on the electrode surface, blocking it and setting up a small opposing e.m.f. This is called polarization. It makes the current fall and the cell quickly become ‘tired’.

The effect is reduced by adding an oxidizing agent called a depolariser, for example manganese(IV) oxide or acidified potassium dichromate(VI), which removes the hydrogen by converting it to water.

  • Chlorine and oxygen are not produced in this cell.
  • Tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid is part of the electrolyte, not the cause.

Hydrogen gas coating the electrode is the cause. Correct option: D (hydrogen).

question: In an endothermic reaction, if there is a loss in entropy the reaction will
solution:
Idea tested: free-energy change and spontaneity.

Whether a reaction occurs on its own is decided by the free-energy change:

ΔG=ΔH−TΔS

A reaction is spontaneous only when ΔG is negative.

  • Endothermic means ΔH is positive (heat is absorbed).
  • Loss of entropy means ΔS is negative, so −TΔS is positive.

The two terms are both positive, so ΔG is positive at every temperature and the reaction cannot occur on its own – it is not spontaneous. It is not ‘indeterminate’ because the signs settle the matter, and there is no tendency towards equilibrium because the forward change is not favoured. Correct option: C (not spontaneous).

question: the minimum amount of energy required for a reaction to take place is
solution:
Idea tested: the meaning of activation energy.

For a reaction to occur, colliding particles must possess at least a certain minimum energy so that old bonds can be stretched and broken before new ones form. This minimum energy is the activation energy, and it is the height of the energy barrier shown as the peak on an energy profile.

Only particles with energy equal to or greater than this value react, which is why raising the temperature (more energetic collisions) or adding a catalyst (lower barrier) speeds up a reaction.

  • Lattice energy is the energy released when gaseous ions form an ionic solid.
  • Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom.
  • Kinetic energy is the energy of motion of a particle – not a threshold value.
