Correct option: C (activation energy).

question: Which of the following compounds is a neutral oxide?
solution:
Idea tested: classification of oxides as acidic, basic, amphoteric or neutral.

Oxides are classified by how they behave with acids and alkalis. A neutral oxide reacts with neither: it does not dissolve in water to give an acid or an alkali, and it does not form a salt with either an acid or a base. Carbon(II) oxide, CO, is the classic neutral oxide, together with water, nitrogen(I) oxide and nitrogen(II) oxide.

  • Carbon(IV) oxide dissolves to give trioxocarbonate(IV) acid – acidic.
  • Sulphur(IV) oxide gives trioxosulphate(IV) acid – acidic.
  • Sulphur(VI) oxide gives tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid – acidic.

Since CO forms no salt with acid or alkali, it is neutral. Correct option: D (carbon(II) oxide).

question: In the laboratory preparation of ammonia, the flask is placed in a slanting position so as to

option.a: prevent condensed water from breaking the reaction flask
option.b: enable the proper mixing of the reactions in the flask
option.c: enhance the speed of the reaction

solution:
Idea tested: the laboratory preparation of ammonia.

Ammonia is made by heating a mixture of ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) in a hard-glass test tube:

2NH4Cl+Ca(OH)2→CaCl2+2H2O+2NH3

The tube is clamped in a slanting position with its mouth lower than the closed end. Water formed in the reaction condenses and runs towards the cooler mouth instead of trickling back onto the hot part of the tube, which could crack it. The gas is collected by downward delivery because ammonia is lighter than air. Slanting does not affect mixing, speed or precipitation. Correct option: A.

question: Which of the gases is employed as an anaesthesia?
solution:
Idea tested: uses of oxides of nitrogen.

Nitrogen(I) oxide, N2O, also called dinitrogen monoxide or laughing gas, is a colourless, fairly unreactive gas that produces insensibility to pain. It is therefore used as a mild anaesthetic in dentistry and surgery, usually mixed with oxygen.

  • NO2 is a reddish-brown, poisonous gas that causes serious lung damage – not an anaesthetic.
  • NH3 is a pungent, alkaline gas that irritates the eyes and nose and is used in making fertilizers.
  • NO is a colourless but toxic gas that reacts at once with oxygen in air to form NO2.

Only nitrogen(I) oxide is safe enough and effective enough to be used as an anaesthetic. Correct option: A (N2O).

question: Sulphur (IV)oxide is a strong reducing agent in the presence of water due to the formation of
solution:
Idea tested: the reducing property of sulphur(IV) oxide.

Sulphur(IV) oxide does not reduce substances on its own; in the presence of water it forms trioxosulphate(IV) acid:

SO2+H2O→H2SO3

This acid, and its salts (trioxosulphate(IV) salts, SO32−), contain sulphur at oxidation number +4, which is easily oxidised to +6 in tetraoxosulphate(VI). By giving up electrons so readily, SO2 bleaches and reduces other substances, for example turning orange dichromate(VI) to green chromium(III). The product is therefore a trioxosulphate(IV) salt.

  • Hydroxide ion is a base, not a reducing species.
  • Sulphur(VI) oxide is the oxidised product, not the cause.
  • Hydrogen sulphide is not formed in this reaction.

Correct option: D.

question: A metal that forms soluble trioxosulphate (IV) ion is
solution:
Idea tested: solubility rules for salts.

All potassium, sodium and ammonium salts are soluble in water (the ‘KNA’ rule). This includes the trioxosulphate(IV) salts, SO32−, so potassium trioxosulphate(IV), K2SO3, dissolves freely to give trioxosulphate(IV) ions in solution.

  • Barium gives an insoluble trioxosulphate(IV), BaSO3, which appears as a white precipitate.
  • Aluminium and manganese trioxosulphates(IV) are also insoluble or only sparingly soluble.

Only the Group 1 metal, potassium, forms a soluble trioxosulphate(IV). Correct option: B (potassium).

question: Copper is displaced from the solution of its salts by most metals because it

option.b: is at the bottom of the activity series

solution:
Idea tested: the reactivity series of metals and displacement reactions.

Metals differ in how easily they lose electrons and form ions. The reactivity (activity) series places the most reactive metals at the top and the least reactive at the bottom, ending with gold and platinum. A metal higher in the series can push (displace) a metal lower down from a solution of its salt.

Copper lies far down the series, below hydrogen, so it loses electrons reluctantly. Most metals (zinc, iron, magnesium, aluminium) are above it, so they displace copper from copper(II) sulphate:

Zn+CuSO4→ZnSO4+Cu

Being a transition element or having a filled 3d orbital does not explain displacement, and copper is certainly not very reactive. Correct option: B.

question: The coloured nature of transition metal ions are associated with their partially filled
solution:
Idea tested: the origin of colour in transition-metal ions.

Transition metals have partially filled d-orbitals. When ligands (water molecules or other ions) attach to the ion, the five d-orbitals split into groups of slightly different energy. Electrons can then jump between these levels by absorbing a particular wavelength of visible light; the light that is not absorbed is what we see. Since the size of the splitting depends on the ion and its ligands, each ion has its own colour – blue for hydrated Cu2+, green for Fe2+, and so on.

  • s- and p-orbitals are fully used in bonding and do not give d–d transitions.
  • f-orbitals give the colours of lanthanide and actinide ions, not the common transition ions.

Correct option: D (d-orbital).

question: Aluminium containers are frequently used to transport trioxonitrate (V) acid because aluminium

option.c: does not react with the acid

solution:
Idea tested: the passivating effect of a protective oxide film on aluminium.

Aluminium is a reactive metal, but when exposed to air it quickly forms a very thin, tough, adherent layer of aluminium oxide, Al2O3, on its surface. This unreactive film protects the metal underneath, a process called passivation. Concentrated trioxonitrate(V) acid thickens this film instead of dissolving it, so the acid appears to have no reaction with the metal – which is why aluminium tankers and containers can carry the acid.

  • Its silvery appearance and low density are merely physical advantages; they do not stop the acid attacking it.
  • ‘Does not corrode’ is only true because of the same oxide film, but the point needed here is that the acid does not attack the metal.

Correct option: C.

question: 2- methylpropan-2-ol is an example of a
solution:
Idea tested: classification of alkanols as primary, secondary or tertiary.

An alkanol is classified by the number of alkyl groups attached to the carbon that carries the −OH group. In 2-methylpropan-2-ol the structure is (CH3)3C–OH. The carbon bearing the hydroxyl group is joined to three other carbon atoms (the two methyl groups of the main chain plus the methyl branch), so it is a tertiary alkanol.

  • Primary alkanols have the −OH carbon joined to one carbon, e.g. ethanol.
  • Secondary alkanols have it joined to two, e.g. propan-2-ol.
  • Dihydric means two −OH groups in the molecule, e.g. ethane-1,2-diol; this compound has only one.

Correct option: B (tertiary alkanol).

question: The reaction between ammonia and ethyl ethanoate produces
solution:
Idea tested: ammonolysis of an ester (formation of an amide).

Esters react with ammonia, which replaces the −O–C2H5 group to give an amide and an alkanol:

CH3COOC2H5+NH3→CH3CONH2+C2H5OH

In words: ethyl ethanoate + ammonia → ethanamide + ethanol. The acyl part (CH3CO–) keeps its two carbon atoms, so the amide is ethanamide, and the alcohol released is the one from the ester’s alkyl group, ethanol.

  • Propanol and propanamide would need three-carbon fragments, which are not present.
  • Ethanol and propanamide mixes the wrong pair.

Correct option: D (ethanol and ethanamide).

question: The decarboxylation of ethanoic acid will produce carbon (IV)oxide and
solution:
Idea tested: decarboxylation of alkanoic acids.

Decarboxylation means loss of carbon(IV) oxide from a compound. When the sodium salt of ethanoic acid is heated with soda lime (a mixture of sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide), the −COO group is removed as CO2 and the rest of the molecule becomes an alkane:

CH3COOH→CH4+CO2

Ethanoic acid has two carbon atoms; removing one as CO2 leaves one carbon, which is methane.

  • Ethane (2 C), propane (3 C) and butane (4 C) are far too large to come from a two-carbon acid.

Correct option: A (methane).

question: A primary amide is generally represented by the formula
solution:
Idea tested: the general formulae of amides.

An amide is formed when the −OH of a carboxylic acid is replaced by an amino group –NH2. The primary amide has the carbonyl carbon joined to a hydrocarbon group R on one side and an unsubstituted −NH2 group on the other:

R−C(=O)−NH2, that is, RCONH2.

  • RCOOR is an ester.
  • RCONHR is a secondary amide, with one hydrogen of the nitrogen replaced by R.
  • RCONR2 is a tertiary amide, with both hydrogens replaced.

Since only RCONH2 has the unsubstituted nitrogen of a primary amide (ethanamide, CH3CONH2, is an example), the answer is B.

question: Which of the following fraction is used as raw material for the cracking process?
solution:
Idea tested: the fractions obtained from crude oil and cracking.

Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into fractions that boil over different ranges. Long-chain fractions are in great demand as petrol, so they are cracked – heated with a catalyst to break big molecules into smaller, more useful ones plus alkenes. The usual feedstock is a fairly heavy but liquid fraction such as diesel oil (gas oil), which has long chains that break down readily into petrol-range molecules.

  • Kerosene is a middle fraction already used directly as fuel for lamps and jets.
  • Lubricating oil is valued for its high viscosity and is not the fraction normally cracked.
  • Bitumen is a semi-solid residue used for surfacing roads.

Diesel oil is therefore the raw material used for cracking. Correct option: D.

question:
An organic compound contains 60% carbon, 13.3% hydrogen and 26.7% oxygen. Calculate the empirical formula
rn(C=12,H =1, O=16)
solution:
Idea tested: calculating an empirical formula from percentage composition.

Step 1 – divide each percentage by the atomic mass:

  • C: 60 ÷ 12 = 5.00
  • H: 13.3 ÷ 1 = 13.3
  • O: 26.7 ÷ 16 = 1.67

Step 2 – divide by the smallest (1.67):

  • C: 5.00 ÷ 1.67 = 3
  • H: 13.3 ÷ 1.67 = 8
  • O: 1.67 ÷ 1.67 = 1

Step 3 – write the ratio: C : H : O = 3 : 8 : 1, so the empirical formula is C3H8O, the formula of propan-1-ol or propan-2-ol.

The other options come from dividing by a wrong number or from not dividing by the smallest value at all. Correct option: B.

question: From the diagram above, an ideal gas is represented by
solution:
Idea tested: the behaviour of an ideal gas shown on a PV against P graph.

For one mole of an ideal gas, PV=nRT. If the temperature is kept constant, the product PV does not change as the pressure changes, so a graph of PV against P is a horizontal straight line. In the diagram, line Z is the only one that stays flat at a constant value, so Z represents the ideal gas.

Curves W, X and Y rise or dip because real gases do not obey the law exactly: at high pressure the molecules themselves occupy space (PV rises above the ideal value), and at low pressure attractive forces pull them together (PV dips below it). Hence real gases are shown by the curved lines, not by Z. Correct option: A (Z).

question: In the graph above, the activation energy of the catalyzed reaction is
solution:
Idea tested: reading activation energy from an energy profile, and the effect of a catalyst.

On the graph, the reactants start at an energy level of 100 kJ. The solid (uncatalysed) curve peaks at 300 kJ, so its activation energy is 300 − 100 = 200 kJ. The broken (catalysed) curve peaks at 200 kJ, so its activation energy is 200 − 100 = 100 kJ.

A catalyst provides an alternative path with a lower energy barrier; it does not change the starting or finishing levels, so the enthalpy change of the reaction stays the same. The 200 kJ option is the uncatalysed value, 300 kJ is the peak energy itself rather than the barrier, and 250 kJ is not read from the graph at all. Correct option: A (100 kJ).

question: Choose the correct option from the graph above . 3Fe(S) + 4H2O(g) ⇌ Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g). The equilibrium constant, K, of the reaction above is represented as
solution:
Idea tested: writing an equilibrium constant expression, omitting pure solids.

For the reaction

3Fe(s)+4H2O(g)⇌Fe3O4(s)+4H2(g)

Kc is the product of the concentrations of the products, each raised to its coefficient, divided by the same product for the reactants. But pure solids have a constant concentration and are given the value 1, so Fe and Fe3O4 are left out. Only the gases appear:

K=[H2]4[H2O]4

Option A wrongly includes the solids, B is upside down, and D uses wrong powers and wrong species. Correct option: C.

question: The IUPAC nomenclature for the compound above is
solution:
Idea tested: IUPAC nomenclature of branched alkenes.

The structure is CH3–CH(CH3)–CH2–CH=CH2.

Rules applied:

  • The longest chain containing the double bond has five carbon atoms → pent.
  • It contains a C=C, so the ending is -ene.
  • Number the chain from the end nearer the double bond, so the C=C carbons are 1 and 2: pent-1-ene.
  • Counting that way, the methyl branch sits on carbon 4.

Combining: 4-methylpent-1-ene.

2-Methylpent-1-ene places the branch wrongly, 3-methylpent-2-ene moves the double bond, and 2-methylpent-4-ene numbers from the far end, which is not allowed because the double bond then gets the higher number. Correct option: A.

question: Use the above option to answer this question. The dehydration of ammonium salt of alkanoic acids produces a compound with the general formula
solution:
Idea tested: dehydration of ammonium alkanoates to amides.

An ammonium alkanoate is the salt formed when an alkanoic acid reacts with ammonia, e.g. ammonium ethanoate, CH3COONH4. When it is heated, a molecule of water is removed (dehydration) and the salt closes up into an amide:

CH3COONH4→CH3CONH2+H2O

The general formula of this product is RCONH2, the primary amide, which is option B.

  • A (RCOOR) is an ester, made from an acid and an alkanol.
  • C (RNH2) is a primary amine.
  • D (RCOR) is a ketone.

Correct option: B.

question: Use the following option above to answer this question. Which of the following compounds in solution will turn red litmus paper blue?
solution:
Idea tested: the basic nature of amines.

Red litmus turns blue only in an alkaline solution, so the compound must behave as a base. In an amine, RNH2, the nitrogen atom carries a lone pair of electrons. This lone pair can accept a hydrogen ion from water, leaving hydroxide ions behind:

RNH2+H2O⇌RNH3++OH−

Because OH− ions are produced, the solution is alkaline and turns red litmus blue. This is option C, RNH2.

  • A (R′OR″, an ether) is neutral.
  • B (a tertiary amide) is practically neutral.
  • D (a ketone) is neutral.

Correct option: C.

question: The compound above is an
solution:
Idea tested: recognising the alkanone (ketone) functional group.

The structure is CH3–CO–CH3, that is, propanone. Its functional group is the carbonyl group, C=O, joined to two carbon atoms (one methyl group on each side). Compounds with this arrangement are alkanones (ketones); the smallest member is propanone, the common laboratory solvent.

  • An alkanal has the carbonyl carbon joined to at least one hydrogen, e.g. ethanal, CH3CHO.
  • An alkanoate (ester) has the carbonyl carbon joined to an −OR group, e.g. ethyl ethanoate.
  • An alkanol has −OH and no C=O.

Since the carbonyl carbon carries no hydrogen, the compound is an alkanone. Correct option: A.

question: A mixture is different from a compound because

option.a: the properties of a compound are those of its individual constituents while those of a mixture differ from its constituents
option.b: a mixture is always homogeneous while a compound is not
option.c: the constituent of a compound are chemically bound together while those of a mixture are not
option.d: a mixture can be represented by a chemical formula while a compound cannot

solution:
This question tests the difference between a mixture and a compound.

In a compound, the elements are joined by chemical bonds in a fixed ratio, so the compound has properties of its own. For example, sodium (a violent metal) and chlorine (a poisonous gas) combine to give common salt. In a mixture the substances are only put together physically, so each one keeps its own properties and can be separated by sieving, filtration or distillation.

Option C says exactly this. Option A is the reverse of the truth, B is wrong because mixtures can be heterogeneous (sand and water), and D is wrong because a mixture has no fixed chemical formula.

question: What is the percentage of sulphur in sulphur (IV) oxide?
solution:
This tests percentage composition worked out from a chemical formula.

The formula of sulphur(IV) oxide is SO2. Its relative molecular mass is 32 + (2 × 16) = 64.

The mass of sulphur in one molecule is 32, so:

% S = (32 ÷ 64) × 100 = 50%

Option 25% is the fraction of one oxygen atom (16 ÷ 64), and 40% would come from using the wrong formula SO3 (32 ÷ 80). Option 66% does not follow from the correct masses. Since sulphur makes up exactly half of SO2, the answer is 50%.

question: A gas X diffuses twice as fast as gas Y. if the relative molecular mass of X is 32, calculate the relative molecular mass of Y.
solution:
This is an application of Graham's law of diffusion: the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its relative molecular mass.

rXrY=MYMX

X diffuses twice as fast as Y, so rX/rY = 2 and MX = 32:

2 = √(MY ÷ 32)
Squaring both sides: 4 = MY ÷ 32
MY = 4 × 32 = 128

Option 8 comes from dividing 32 by 4, 16 from halving 32, and 64 from doubling it. All three ignore the square root in Graham's law.

question: 200 cm3 of a gas at 25°C exerts a pressure of 700 mmHg. Calculate its pressure if its volume increase 350 cm3 at 75°C.
solution:
This question uses the combined gas law for a fixed mass of gas:

P1V1T1=P2V2T2

Convert to kelvin: T1 = 25 + 273 = 298 K and T2 = 75 + 273 = 348 K. Also P1 = 700 mmHg, V1 = 200 cm3 and V2 = 350 cm3.

P2 = (700 × 200 × 348) ÷ (298 × 350) = 48 720 000 ÷ 104 300 = 467.11 mmHg

Option 1430.54 comes from inverting the temperature ratio, 342.53 from mixing up the volumes, and 400.00 simply doubles the volume without allowing for the rise in temperature.

question: An element X has electron configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p5. Which of the following statements is correct about the element?

option.a: lt has a completely filled p-orbital
option.b: lt has 5 electrons in its outermost shell.
option.c: lt belongs to group ll on the periodic table

solution:
This tests electron configuration and position in the periodic table.

Add the superscripts: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17 electrons, so a neutral atom has 17 protons — the element X is chlorine.

The outermost shell is the third shell, holding 3s2 3p5 = 7 electrons. Seven outer electrons place the element in group VII (17), the halogen family, so it forms ions with a single negative charge.

Option A is wrong because the 3p subshell needs six electrons but has only five, so it is not completely filled. Option B is wrong because there are 7 outer electrons, not 5, and C is wrong because group II elements have only two outer electrons.

question: Beryllium and aluminum have similar properties because they?

option.d: are positioned diagonally to each other

solution:
This tests the diagonal relationship in the periodic table.

Beryllium is in group 2, period 2, while aluminium is in group 13, period 3. Going down a group the elements become more metallic, but going across a period they become less metallic. For elements placed diagonally, these two effects almost cancel, so Be and Al end up with nearly the same charge density and electronegativity.

As a result both form mainly covalent compounds, both have amphoteric hydroxides (Be(OH)2 and Al(OH)3 dissolve in both acid and alkali), and both resist attack by water. Lithium and magnesium show the same kind of relationship.

They are not in the same group or period, and being metals alone does not explain such close similarity.

question: If the difference in electronegativity of elements P and Q is 3.0. The bond that will be formed between them is
solution:
This tests how the electronegativity difference between two atoms decides the type of bond.

Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts the shared electrons. A difference of 3.0 is very large:

  • 0 to about 0.4: non-polar covalent
  • about 0.4 to 1.7: polar covalent
  • above about 1.7: ionic

With a difference of 3.0, the more electronegative atom pulls the electron completely away from the other, so ions are formed and electrostatic attraction packs them into a giant lattice — an ionic bond.

A metallic bond occurs between metal atoms, a covalent bond needs fairly equal sharing, and a co-ordinate bond is a special covalent bond where one atom donates both electrons.

question: How many protons, neutrons and electrons respectively are present in the element 60/27 Co?
solution:
This tests the meaning of the numbers written with a nuclide symbol.

For cobalt-60 written as Co27, the lower number is the atomic number Z = 27 (protons) and the upper number is the mass number A = 60 (protons + neutrons).

  • Protons = 27
  • Neutrons = 60 − 27 = 33
  • Electrons = 27, because a neutral atom has one electron for every proton

So the order is 27, 33, 27. Option A wrongly makes electrons equal neutrons, B puts the neutrons first, and D uses 60 for both protons and electrons.

question: The radioactive radiation used in studying the arrangement of particles in giant organic molecules is
solution:
This question tests the use of radiations in studying matter.

To find out how atoms are arranged in a giant molecule, the radiation used must have a wavelength about the size of a chemical bond (about 10−10 m). X-rays have exactly this wavelength, so a crystal scatters them and the pattern formed (X-ray crystallography) reveals where the atoms sit. This is how the structure of DNA and of proteins was worked out.

Alpha and beta particles are relatively heavy and charged, so they are stopped by a thin layer of matter and cannot pass through a crystal. Gamma rays are far too penetrating and give no useful diffraction pattern in this experiment. Hence X-rays is the answer.

question: A silicon -containing ore has 92% 28Si, 5% 29Si and 3% 30Si. Calculate the relative atomic mass of the silicon.
solution:
This tests relative atomic mass from isotopic abundances.

The relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the masses of the isotopes:

RAM = (92 × 28 + 5 × 29 + 3 × 30) ÷ 100

RAM = (2576 + 145 + 90) ÷ 100 = 2811 ÷ 100 = 28.11

Option 28.00 wrongly ignores the heavier isotopes, 29.00 is just the mass of the middle isotope, and 14.00 is roughly half the correct value. Because the ore also contains some 29Si and 30Si, the average is slightly above 28, which confirms 28.11.

question: Water is said to be temporarily hard when it contains
solution:
This tests the types of hardness of water.

Temporary hardness is caused by the hydrogencarbonates (hydrogen trioxocarbonates(IV)) of calcium and magnesium, Ca(HCO3)2 and Mg(HCO3)2. These salts break down on boiling:

Ca(HCO3)2 → CaCO3 + H2O + CO2

so the hardness disappears when the water is boiled.

Hardness that remains after boiling is permanent, and it is caused by sulphates and chlorides such as CaSO4 and MgSO4. Options C and D include CaSO4, and option B includes CaCO3, which is insoluble and not the cause of temporary hardness. Option A is therefore correct.

question: On exposure to the atmosphere, a hydrated salt loses its water of crystallization to become anhydrous. This phenomenon is referred to as
solution:
This tests the behaviour of salts in moist air.

Efflorescence is the loss of water of crystallisation by a hydrated salt when it is exposed to the atmosphere, leaving an anhydrous powder:

Na2CO3·10H2O → Na2CO3 + 10H2O

It happens when the vapour pressure of the water in the salt is higher than that of the surrounding air, so the water escapes.

Deliquescence is the opposite: a salt absorbs moisture until it dissolves (e.g. CaCl2). Hygroscopy is absorbing moisture without dissolving, and hydrolysis is a reaction with water. Only efflorescence means losing water of crystallisation.

question:
16.55g of lead (II) trioxonitrate (V) was dissolved in 100g of distilled water at 20 °C. Calculate the solubility of the solute in mol dm-3.
[Pb = 207, N = 14, O = 16]
solution:
This tests solubility in mol dm−3.

First find the molar mass of lead(II) trioxonitrate(V), Pb(NO3)2:

207 + 2(14 + 48) = 207 + 124 = 331 g mol−1

Moles dissolved = 16.55 ÷ 331 = 0.05 mol

100 g of water has a volume of about 100 cm3 = 0.1 dm3.

Solubility = 0.05 ÷ 0.1 = 0.50 mol dm−3

Option 0.05 is just the number of moles, 1.00 comes from forgetting to divide by the 0.1 dm3 of water, and 2.00 comes from using a much smaller volume. The unit printed on the options is a misprint for mol dm−3.

question: The dispersion of a liquid in a liquid medium will give
solution:
This tests types of colloidal dispersion, which are named from the two phases involved.

When one liquid is spread as tiny droplets throughout another liquid, the dispersion is an emulsion. Milk (fat droplets in water) and mayonnaise are everyday examples, and an emulsifying agent is often needed to keep the droplets from joining.

  • Fog is liquid droplets dispersed in a gas.
  • Gel is a liquid held in a solid network, like jelly.
  • Aerosol is solid or liquid particles dispersed in a gas.

Only an emulsion has a liquid dispersed in a liquid medium, so option A is correct.

question: The major and most effective way of controlling pollution is to

option.a: improve machinery so that the substances released from combustion are less harmful
option.b: pass strict laws against it by individuals and companies
option.c: educate people on the causes and effects of pollution
option.d: convert chemical wastes to harmless substances before releasing them into the environment

solution:
This question tests methods of controlling pollution.

Pollution is best controlled by prevention — stopping the harmful substance from entering the environment at all. Educating people about the causes and effects of pollution is the major and most effective step, because people who understand the harm change their habits: they stop dumping refuse in drains, stop bush burning, handle chemicals carefully and obey rules willingly.

The other options are useful but secondary. Treating wastes, improving machinery and passing laws all deal with pollution after it has been produced; they are costly, and laws cannot succeed without people who understand and support them. Education therefore remains the most fundamental control measure.

question: The basicity of CH3COOH is
solution:
This tests the meaning of basicity of an acid.

Basicity is the number of replaceable hydrogen ions (H+) that one molecule of the acid can give up.

Ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, contains four hydrogen atoms, but only the one in the carboxyl group (−COOH) is released:

CH3COOH ⇌ CH3COO− + H+

The three hydrogen atoms of the methyl group (CH3) are held firmly by carbon and are not acidic. So the basicity is 1, and ethanoic acid is monobasic. Options 2, 3 and 4 wrongly count all the hydrogen atoms in the molecule.

question: The colour of litmus in a neutral medium is
solution:
This tests acid–base indicators.

Litmus is a dye that changes colour with the acidity of a solution. A neutral medium is neither acidic nor alkaline, that is pH 7, and in such a medium litmus is purple.

  • In an acid it turns red.
  • In an alkali (base) it turns blue.

Pink, yellow and orange are the colours of other indicators; methyl orange, for example, is red in acid and yellow in alkali. Pure water and sodium chloride solution are neutral and leave litmus purple, so option A is correct.

question: The mathematical expression of pH is
solution:
This tests the definition of pH.

pH is the negative logarithm to base 10 of the concentration of hydrogen (oxonium) ions:

pH = −log10[H3O+]

Since −log x = log(1/x), the same expression can be written as:

pH=log101[H3O+]

That is exactly option B. Option C leaves out the negative sign, while options A and D use the hydroxide ion concentration, which gives pOH and not pH.

question: Which of the following salts will turn blue litmus red?
solution:
This tests acidic, basic and neutral salts. A salt turns blue litmus red only if its solution is acidic.

Sodium hydrogentetraoxosulphate(VI), NaHSO4, is an acid salt: it still has one replaceable hydrogen atom, so in water it ionises to give H+ and the solution is acidic.

The others are not acidic. Sodium tetrahydroxozincate(II) and zinc chloride hydroxide are basic salts, and sodium trioxocarbonate(IV), Na2CO3, is the salt of a weak acid, so it hydrolyses to give an alkaline solution. That is why only option B turns blue litmus red.

question:
Zn (s) + CuSO 4(aq) → ZnSO 4(aq) + Cu (s)
In the reaction above, the oxidation number of the reducing agent changes from
solution:
This tests oxidation numbers in redox reactions.

In Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu, zinc is the reducing agent because it gives electrons away and is itself oxidised.

  • In the free element Zn the oxidation number is 0.
  • In ZnSO4 the tetraoxosulphate(VI) ion carries −2, so zinc must be +2.

Zinc therefore changes from 0 to +2, losing two electrons: Zn → Zn2+ + 2e−. At the same time copper falls from +2 to 0 and is reduced. Options containing +1, +3 or +4 describe other elements, not zinc, so option B is correct.

question:
H2O(g) + C(s) → H2(g) + CO(g)

The oxidizing agent in the reaction above is
solution:
This tests oxidising and reducing agents.

In H2O(g) + C(s) → H2(g) + CO(g):

  • Hydrogen in water is +1 and becomes 0 in H2. It gains electrons, so it is reduced.
  • Carbon is 0 and becomes +2 in CO. It loses electrons, so it is oxidised.

The substance that is reduced is the oxidising agent, so H2O is the oxidising agent, while carbon is the reducing agent. CO and H2 are simply the products of the reaction, so neither of them can be the oxidising agent.

question:
Calculate the quantity of electricity in coulombs required to liberate 10g of copper from a copper compound

[Cu=64, F = 96500 Cmol-1]
solution:
This tests Faraday's laws of electrolysis.

At the cathode: Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu. So 2 moles of electrons (2 faradays) deposit 1 mole of copper.

Moles of copper = 10 ÷ 64 = 0.15625 mol

Moles of electrons needed = 2 × 0.15625 = 0.3125 mol

Quantity of electricity Q = 0.3125 × 96 500 = 30 156.3 C

Option 15 196.5 uses only one electron per copper ion, and 60 784.5 uses about four electrons per ion. Option 32 395.5 does not match the correct mole ratio either. Hence option B is right.

question: How many faraday of electricity is required to produce 0.25 mole of copper?
solution:
This tests the link between moles of a substance and faradays in electrolysis.

Copper is deposited by the half-equation:

Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu

This shows that 2 moles of electrons are needed for every 1 mole of copper. One mole of electrons is one faraday (96 500 C).

For 0.25 mole of copper:
Faradays = 0.25 × 2 = 0.50 F

Option 1.00 F would deposit 0.5 mole of copper, 0.05 F divides when it should multiply, and 0.01 F is far too small. So 0.50 F is correct.

question: If the change in free energy of a system is -899 Jmol-1 and the entropy change is 10Jmol-1k-1 at 250C, calculate the enthalpy change.
solution:
This tests the Gibbs free energy equation:

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS

Temperature must be in kelvin: T = 25 + 273 = 298 K. Given ΔG = −899 J mol−1 and ΔS = 10 J mol−1 K−1:

TΔS = 298 × 10 = 2980 J mol−1

ΔH = ΔG + TΔS = −899 + 2980 = +2081 J mol−1

The positive sign shows the reaction is endothermic; it can still occur because the large entropy increase makes TΔS bigger than ΔH. Option −649 comes from using 25 K instead of 298 K, and +649 is the same error with the sign changed.

question: In an equilibrium reaction, which of the following conditions indicates that maximum yield of the product will be obtained?

option.d: Equilibrium constant is less than zero

solution:
This tests the equilibrium constant and the yield of product.

At equilibrium, K = [products] ÷ [reactants], each raised to the power of its coefficient. A very large K means the top of the fraction is far bigger than the bottom, so the equilibrium lies well to the right and the yield of product is maximum. The link ΔG° = −RT ln K also gives a large negative ΔG°, showing the forward reaction is strongly favoured.

Option B (ΔH − TΔS = 0) describes a system already at equilibrium, not a large yield. Option C gives a positive ΔG, so the reaction is not even feasible. K can never be less than zero, so D is impossible.

question: In a chemical reaction, the change in concentration of a reactant with time is
solution:
This tests the definition of reaction rate.

The rate of a reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time:

rate = −Δ[reactant] ÷ Δt or rate = +Δ[product] ÷ Δt

For a reactant the concentration falls with time, so a minus sign is used to keep the rate positive. The unit is mol dm−3 s−1.

Enthalpy is the heat change at constant pressure, entropy measures disorder, and the order of a reaction is the power to which a reactant concentration is raised in the rate law. None of these describes change in concentration with time, so option C is correct.

question: Fluorine does not occur in the free state in nature because

option.b: it belongs to the halogen family

solution:
This tests the reactivity of fluorine, a halogen.

Fluorine is the most electronegative and most reactive of all the elements. It attacks almost everything — even water and glass — so any fluorine set free would quickly combine with another substance. That is why fluorine is never found free in nature; it occurs only in compounds such as fluorspar, CaF2, and cryolite, Na3AlF6.

Being poisonous (A) does not stop an element occurring free, since many poisonous gases exist naturally. Belonging to the halogen family (B) is no reason either, because family membership alone does not decide this. Fluorine is certainly not inert (C) — it is the very opposite.

question: In the extraction of sodium from fused sodium chloride, the anode is made of platinum because

option.a: sodium is formed at the anode
option.b: chlorine is formed at the anode
option.c: sodium does not react with platinum
option.d: chlorine does not react with platinum

solution:
This tests the electrolysis of fused sodium chloride (Down's process).

In the molten salt, Na+ and Cl− ions are free to move.

  • Cathode: Na+ + e− → Na
  • Anode: 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−

Hot chlorine gas is set free at the anode and attacks most metals, but platinum is inert and is not corroded by it, so the anode lasts. Option A is wrong because sodium forms at the cathode. Option B states correctly what is produced at the anode but does not explain why platinum is chosen. Option C is irrelevant, since no sodium forms at the anode at all.

question: In the electrolytic extraction of calcium from calcium chloride, the cathode is
solution:
This tests the electrolytic extraction of calcium from fused calcium chloride.

Calcium ions, Ca2+, are positively charged, so they travel to the negative electrode (cathode) and gain electrons:

Ca2+ + 2e− → Ca

The cathode is a rod of iron: it conducts well, it does not react with the calcium produced, and it is much cheaper than platinum. Graphite is used for the anode, where chlorine is liberated, because it resists the chlorine; platinum would be too expensive for a large cathode, and zinc would melt and react. So iron is correct.

question: A compound that gives a brick-red colour to a non-luminous flame is likely to contain
solution:
This tests flame tests for metal ions.

When a compound is heated in a non-luminous flame, its electrons absorb energy and then fall back, giving out light of a colour that identifies the metal:

  • Sodium — golden yellow
  • Potassium — lilac
  • Calcium — brick-red
  • Copper — blue-green

A brick-red flame therefore points to calcium ions. Copper ions give blue-green, sodium ions give yellow and potassium ions give lilac, so options A, B and D are ruled out.

question: A few drops of NaOH solution was added to an unknown salt forming a white precipitate which is insoluble in excess solution. The cation likely present is
solution:
This tests the test for cations using sodium hydroxide solution.

Ca2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) → Ca(OH)2(s), a white precipitate.

Calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble and does not dissolve in excess NaOH, so the white precipitate stays. Zinc, lead and aluminium ions also give white precipitates, but these dissolve in excess NaOH to form soluble zincate, plumbate and aluminate ions. That difference points to Ca2+; a precipitate that cleared in excess would suggest Zn2+, Pb2+ or Al3+ instead.

question: The general formula of haloalkanes where X represents the halide is
solution:
This tests the general formula of haloalkanes.

An alkane has the formula CnH2n+2. A haloalkane is obtained by replacing one hydrogen atom with one halogen atom X, so one hydrogen is lost:

CnH2n+2 − H + X = CnH2n+1X

For example, with n = 1 we get CH3Cl, chloromethane, which is correct. Option C keeps all the alkane hydrogens, which would give carbon five bonds. Options A and B have too few hydrogens for a saturated halide, so they fit unsaturated or ring compounds, not a simple haloalkane.

question: The alkanol obtained from the production of soap is
solution:
This tests saponification (soap making).

Soap is made by boiling fats or oils, which are triesters of propane-1,2,3-triol with long-chain fatty acids, with concentrated sodium hydroxide:

fat + 3NaOH → sodium salt of the fatty acid (soap) + propane-1,2,3-triol

The alkanol released is the triol glycerol, also called glycerine. The soap is salted out, while glycerol stays in solution.

Methanol, ethanol and propanol are simple alkanols with only one −OH group each and are not obtained from fats, so options A, B and D are wrong.

question: Ethyne is passed through a hot tube containing organo-nickel catalyst to produce
solution:
This tests the polymerisation of ethyne.

When ethyne (acetylene) is passed through a red-hot tube containing an organo-nickel catalyst, three molecules join in a cyclic trimerisation:

3C2H2 → C6H6

The product is benzene, a six-membered ring with alternating double bonds.

Polythene is made by addition polymerisation of ethene, isoprene comes from 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene, and ethanol is made by hydrating ethene with steam and acid. None of these is obtained from ethyne in a hot nickel tube, so option D is correct.

question: Due to the unstable nature of ethyne, it is stored by dissolving in
solution:
This tests the storage of ethyne.

Ethyne is a gas that is dangerous when compressed or liquefied, since it can decompose explosively, though it burns with a very hot flame used for welding. To store it safely, cylinders are packed with a porous material soaked in propanone (acetone), in which ethyne dissolves readily. The gas is released as needed, and the dissolved form is far safer.

Ethane-1,2-diol, propanol and ethanoic acid do not dissolve ethyne well, so they would not serve the purpose. That is why propanone, option D, is the correct answer.

question: The process of converting starch to ethanol is
solution:
This tests the production of ethanol from starch.

Starch is first broken down to maltose and then to glucose by enzymes (diastase and maltase) in germinating grain. Yeast is then added, and its enzyme zymase converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide:

C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2

This breakdown by micro-organisms without air is called fermentation. Cracking breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller alkenes, distillation separates liquids with different boiling points, and oxidation adds oxygen or removes hydrogen. None of these turns starch into ethanol.

question: The polymer used in making car rear lights is
solution:
This tests the uses of polymers.

Perspex is the trade name of poly(methyl methacrylate), a transparent, tough, shatter-proof plastic. Because it lets light through and can be coloured red or amber, it is moulded into car rear-light covers and lenses. It is also lighter and safer than glass.

Bakelite is a dark, hard thermosetting plastic used for plugs and pot handles, not for light covers. Polystyrene is clear but brittle, and polyacrylonitrile is used mainly for synthetic fibres such as acrylic wool. Only perspex combines transparency with toughness, so option A is correct.

question:
CH3COOC2H5(1) + H2O(1) ⇌ CH 3COOH (aq) + C 2H 5OH (aq)

The purpose of H+ in the reaction above is to

option.b: maintain the solution at a constant PH
option.c: increase the rate of the hydrolysis
option.d: decrease the rate of the reverse reaction

solution:
This tests catalysis in the hydrolysis of an ester.

Ethyl ethanoate reacts with water to give ethanoic acid and ethanol:

CH3COOC2H5 + H2O ⇌ CH3COOH + C2H5OH

The reaction is very slow on its own, so a little dilute acid is added. The H+ ions act as a catalyst: they speed up both the forward and the reverse reaction equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner. A catalyst is not used up and does not shift the position of equilibrium.

So H+ does not increase the yield (A), does not act as a buffer (B) and does not slow the reverse reaction (D). It only increases the rate of hydrolysis.

question:
A hydrocarbon has an empirical formula CH and a vapour density of 39. Determine its molecular formula.

[C = 12, H = 1]
solution:
This tests the link between empirical formula, vapour density and molecular formula.

Vapour density is half the relative molecular mass:

Mr = 2 × vapour density = 2 × 39 = 78

The empirical formula CH has mass 12 + 1 = 13, so:

n = Mr ÷ empirical formula mass = 78 ÷ 13 = 6

Molecular formula = (CH)6 = C6H6

C2H6 (30), C3H8 (44) and C3H4 (40) all have the wrong relative molecular mass, so they are ruled out. The compound is benzene.

question: Polystyrene is widely used as packaging materials for fragile objects during transportation because of its
solution:
This tests the properties and uses of polystyrene.

Polystyrene foam, often called styrofoam, is made by expanding the polymer with gas so that it is full of tiny air pockets. Because of these pockets the foam is highly compressible: when a fragile object is packed in it, the foam squashes and absorbs the shock of knocks during transport instead of passing the force to the object.

Lightness and low density are true of the foam, but they only make the package easy to carry; they do not protect the contents. High density is false for the foam. The property that actually protects fragile goods is therefore compressibility, option D.

question: The filter in the cigarette reduces the nicotine content by
solution:
This question tests the difference between adsorption and absorption. In adsorption, particles of a gas or liquid stick to the surface of a solid; in absorption, they go right into the bulk of the material, like water soaking into a sponge.

  • The cigarette filter is packed with cellulose acetate fibres, giving a very large surface area.
  • Nicotine and tar particles in the smoke collide with this surface and are held there by weak van der Waals forces, so less nicotine reaches the smoker.

Burning would destroy nicotine rather than trap it, and evaporation is a change of liquid to vapour, not a trapping process. Absorption is the closest distractor, but it means taking particles into the body of the filter, not onto its surface.

question: Which of these require crystallization most?
solution:
This question tests the use of crystallisation as a purification technique. Crystallisation works because a substance dissolves in a hot solvent, then comes out as pure crystals when the solution cools; impurities stay behind in the mother liquor.

Drugs (pharmaceuticals) must be extremely pure and their doses exact, so the active ingredient is repeatedly crystallised to remove impurities before tablets or injections are made. This is why drug making needs crystallisation most.

Cement making depends on roasting limestone and clay in a kiln, paint making on mixing pigments with oil or water, and perfume making on distillation and extraction of essential oils. None of these depends mainly on growing pure crystals, so options B, C and D are not the best answers.

question: Iron is often galvanized in order to
solution:
The idea here is rust prevention by coating. Galvanising means dipping iron or steel in molten zinc so that a thin zinc layer covers the surface.

  • The zinc coat is a physical barrier that keeps out oxygen and water, which are both needed for rusting.
  • Zinc is more electropositive than iron, so even if the coat is scratched, zinc corrodes first and protects the iron sacrificially.

Galvanising does not soften the metal; malleability comes from the iron itself. It does not remove impurities from the iron either; that is done during smelting. "Rendering passive" refers to the unreactive oxide film formed on metals such as aluminium by concentrated trioxonitrate(V) acid, not to zinc coating.

question: In the industrial production of H2 from water gas the CO2 produced along with the H2 is removed by

option.c: passing the mixture to the limewater

solution:
This question is about the industrial preparation of hydrogen from water gas. Water gas is a mixture of carbon(II) oxide and hydrogen, made by passing steam over red-hot coke:

C(s)+H2O(g)→CO(g)+H2(g)

The carbon(II) oxide is then converted to carbon(IV) oxide, which is removed by washing the gas under pressure with water, because carbon(IV) oxide dissolves readily in water at high pressure while hydrogen hardly dissolves.

Drying over phosphorus(V) oxide only removes water vapour. Limewater can only test or remove small amounts of carbon(IV) oxide, not treat large industrial volumes. Ammoniacal copper(I) chloride absorbs carbon(II) oxide, not carbon(IV) oxide.

question: The gas that is most useful in protecting humans against solar radiation is
solution:
The gas described is ozone, O3, which forms a layer in the stratosphere. ("Solar marathon" in the question means solar radiation.)

Ozone molecules absorb most of the sun's ultraviolet radiation, especially the harmful UV-B and UV-C rays, and turn that energy into heat. Without this shield, more ultraviolet light would reach the earth, causing skin cancer, eye cataracts and damage to plants and DNA.

Chlorine itself is a poisonous green gas, and chlorine atoms released from chlorofluorocarbons actually destroy ozone. Carbon(IV) oxide traps heat and causes global warming, but it does not absorb ultraviolet rays. Hydrogen sulphide is a toxic gas with no protective role in the atmosphere.

question: Vulcanization involves the removal of
solution:
This question tests vulcanisation, the process of heating natural rubber with sulphur. Natural rubber is polyisoprene, a long chain with carbon-carbon double bonds (C=C) along it; the rubber is soft and sticky because the chains slide over one another.

During vulcanisation, sulphur atoms add across these double bonds and form disulphide (-S-S-) bridges between neighbouring chains. In effect the double bonds are removed (saturated), and the chains become cross-linked into a strong network.

The result is rubber that is harder, stronger and more elastic, and less affected by heat.

The monomer units stay in the chain, so option A is wrong. Single bonds are formed, not removed, so option B is wrong. The polymer is not removed at all; it is only cross-linked, so option D is wrong.

question: The acid in electrolysis of water is dilute
solution:
This question tests the electrolysis of water and the choice of electrolyte. Pure water conducts electricity only very slightly, so a little acid is added to supply mobile ions.

Dilute tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid is preferred because:

  • it is a strong electrolyte, giving many ions for conduction;
  • SO42− is not easily discharged, so oxygen is liberated at the anode instead;
  • it is non-volatile and stable, so it is not lost with the gases.

The overall change is 2H2O→2H2+O2, giving hydrogen and oxygen in a 2:1 volume ratio.

Dilute hydrochloric acid is volatile and gives chlorine at the anode. Ethanoic acid is a weak electrolyte with few ions. Trioxonitrate(V) acid is an oxidising acid and is decomposed during electrolysis.

question: A small quantity of solid ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) heated gently in a test tube, the solid gradually disappear produce two gases. Later, a white cloudy deposit was absence on the cooler part of the test tube. The ammonium chloride is to have undergo
solution:
This question tests sublimation. On gentle heating, solid ammonium chloride does not melt; it breaks up into two gases:

NH4Cl(s)⇌NH3(g)+HCl(g)

On reaching the cooler part of the tube the two gases recombine to give a white solid deposit of ammonium chloride. This change of a solid straight to vapour and back to solid is called sublimation (here, dissociative sublimation).

Distillation also involves vapour, but starts from a liquid and the vapour is condensed to liquid. Precipitation is the formation of an insoluble solid from solution. Evaporation is a liquid changing to vapour, leaving no solid deposit on the cool part.

question: When salt loses its water of crystallization to the atmosphere on exposure, the process is said to be
solution:
The idea tested is the behaviour of hydrated salts in air. Many salts contain water of crystallisation, for example washing soda, Na2CO3·10H2O.

When such a salt is exposed to air and loses this water vapour to the atmosphere, it crumbles into a powder. This spontaneous loss of water of crystallisation is called efflorescence.

The other terms describe different changes:

  • Deliquescence is the opposite: a substance absorbs water from the air and dissolves in it, e.g. calcium chloride.
  • Effervescence is the fizzing that occurs when a gas, usually carbon(IV) oxide, is given off.
  • Fluorescence is the giving out of light by a substance after absorbing light.

Only efflorescence means losing water of crystallisation to the air.

question: Atomicity of ozone is
solution:
This question tests the meaning of atomicity, which is the number of atoms in one molecule of a substance.

Ozone is O3: each molecule is built from three oxygen atoms joined together, so its atomicity is 3. It is therefore a triatomic molecule.

For comparison:

  • Atomicity 1 (monoatomic) - the noble gases such as helium and neon.
  • Atomicity 2 (diatomic) - hydrogen, H2, and oxygen, O2.
  • Atomicity 4 (tetraatomic) - white phosphorus, P4.

Options 1, 2 and 4 describe those other molecules, not ozone.

question: Which of the noble gases has the greatest ionization energy
solution:
This question tests the trend of first ionisation energy, the energy needed to remove one electron from a gaseous atom:

X(g)→X+(g)+e−

Helium has only one shell, holding two electrons, and its outer electron is held very strongly by the +2 nucleus with almost no shielding. This gives helium the highest ionisation energy of all elements.

Going down the group, atomic radius increases and inner shells shield the outer electron from the nucleus, so the outer electron is held less tightly. Hence ionisation energy falls from helium through neon and argon to xenon, which is the lowest here.

"Rr" is not a real element symbol, so option D can be ignored.

question: The weakest attractive force that can be observed between two molecules is
solution:
This question tests intermolecular forces - the attractions between separate molecules. These are much weaker than the forces holding atoms together inside a molecule.

Van der Waals forces are the weakest of them. They arise from temporary or uneven distribution of electrons, which produces small dipoles that attract one another, and they need only a few kilojoules per mole to overcome. That is why substances held only by van der Waals forces, such as methane, are gases at room temperature.

Ionic bonds are strong attractions between oppositely charged ions, and covalent and co-ordinate covalent bonds are strong bonds sharing electron pairs within a molecule or ion. They require far more energy to break, so they are not weak intermolecular attractions.

question: An elements used in production of matches is
solution:
The idea tested is the composition of match heads. A match head is a mixture of sulphur, potassium trioxochlorate(V) and a little antimony(III) sulphide, held together with glue.

  • Sulphur is the fuel; it burns readily in air, giving sulphur(IV) oxide and heat.
  • Potassium trioxochlorate(V) supplies oxygen so the match burns strongly even in a draught.
  • Red phosphorus on the striking surface helps the match to light.

Nitrogen is unreactive and is used for inert atmospheres, not as a fuel. Aluminium is a light metal used for foil, cables and alloys. Copper is used for electrical wiring and alloys such as brass. Neither metal is suitable for a match head, which must ignite easily.

question: Cathode rays cause an object placed behind a perforated anode to cast a shadow on the screen. This observation shows that cathode rays
solution:
This question tests how we know that cathode rays travel in straight lines. When the rays pass through the hole in the anode, an object placed in their path throws a sharp shadow on the screen behind it.

A shadow is formed only if the rays move in straight lines; if they spread out or bent round the object, the shadow would be blurred or absent. This same straight-line motion is why cathode rays can turn a small paddle wheel placed in their path.

Other properties are proved differently:

  • their negative charge is shown by their deflection towards the positive plate;
  • their mass and momentum are shown by the spinning paddle wheel.

So the shadow experiment demonstrates straight-line travel, not charge.

question: Flow of current in electrolytes is due to the movement of
solution:
This question tests conduction in electrolytes. An electrolyte is a substance that conducts electricity when molten or dissolved in water because it contains free-moving ions.

When a direct current is passed:

  • positive ions (cations) move towards the cathode;
  • negative ions (anions) move towards the anode;
  • the ions are discharged at the electrodes, and this movement of ions carries the current through the solution.

For example, in dilute sodium chloride solution, Na+ and H+ move to the cathode while Cl− and OH− move to the anode.

Electrons carry current in metals, not in electrolytes. Holes occur in semiconductors, and "charges" is too general - the charged particles here are ions.

question: A suitable reagent for distinguish between ethanoic and ethanol is
solution:
This question tests a simple chemical test for the carboxyl group (-COOH). Ethanoic acid is a carboxylic acid, while ethanol is an alkanol; only the acid reacts with a trioxocarbonate(IV).

When a little sodium hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV), NaHCO3, is added:

CH3COOH+NaHCO3→CH3COONa+H2O+CO2

The brisk effervescence of carbon(IV) oxide shows the acid. Ethanol gives no effervescence, so the two are easily distinguished.

Bromine water tests for unsaturation (C=C). Fehling's solution and ammoniacal silver trioxonitrate(V) test for aldehydes and reducing sugars. Neither reagent reacts clearly with both liquids here.

question: The above orbital diagram shown the electronic configuration of
solution:
This question tests electronic configuration and orbital diagrams, especially Hund's rule. The diagram shows the 2p subshell with three orbitals, each holding a single electron (three unpaired electrons).

Nitrogen has atomic number 7, so its configuration is

1s2 2s2 2p3

By Hund's rule, the three 2p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, so the p boxes each contain one arrow. That is exactly the diagram shown.

Chlorine (17) ends in 3p5 with one pair and two single electrons, calcium (20) ends in 4s2, and neon (10) has a full 2p6 with all orbitals paired.

question: Which of the following metals burns with brick red
solution:
This question tests flame tests, used to identify metal ions. A clean platinum or nichrome wire is dipped in the metal compound and held in a non-luminous flame; the colour seen is characteristic of the metal.

  • Calcium and its compounds give a brick-red flame, so option B is correct.
  • Sodium gives a persistent golden-yellow flame.
  • Magnesium burns with a dazzling white light, not a brick-red flame.
  • Lead gives a pale blue or greyish flame.

The heat of the flame excites electrons in the metal ions to higher energy levels; as they fall back, light of a particular wavelength is emitted. Since each metal has its own energy levels, each gives its own flame colour, which makes the test useful for identification.

question: In the production of soap, concentrated sodium chloride solution is added to

option.b: decrease the solubility of the soap

solution:
This question tests the salting-out stage in soap making. Soap is the sodium salt of a long-chain fatty acid, made by boiling fat or oil with concentrated sodium hydroxide (saponification). The product mixture contains soap, glycerol and excess alkali.

When concentrated sodium chloride solution is added, the solution becomes rich in sodium ions. By the common ion effect, this reduces the solubility of the soap, so the soap separates out as a solid curd that floats and can be skimmed off. Glycerol remains dissolved and is recovered separately.

The salt does not increase soap solubility. It does not saponify the soap - saponification is the alkali hydrolysis of fat. It also does not emulsify the soap; emulsification is what soap does to grease, not what salt does to soap.

question: A liquid that will dissolve fat is
solution:
This question tests the rule "like dissolves like". Fats and oils are made of long hydrocarbon chains, so they are non-polar molecules held together by weak van der Waals forces.

Kerosene is a mixture of non-polar hydrocarbons. Its molecules attract the fat molecules in the same weak way that fat molecules attract one another, so the fat breaks up and mixes with the kerosene. That is why kerosene is used as a dry-cleaning solvent for greasy stains.

Water is polar and is held by hydrogen bonds, so it cannot mix with non-polar fat. Hydrochloric acid is a polar acid and also does not dissolve fat. "Calcium hydrochloride" is not a proper chemical name; the real compound, calcium chloride, is an ionic salt and would not dissolve fat either.

question: Tartaric acid is used industrially to
solution:
This question tests the use of tartaric acid in baking powder. Baking powder is a mixture of sodium hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV) and a solid weak acid, usually tartaric acid or cream of tartar.

When the powder is moistened in dough, the acid reacts with the hydrogen trioxocarbonate(IV):

NaHCO3+H2A→NaA+H2O+CO2

where HA stands for tartaric acid. The carbon(IV) oxide bubbles make the dough rise and become light and porous.

Fruit juice is made from fruit, not tartaric acid. Rust removal needs dilute mineral acids that dissolve the oxide. Drying substances requires drying agents such as calcium chloride or silica gel, not an acid.

question: P1V1 = P2V2 supports ?
solution:
This question tests the gas laws. The equation P1V1=P2V2 states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional.

This is Boyle's law: if the pressure is doubled, the volume is halved, so the product PV stays the same. Squeezing a sealed syringe gives a practical example.

The other laws are different:

  • Charles's law: V1/T1=V2/T2 at constant pressure.
  • Graham's law: rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass.
  • Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules at the same temperature and pressure.

question: A fixed mass of gas occupies 92 cm3 at 3 °C. What will be its volume at 18 °C if the pressure remains constant?
solution:
This question tests Charles's law: at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.

V1/T1=V2/T2

Temperatures must be in kelvin:

  • T1=3+273=276K
  • T2=18+273=291K

V2=V1T2/T1=(92×291)/276=97.0cm3

The gas expands on warming, so the volume must be greater than 92 cm³. 87.3 cm³ comes from turning the ratio upside down (92 × 276/291). Using 3 and 18 directly, without converting to kelvin, is another common mistake.

question: Which of the following ions requires the largest quantity of electricity for discharge at an electrode?
solution:
This question tests the quantity of electricity needed to discharge ions, using Faraday's idea that one mole of electrons carries about 96 500 C.

The charge carried by a mole of ions equals the number of moles multiplied by the size of the charge on each ion:

  • Q3+: 2.0 × 3 = 6.0 mol of electrons
  • R2+: 2.5 × 2 = 5.0 mol of electrons
  • T-: 3.0 × 1 = 3.0 mol of electrons
  • Y-: 4.0 × 1 = 4.0 mol of electrons

Q3+ needs the greatest number of moles of electrons, so it needs the largest quantity of electricity (about 6 × 96 500 C).

The distractors fail because a larger number of moles does not automatically mean more electricity; the charge on each ion must also be counted. The 3+ charge on Q makes the difference.

question: Hydrogen can be displaced from a hot alkaline solution by
solution:
This question tests the reaction of amphoteric metals with hot alkali. Metals such as tin, aluminium and zinc can react with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide solution, giving hydrogen gas and a soluble salt. For tin:

Sn+2NaOH+2H2O→Na2Sn(OH)4+H2

Copper does not react with alkali, and iron is not amphoteric, so neither displaces hydrogen from hot alkali. Calcium is the metal whose hydroxide forms the alkali, and it reacts with water itself rather than displacing hydrogen from an alkaline solution. Tin is therefore the correct choice.

question:
Which of the following types of alkanols undergo oxidation to produce alkanoic acids.

I. Primary alkanols
II. Secondary alkanols
III. Tertiary alkanols
solution:
This question tests the oxidation of alkanols. The position of the -OH group decides the product.

  • Primary alkanols have the -OH on a carbon joined to only one other carbon. On oxidation they first give an alkanal, then an alkanoic acid. Ethanol, for example, gives ethanal and then ethanoic acid with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) or potassium tetraoxomanganate(VII).
  • Secondary alkanols give ketones, which are not oxidised further to acids under these conditions.
  • Tertiary alkanols have no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the -OH group, so they resist oxidation; strong oxidation would break the carbon chain.

Hence only primary alkanols, I, give alkanoic acids.

question: Rare gases are stable because they

option.c: have duplet or octet electronic configuration in the outermost shells in their atoms

solution:
This question tests why the noble (rare) gases are unreactive. Chemical stability depends on the arrangement of electrons in the outermost shell.

  • Helium has two electrons in its only shell - a stable duplet.
  • Neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon have eight electrons in their outermost shell - a stable octet (the ns²np⁶ arrangement).

Because their outer shells are full, these atoms have no need to gain, lose or share electrons, so they hardly form compounds.

Being monoatomic is a result of this stability, not its cause. They do not form ions easily; their high ionisation energies make ion formation very difficult. Being volatile gases is a physical property and does not explain chemical inertness.

question: A major source of oxide of nitrogen is from the burning of
solution:
This question tests the sources of nitrogen oxides and air pollution. At the very high temperature inside motor engines and furnaces, nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine directly:

N2(g)+O2(g)→2NO(g)

The nitrogen(II) oxide is then oxidised in air to brown nitrogen(IV) oxide. Burning fuels such as petrol and diesel in vehicles is therefore a major source of these oxides, which cause acid rain and photochemical smog.

Burning coal and wood produce mainly carbon(IV) oxide, carbon(II) oxide and sulphur(IV) oxide. Chlorofluorocarbons release chlorine atoms that destroy ozone; they are not a source of nitrogen oxides.

question: Which of these radioactive elements is commonly used as a nuclear fuel
solution:
This question tests nuclear fuels. A nuclear fuel is a substance whose nuclei can undergo fission, splitting into smaller nuclei and releasing large amounts of energy.

Uranium, particularly the isotope uranium-235, is the commonest nuclear fuel. When a slow neutron strikes a U-235 nucleus, it splits into two lighter nuclei and releases two or three more neutrons plus energy:

U235+n1→Ba141+Kr92+3n1+energy

The extra neutrons keep the chain reaction going. Palladium is a catalyst metal, not a fuel. Actinium is radioactive but not used as a reactor fuel. Thorium can be converted into fissile uranium-233, but it is not the fuel commonly used.

question: All these are electromagnetic waves except
solution:
This question tests the electromagnetic spectrum. Electromagnetic waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields that travel through space and need no medium. They include radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.

  • White light is the visible part of the spectrum, a mixture of colours from red to violet.
  • X-rays are very short-wavelength electromagnetic waves used in radiography.
  • Infrared radiation is the heat radiation just beyond the red end of the visible spectrum.

A photon is not a kind of wave; it is a quantum, or packet, of electromagnetic energy. Light behaves as both a wave and a stream of photons, but a photon itself is a particle-like quantity, so it is the odd one out.

question:
Cu2S(s) + O2(g) → 2Cu(s) + SO2(g)

In the above reaction, the oxidation number of Cu changes from ___ to ______?
solution:
This question tests oxidation numbers in a redox reaction. In copper(I) sulphide the sulphur atom has an oxidation number of -2, and the compound is neutral, so the two copper atoms together carry +2. Thus each copper is +1.

In the products, copper appears as the free element Cu(s), whose oxidation number is 0, while sulphur is oxidised to +4 in sulphur(IV) oxide.

So copper changes from +1 to 0, which is a decrease, so copper is reduced. The change 0 to +2 is the opposite (oxidation), +2 to +1 would be a small reduction starting from copper(II), and 0 to +1 is oxidation. Only +1 to 0 fits the reaction.

question: The number of isomers formed by C6H14 is
solution:
This question tests structural isomerism in alkanes. Isomers have the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms. For C6H14, the isomers are found by shortening the main chain and adding branches:

  • straight chain: hexane
  • five-carbon chain: 2-methylpentane and 3-methylpentane
  • four-carbon chain: 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane

That gives 5 isomers in total.

Four would miss one of the branched structures, and three or two are far too few. Remember that moving a branch along a chain can create a new isomer, but placing it at the end merely lengthens the chain.

question: The basic particles from which matter could be made up of are as follow, except?
solution:
This question tests the basic particles of matter. Matter is built from three kinds of particles:

  • Atoms - the smallest particles of an element that can take part in a chemical change, e.g. an oxygen atom.
  • Ions - atoms or groups of atoms that have gained or lost electrons and carry a charge, e.g. Na+ and Cl−.
  • Molecules - two or more atoms joined together, e.g. H2O.

Salt is not a basic particle. It is a compound, such as sodium chloride, and it is itself made up of ions. So salt is the exception.

question: The energy value of petrol can be determined by
solution:
This question tests how the energy value (calorific value) of a fuel is measured. A bomb calorimeter is a strong steel vessel in which a known mass of the fuel is burnt completely in excess oxygen at constant volume. The vessel sits in a known mass of water, and the rise in water temperature is measured.

heat=mcΔT

Dividing this heat by the mass of fuel burnt gives the energy value, usually in kJ per gram or kJ per dm³.

A catalytic cracker breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller ones; it does not measure energy. A fractionating column separates crude oil by boiling point. A thermometer only measures temperature and is just one part of the calorimeter.

question: What volume of 0.5 mol dm-3 H2SO4 will exactly neutralize 20 cm3 of 0.1 mol dm-3 NaOH solution?
solution:
This question tests acid-base titration calculations. Write the equation first:

H2SOO4+2NaOH→Na2SOO4+2H2O

Moles of sodium hydroxide = 0.1×20/1000=0.002 mol.

One mole of the acid neutralises two moles of the base, so moles of acid = 0.002/2 = 0.001 mol.

Volume of acid = n/c=0.001/0.5=0.002dm3 = 2.0 cm³.

Forgetting the 1:2 mole ratio doubles the answer, which is the common error behind the larger values.

question: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen. If the molar mass of the compound is 180, Find the molecular formula [H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
solution:
This question tests empirical and molecular formulae. First divide each percentage by the atomic mass:

  • C: 40.0/12 = 3.33
  • H: 6.7/1 = 6.7
  • O: 53.3/16 = 3.33

Divide by the smallest value (3.33): C = 1, H = 2, O = 1, giving the empirical formula CH2O, whose mass is 12 + 2 + 16 = 30.

The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of this:

n=180/30=6, so the formula is C6H12O6 (glucose).

CH2O is only the empirical formula, and C3H6O3 has mass 90, half of 180. Option D has the wrong numbers of hydrogen and oxygen atoms.

question: An oxidation state of Cr in K2Cr2O7
solution:
This question tests oxidation numbers in a compound. The sum of the oxidation numbers of all the atoms in a neutral compound is zero.

In potassium dichromate(VI), K2Cr2O7:

  • potassium, a group 1 metal, is always +1;
  • oxygen is usually -2.

Let the oxidation number of chromium be x:

2(+1)+2x+7(−2)=0

2+2x−14=0, so 2x=12 and x=+6.

The other values would not make the total charge zero.

question: The elements that belong to the third period of periodic table are
solution:
This question tests the periodic table. A period is a horizontal row. The period number equals the number of electron shells in the atoms of its elements.

The third period runs from sodium (atomic number 11) to argon (18):

Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar

All these atoms have electrons in three shells (2, 8 and the outer shell).

Checking the options:

  • A contains Li and Be, which are in period 2, and "D" is not an element symbol.
  • B contains Na, P and Cl from period 3, but oxygen is in period 2.
  • C has B, C, N and O, all period 2 elements.
  • D has Na, Mg, S and Ar, and every one of them is in the third period.

So D is the only list made up completely of third-period elements.

question: When sugar is dissolved in tea, the reaction is accompanied by a
solution:
This question tests entropy, a measure of the disorder or randomness of a system. When sugar dissolves in tea, the ordered sugar crystals break up and the sugar molecules spread randomly throughout the liquid. The disorder of the system therefore increases, so the entropy change is positive (ΔS>0).

A positive entropy change favours a spontaneous process, as shown by

ΔG=ΔH−TΔS

The negative values are wrong because entropy does not decrease or stay constant when a solid spreads through a liquid. "Minimum entropy change" is also incorrect, since the change is clearly an increase.

question:
NH3(g) + HCl(g) → NH4Cl(s)
The entropy change in the system above is
solution:
This question tests how the entropy change of a reaction depends on the physical states involved. Gases have far more disorder than solids, because their molecules move freely and fill the container.

In the reaction

NH3(g)+HCl(g)→NH4Cl(s)

two gases combine to form one solid. The number of moles of gas falls from 2 (or from 1 if the hydrogen chloride is taken as a solid) to zero, so the freedom of movement is lost and the system becomes more ordered.

Entropy therefore decreases, giving a negative entropy change (ΔS<0). A positive or zero change would require more gas molecules after the reaction.

question: In an electrochemical cell, polarization is caused by
solution:
Idea tested: polarization of an electrochemical (voltaic) cell.

When a metal such as zinc dissolves in the cell, hydrogen gas is produced at the other electrode. Tiny bubbles of hydrogen cover that electrode and insulate it, so it can no longer receive electrons easily. The current therefore falls quickly and the cell is said to be polarized or "tired". The cure is to add a depolarizer such as potassium dichromate(VI) or manganese(IV) oxide, which removes the hydrogen.

So hydrogen is the correct answer. Oxygen, tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid and chlorine do not form that insulating film on the electrode, so options A, C and D are wrong.

question: The condition required for corrosion to take place is the presence of

option.c: Water and Carbon (IV) oxide and Oxygen

solution:
Idea tested: the conditions needed for the rusting (corrosion) of iron.

Rusting is an electrochemical change. Iron loses electrons (oxidation) at one region, and oxygen from the air gains those electrons at another. Water is needed as the electrolyte that lets ions move between the two regions. So water and oxygen must be present together; remove either one and rusting stops. That is why iron is painted, greased or coated with zinc (galvanising).

Carbon(IV) oxide is not essential — it only makes rain slightly acidic and speeds rusting up. Options A, C and D all demand carbon(IV) oxide as a must, so they are wrong.

question: The enzyme used in the hydrolysis of starch to dextrin and maltose is
solution:
Idea tested: enzymes that hydrolyse carbohydrates.

Starch is a very large polysaccharide. The enzyme amylase, found in saliva and in malt, catalyses its hydrolysis by breaking the glycosidic links, so starch first becomes dextrin and finally maltose, a disaccharide:

starch→dextrin→maltose

Zymase (A) changes sugars into ethanol and carbon(IV) oxide during fermentation, sucrase (B) hydrolyses sucrose, and lactase (D) hydrolyses lactose in milk. None of these three attacks starch, so only amylase is correct.

question: In the laboratory preparation of chlorine from concentrated hydrochloric acid in the presence of potassuim tetraoxomanganate(VII) the produced is dried by passing it through
solution:
Idea tested: drying a gas with an agent that will not react with it.

Chlorine is prepared by heating concentrated hydrochloric acid with potassium tetraoxomanganate(VII):

16HCl+2KMnO4→2KCl+2MnCl2+8H2O+5Cl2

The moist gas is then bubbled through concentrated tetraoxosulphate(VI) acid, which absorbs the water vapour and leaves chlorine unchanged.

Anhydrous calcium chloride (B) and calcium oxide (C) combine with chlorine, while sodium hydroxide (D) is alkaline and absorbs the acidic gas. So only option A can be used.

question: The monomer of nylon is
solution:
Idea tested: condensation polymerisation and the monomers of nylon.

Nylon is a polyamide. It is made when hexanedioic acid (adipic acid) condenses with hexane-1,6-diamine: the acid group of one molecule reacts with the amine group of the other, a molecule of water is lost, and a strong amide link joins the units into a long chain. The name nylon-6,6 shows that each monomer supplies six carbon atoms.

Hydroxybenzene (A) is used in making resins, while benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (C) and ethane-1,2-diol (D) condense to give the polyester Terylene. Only hexanedioic acid is a monomer of nylon.

question: The principle of column chromatography is based on the ability of the constituents to

option.a: React with the solvent in the column
option.b: React with each other in the solvent in the column
option.c: Dissolve in each other in the column
option.d: Move at different speeds in the column

solution:
Idea tested: the principle of column chromatography.

In column chromatography the mixture is put at the top of a column packed with a stationary phase such as alumina or silica gel, and a solvent (the mobile phase) is allowed to run down. Each component is attracted to the stationary phase by a different strength: the one held weakly is swept along quickly by the solvent, while the one held strongly lags behind. Since the components therefore move at different speeds, they separate into bands that can be collected one after another.

The components do not react with the solvent (A) or with each other (B), and they do not simply dissolve in one another (C). Separation depends only on different rates of movement, so D is correct.

question: Ammonium chloride can be separated from its mixture with common salt by
solution:
Idea tested: choosing a separation method from the physical properties of the components.

Ammonium chloride sublimes: on gentle heating it changes straight into a vapour without melting first, and the vapour solidifies again on a cool surface. Common salt (sodium chloride) does not sublime; it melts only at a very high temperature. So when the mixture is heated in a covered crucible, pure ammonium chloride collects as a white sublimate on the cooler lid while the salt is left behind.

Distillation (A) suits liquids, evaporation (B) would leave both solids together in the dish, and decantation (C) works only for a solid suspended in a liquid. Hence sublimation is the right method.

question: The ability of carbon to form long chains is referred to as
solution:
Idea tested: the self-linking property of carbon atoms.

Catenation is the ability of an element to form strong covalent bonds with atoms of the same element, producing long chains, branches and rings. Carbon does this best because the C–C bond is strong and each carbon atom can bond in four directions. This is why millions of organic compounds exist, from methane with one carbon atom to giant molecules such as starch and poly(ethene).

Alkylation (A) and acylation (B) are reactions that attach alkyl or acyl groups to a molecule, while carbonation (C) means saturating a substance with carbon(IV) oxide, as in soft drinks. Neither means chain building, so D is correct.

question: The industrial preparation of hydrogen gas from water gas is referred to as
solution:
Idea tested: named industrial processes and the products they give.
